doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Key action
Provide help while maintaining personal safety and the safety and security of the ill or injured
person and bystanders.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Introduction
The initial actions of individuals and groups can help or hurt an effective response. The
recognition of safety and health hazards to self and others is taught in the Early recognition
domain of the chain of survival behaviours. A systematic approach helps with remembering and
doing the initial behaviours in a general approach. Ongoing scene hazards (e.g. fire, violence or
hot environment) must be addressed by removing the hazard, removing people from the
hazard or calling for help.
Once the scene is safe enough to initiate care, a systematic approach to identifying
life-threatening injuries is important to prioritizing care. After life-threatening issues are treated,
first aid providers can identify all other first aid ailments to either care for or to inform advanced
care.
First aid scenarios require critical thinking, and a general approach helps individuals navigate
this process. Although we often teach first aid in distinct modules (e.g. breathing, bleeding, CPR,
poisoning), the hazards and their consequences complicate first aid actions. The general
approach allows for life-threatening illnesses or injuries to be identified and managed through a
primary survey of the person. The types of injuries or illnesses may overlap, and judgement may
be required on what to treat first and how to do it. For the purpose of these Guidelines,
life-threatening issues are:

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Introduction
● Unresponsiveness: When a person does not react to external stimuli (i.e. anything around
them).
● Breathing problems: Difficulty or inability to breathe normally.
● Trauma: Physical harm to the body that will not maintain life (e.g. arterial bleeding).
● Medical: An acute biological response to an illness or assault to the body (e.g. Poisoning or
sepsis).
● Environmental: Harm to the body from the weather conditions or surroundings.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Introduction
● Mental distress: Psychological response that prevents a person from carrying out safe
behaviours. First aid requires a responder to identify these life-threatening injuries or illnesses and to
prioritize care. Effective first aid education must go beyond individual skills and emphasize the
importance of situational awareness, personal safety and decision-making in dynamic and often
stressful conditions. In practice, many situations will be complex. In real life, they may be more
complex. Providers may need to care for multiple things at once, for example, applying pressure
to a serious cut to stop the bleeding while speaking with the injured person to help calm them
down during a panic attack. In most situations, providers will need to care for the physical illness
or injury while also applying psychological first aid skills. Psychological first aid
Psychological first aid (PFA) is integrated with physical first aid competencies during
training. Acknowledging emotions and reactions to situations in the domain of Early
recognition and addressing them simultaneously reduces stress for the individual and the
first aid provider. Research and guidance for psychological first aid is led within the Movement by the Red
Cross and Red Crescent Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Hub (MHPSS Hub).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Introduction
The
General approach section integrates considerations for psychological first aid into the
chain of survival behaviours to increase awareness of psychological first aid and support
first aid educators and providers in caring for the whole person. See the psychological first aid section for background and specific skills for supporting
people in distress.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Good practice points
Assess the scene
● First aid providers should be taught about the ambiguity of emergencies and that
deciding to act is the most important first step.
● First aid providers should assess the scene for dangers to themselves and others before
providing direct help.
● In assessing a scene that contains areas of danger, first aid providers should also observe
which areas are safe (or have fewer dangers) to provide options for themselves and the ill
or injured person.
● If scene safety cannot be guaranteed, then the provider needs to adjust their approach
(e.g. calling for help or providing support from a distance), prioritizing their well-being
first.
● Where possible, the first aid provider should take steps to protect private information. This
can also help enhance the person’s feeling of personal safety.
Assess the person

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Good practice points
● First aid providers should be taught a standard approach to assessment to help them
appropriately prioritize care for time-sensitive conditions and to feel more confident in
their competencies.
● If possible, first aid providers should approach the ill or injured person so the person can
see them. This will reduce the risk of scaring the injured or ill person or causing them to
move unnecessarily. It may also help keep them at ease.
● First aid providers should assess the ill or injured person by checking for a response,
normal breathing and normal blood circulation. These conditions should be treated as a
priority if abnormal.
● If the ill or injured person can talk or cry, it should be assumed their airway is open and
their breathing is adequate.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Good practice points
● An ill or injured person should be left in the position of most comfort (usually the position
in which they are found) unless there is a need to move them to a different location or
position for safety or well-being purposes.
● First aid providers may assess an ill or injured person further by asking them questions to
determine their mental status or medical history or more closely examining part of their
body (with consent). Providers should get as much information as possible about what
happened by using a calm, non-intrusive manner that respects the person’s needs.
● The first aid provider should communicate with the ill or injured person, explain what
they are doing to help, and act with respect and empathy.
Provide care or access help

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Good practice points
● The first aid provider should access emergency medical services (EMS) as soon as they
think help is needed. If using a phone, care to the ill or injured person should be provided
simultaneously by activating the phone’s speaker function.
● A lack of first aid equipment should not be a barrier to providing care; first aid providers
should use whatever resources are available to them.
● Immediate basic and practical needs are also priorities. Check whether the person needs
water, shelter, clothing or a blanket, and try to provide them as quickly as possible. It is
difficult for someone to solve problems or reach out to others when feeling cold or thirsty.
● Providers should ask if the person needs social support such as restoring family links or
medical or legal assistance.
● In cases of children, connecting them with caregivers is a basic need that should be
prioritized.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Good practice points
● Filming an emergency incident is inappropriate, particularly if it blocks the path of
professional responders. First aid education should raise awareness of this fact.
Multiple casualties
● The first aid provider should protect themselves at all times from danger, aim to preserve
life and reduce injury and suffering.
● If there is more than one ill or injured person, it may be appropriate to call EMS first to
inform them of a potentially critical situation, and then call again once more detailed
information has been gathered.
● In a multiple-casualty incident, the first aid provider should assess the ill or injured, then
treat those with the most life-threatening conditions relating to breathing and circulation
first.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Prevent and prepare
● Know the common risks in your environment and the steps you can take to help
minimize the risk of an incident occurring or worsening.
● Ensure you have access to a first aid kit or the specific equipment (a disaster kit,
hi-visibility signs or clothing, etc.) according to your assessed needs and risks.
● Be aware that diffusion of responsibility (e.g. thinking someone else will help) and
ambiguity (e.g. wondering if the person really needs help) are common barriers to
overcome in helping an ill or injured person. Being prepared and empowered to assist
people not only provides care but also empowers individuals to act and can lessen
feelings of helplessness.
● Learn about the emergency services available in your context and how to access them.
This may involve knowing their phone number, location or the types of questions they
may ask.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Prevent and prepare
● Understand the potential resistance an ill or injured person may have to certain
procedures, such as the associated costs of services. Advocate for them accessing care
when it is needed.
● Learn proactive means to de-escalate volatile situations.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Early recognition
Upon entering a first aid situation, be aware of the thoughts and feelings you may have that
may affect the help you provide. Be alert to the fact that people read situations differently, and
just because no one is responding does not mean that everything is fine (the bystander effect).
Assess the scene
A scene assessment involves identifying any potential safety risks (to you, the ill or injured person
or bystanders), such as fire or exposed electrical wires. The location itself may be unsafe. If the
person is in or near a body of water or ice, in a conflict area or in a closed or confined space with
minimal oxygen or poisonous gas, extra care must be taken. Additionally, if there is an active
shooter, contamination by a chemical, radiological or biological agent, or any other risk you
cannot minimize, stay away and inform the relevant authorities (fire or police).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Early recognition
● If possible, seek the support of another person who can help you.
● Assess the scene for potential danger to yourself or the ill or injured person and try to
identify the potential cause of the illness or injury.
● If necessary, observe areas of safety (or ones with fewer dangers) to provide a safe place
for you and the ill or injured person.
● Take steps to make the scene safe. This could include accessing additional help or
equipment, or changing your approach based on the danger. Do not approach the scene
if it is not safe.
● Identify the number of ill or injured people.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Early recognition
● Remain aware of your surroundings and maintain your personal safety. This will be
particularly important in conflict, disaster or multiple casualty contexts.
Assess the person
Approach carefully, calmly, and in an appropriate manner. Both the behaviour and attitude will
influence how people in distress react to an offer of help. If they meet someone who is calm and
focused, this will help them to feel calm and safe. The first aid provider should introduce
themselves by name, and if relevant, by the name of the National Society or other organization
in a caring and non-threatening or interruptive manner. Tell them what you are doing before
you do it.
Identify any life-threatening emergencies requiring immediate action (e.g. the person is not
breathing) and what kind of first aid can support their condition.
● Is the person responsive?
● Is the person’s airway open and clear?

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Early recognition
● Is the person breathing normally?
● Has the person got an injury that is bleeding severely?
This is often called the “ABC check” or “primary survey”. If there is any concern about
cross-infection, do this assessment by observing the person’s chest or abdomen for signs of
breathing.
Look directly at the person; do not use a phone while talking to someone; focus on what the
person says. Try to be at the same physical level as the other person. For example, if the person is
sitting on the ground, kneel to be at the same eye level. Practise active listening using both
verbal and non-verbal communication skills.
If the person does not have any life-threatening conditions, you may be able to identify and
provide support for any non-life-threatening conditions.
● Is the person showing signs of an altered mental status (confusion, aggression, etc.)?

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Early recognition
● Does the person have any signs of injury? You may need to examine them more closely.
● Does the person have any history of an allergy or medical condition?
● How does the person say they feel?
● What other signs can you observe in them (temperature, movement, etc.)?
Immediate basic and practical needs are also priorities.
● Does the person need warmth, shelter or clothing?
● Does the person need social support (restoring family links, medical or legal assistance,
etc.)?

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Early recognition
● If the person is a child, do they need to be connected with their caregiver?
Knowing how to help people access basic needs is an important PFA skill. While the first aid
provider does not need to have contact details for all the resources in the community, it is vital to
know how and where to get this information when needed.
A key part of first aid is recognizing emotional reactions, accepting these without judgment, and
responding in a caring, empathetic and understanding way. It is important to remain calm and
be mindful of your own verbal and non-verbal communication to support the person in distress.
If the person in distress has strong emotional reactions that endanger themselves or others or
begin to interfere with daily functioning over a longer period of time, they should be referred for
professional mental health support.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● Provide care for the conditions you find in the order of severity, focusing first on the
person’s breathing and circulation, which are critical to survival.
● Access help if necessary.
● Continue to assess and observe the person. Be alert to any changes in their condition.
Take note of any vital signs if necessary.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● Provide care until professional medical care can take over or the person and their support
network become self-sufficient. It may be helpful to share information about onward care
options if available.
The first aid provider will need to ask questions that can help the distressed person identify what
support they need. If someone does not want help, do not impose it. The questions should focus
on the help needed and the priorities, not on the details of what happened. Remember, it is
important to empower people to make their own decisions rather than making decisions for
them, particularly at a time when they may feel very disempowered or lacking control over a
difficult situation.
Handling sensitive disclosures
● Protect the person’s dignity and emotional safety by gently pausing the disclosure if it
becomes too personal.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● Offer to continue the conversation privately after the session.
● Set the expectation that a person does not have to share information in a group setting if
it may lead to regret or vulnerability.
Techniques to calm a person in distress
To help stabilize and comfort individuals experiencing acute distress, apply the following
techniques:
● Use a calm, soft tone of voice to convey safety and reassurance.
● Invite the person to share what is upsetting them and provide individual PFA if needed.
● If culturally appropriate, maintain eye contact (without staring) to show attentiveness and
empathy. Offer comfort through appropriate, culturally sensitive physical gestures (e.g. a
hand on the shoulder).
● Reassure the person of their safety and your intent to help, but only if the situation allows
and the statement is truthful.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● Engage in grounding or distracting activities to restore a sense of normalcy, such as:
○ taking a short walk
○ moving away from distressing sights
○ offering a drink or performing a simple task together.
● Allow space for grief and use the moment to introduce positive coping strategies through
group sharing.
Special situations
Managing agitated behaviours in emergencies
During emergencies, first aid providers may encounter individuals experiencing acute
psychological distress or trauma. This distress may stem from pre-existing conditions, be
triggered by the crisis itself, or emerge as a reaction to overwhelming circumstances. In some
cases, individuals may become emotionally agitated, or even pose a risk to themselves or others.
Understanding distress reactions
Distress reactions can appear in various ways, including:
● disorientation or confusion
● heightened anxiety or panic

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● verbal aggression or shouting
● physical agitation or restlessness
● withdrawal or unresponsiveness
Principle of safety
In rare but serious cases, these reactions may escalate into violent or self-harming behaviour.
Such behaviours may be driven by fear, trauma or a perceived loss of control. The safety of the
first aid provider, the affected individual and bystanders is most important. Before engaging
with an agitated person:
● Assess the environment for safety risks.
● Do not intervene if the situation poses a threat to your own safety.
● Maintain a safe distance and avoid physical contact unless absolutely necessary.
● Seek assistance from security personnel, law enforcement or trained professionals if the
individual becomes violent or unmanageable.
If safe to do so, apply calming techniques such as:
● speaking slowly in a calm, non-threatening tone

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● avoiding sudden movements or loud noises
● offering reassurance without confrontation
● redirecting attention to neutral or grounding activities.
Referral and follow-up
If the individual’s behaviour indicates a need for specialized care—such as persistent confusion,
inability to function, threats of harm, or substance misuse—refer them to appropriate mental
health and psychosocial services. Ensure follow-up where possible to confirm they have received
the necessary support.
Medication administration
Generally, a first aid provider is not authorized to prescribe or give medication. In some
countries, these legal restrictions are evolving. Depending on the scope of practice, the target
audience, medical oversight, as well as the extent and depth of the educational programme
offered, medication administration may be appropriate and used in particular first aid situations.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● In situations where a person has prescribed medication (such as an inhaler or
auto-injector), first aid providers may assist the person, if local regulations allow.
● First aid providers should learn about the common conditions they may encounter and
the types of medication that may be used by an ill person.
● First aid providers should become familiar with the various methods of administration
(e.g. how to use the auto-injector or inhaler).
● First aid providers should try to contact EMS before administering medication if possible.
● First aid providers should inform EMS of any medication the person has taken or been
administered, especially if the person is unable to communicate this information
themself.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● First aid providers should advise or assist the ill person to take their medication in
accordance with the prescribed dose and administration route.
First aid providers may typically administer or assist with medication for the following
conditions:
● heart attack (aspirin, nitroglycerin)
● asthma attack (inhaler)
● allergic reaction (antihistamine)
● anaphylactic reaction (epinephrine)
● decompression sickness and hypoxia (oxygen)
● opioid overdose (naloxone)
● fever (antipyretic)
● earache, headache, sore throat, period pain, Back pain (painkiller)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
● diabetic emergency (insulin, glucose).
Multiple casualty incident
In a multi-casualty event, large numbers of people are affected simultaneously. The scene is
often chaotic, with survivors, families of victims and bystanders all experiencing varying levels of
psychological distress. When responding to a multiple casualty incident, call EMS first to inform
them about a potentially critical situation, and then call them again when you have detailed
information to give them.
Quickly assess all the ill or injured before providing care, and provide care first to those with the
most life-threatening conditions relating to breathing and circulation.
Who is affected and how they may react
1.
Survivors
○ May be in shock, confusion, disorientation, or panic.
○ Some may be numb or silent, while others may cry, scream or express guilt for
surviving.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - First aid steps
○ Physical injuries may compound emotional distress.
2. Family members
○ Often arrive at the scene or hospitals in a state of desperation and fear.
○ May express anger, helplessness or overwhelming grief, especially if loved ones are
missing or deceased.
○ Some may demand information or become agitated due to lack of updates.
3. Bystanders and witnesses
○ Even if not directly harmed, they may experience trauma due to the exposure.
○ Reactions include anxiety, nausea, trembling or feeling frozen.
○ Children and elderly bystanders may be especially vulnerable.
First aid providers are often the first point of human contact in these situations. While attending
to physical injuries, they can also provide basic emotional support using PFA principles.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Access help
● Identify what type of help is needed to address immediate needs and problems and
support the person’s ability to cope with the situation. It may be more than one type of
help. For example, the person may need rescue service, PFA and medical care.
● Access the next level of care as soon as the need is expected. This will get help to you
quicker, and if you are phoning, the call-taker may be able to guide and support your first
aid actions.
● Identify additional resources that could help you in accessing help or providing care, such
as bystanders or transport options.
● If life-saving first aid is being provided, access care in the most efficient way possible. This
may mean making a call using the speakerphone function or arranging transport that
allows care to be continued during the journey.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Access help
● Help the person prioritize their needs and find helpful solutions to the issues. The first aid
provider may have to accompany the person in taking the first steps and continue to
empower them to act. PFA aims to enable people to make their own informed decisions.
● In some cases, it might be better to access EMS quickly with incomplete information. For
example, accessing EMS early for a full bus crash, even without knowing the exact
number of injured, will start the process of getting help. In other contexts, more detailed
information may be needed. For example, a message sent from a remote setting should
have detailed information so EMS can send adequate resources to help.
● If calling EMS, remain calm and answer their questions as clearly and accurately as you
can. This will help them prioritize your call.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Recovery
In the case of minor illnesses or injuries, the role of the first aid provider is one of support and
empowerment to allow people to cope with the difficulties and be responsible for themselves.
Accurate information about the event, the rescue, as well as information about loved ones or
others who are impacted, their safety, rights and how to access the services and things needed
are essential for anyone in a crisis. Provide accurate and useful information relevant to the
individual. This could range from practical information on what happened, where to access
different resources, or what is possible and important to do at the moment, to psycho-education
that helps normalize the reaction of distress and prepare the person for possible reactions that
may follow in the coming days and weeks. Information helps people feel empowered to make
informed decisions about their situation.
It is a priority to connect a distressed person with their family or friends, either in person or by
phone, to update them on what is happening and check if the loved ones are fine. The first aid
provider should also know the services to help link people to their family in emergencies. Ask
about who should be informed and called upon in the social network.
Examples of helpful practical support are:

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Recovery
● contacting someone who can stay with the ill, injured, or distressed person
● arranging for the pick-up of children, or the provision of food, shelter, clothing and
reassurance to children
● helping the person with transport to a safe place

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Recovery
● helping the person to access a hospital or other support services.
Encouraging the use of helpful coping strategies and avoiding unhelpful ones is also essential.
Examples of unhelpful coping strategies include using alcohol or substances to try to forget the
problems, denial or isolating oneself. While these strategies may feel like they are helping the
person cope in the moment, if continued over long periods, they are likely to impact the person
negatively and cause more challenges. Having information on natural and normal reactions to a
crisis event can also help the person use healthy coping strategies.
Referrals
Referral means linking a person in distress with the appropriate care provided by other people,
agency or facility, either by contacting the other service directly or giving contact details to the
affected person. When a first aid provider assesses that the person needs help beyond that
which they can provide, they make a referral. It is good practice to follow up with the person
afterwards to ensure that they have received the support needed.
Refer specialized psychological help if someone:

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Recovery
● has not been able to sleep for the last week and appears confused and disoriented
● is so distressed that they are unable to function normally and care for themselves or their
children
● loses control over their behaviour and behaves unpredictably or destructively
● threatens to harm themselves or others

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Recovery
● uses substances or alcohol excessively. Self-care for the first aid provider
In order to provide help responsibly, first aid providers must take care of their own health and
well-being. Providers can be affected by supporting others in crises or by their own distress. Providing first aid can be difficult both physically and emotionally. It is not easy interacting with
people who are in distress and this could lead to feelings of guilt, sadness and frustration if first
aid providers feel they have not done enough. These may also result in cumulative stress and
burnout. It is also important to acknowledge that different situations may affect or resonate with
first aid providers who are unique individuals, shaped by their own experiences. There is no
shame in finding things difficult and it is essential to practise proper self-care in the first aid
providers’ own lives. First aid providers can apply the PFA principles of Look, Listen and Link, and learn to recognize
their own risk factors to well-being, their own limitations and what kinds of situations may be
overwhelming. They can also discover what protective factors such as support systems and
healthy stress coping strategies they have in place.. Building awareness of their own strengths
and weaknesses as a first aid provider and knowing when to call for help from others can act as
preventive measures.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
General approach - Recovery
It is imperative that all first aid providers and volunteers are given supervision and continuous
support while providing care and assistance for others during times of crisis to ensure they are
not overwhelmed by the circumstances and can maintain their own psychological well-being. It
is recommended that all National Society staff and volunteers providing emotional support
within the principles of PFA have access to a support system where they can receive the
assistance they need. The support system team should take time to come together before,
during and after providing emotional support.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hand hygiene - Introduction
Good hand hygiene is a crucial measure to prevent the spread of germs, which can cause
people to get sick. The Global Handwashing Partnership estimates that inadequate hand
hygiene results in nearly 300,000 deaths each year, with most deaths being among children
younger than five years old (Tharaldson & Moore, 2018). First aid providers must practise good
hand hygiene to prevent the spread of germs and reduce the likelihood of getting or spreading
infections. During a pandemic, more frequent handwashing is recommended.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hand hygiene - Guidelines
● Handwashing should be done with soap and water.**
● Hand hygiene can be achieved using an alcohol-based hand gel with at least 70% volume
of ethanol or 60% of another alcohol for maximum efficacy.*
● Hand hygiene education and access to soap and water may improve hand hygiene
compliance in healthcare workers and within the community, including schools.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hand hygiene - Good practice points
● First aid providers should wash their hands before and after providing first aid care to an
ill or injured person. If there is not an opportunity to wash hands in an emergency, do not
delay providing first aid.
● Hands should also be washed at the critical times listed below, at minimum:
○ after using the toilet or changing a diaper
○ before, during and after food preparation
○ before eating
○ after blowing or wiping the nose
○ after coughing or sneezing
○ after touching an animal, animal food or animal waste
○ when hands are visibly soiled.
● Access to clean running water and soap is ideal. Any kind of soap should suffice.
● Handwashing should be continuous for at least 20 seconds, covering all parts of the
hands, fingers and nails. Initially, the user should cover these areas with water, then
introduce soap and rub the lather repeatedly across all areas of the hand.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hand hygiene - Good practice points
● After handwashing, hands should be rinsed and dried with a clean towel.
● If any type of gel is used (alcohol, ethanol or non-alcoholic), the amount used should cover
the hands and fingers entirely and be rubbed in until dry, usually for a minimum of 30
seconds.
● If gloves are being used after handwashing, hand lotion that does not compromise the
integrity of the gloves can be used twice daily to minimize skin irritation.
● Fingernails should be kept short and trimmed.
● Dispose of dressings, bandages, sharps, gloves and soiled clothing safely and correctly,
while continuing to cover your hands (e.g. use gloves or banana leaves). Wash your hands
immediately afterwards.
● When soap is not available, ash can be used as an alternative to clean hands.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Oxygen administration - Key action
If specifically trained to do so, give supplementary oxygen in the circumstances defined below
until emergency medical care is available.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Oxygen administration - Introduction
Giving oxygen to a person with a severe illness or injury is generally accepted practice, although
there is no evidence for its overall effectiveness. Providing supplementary oxygen is not a routine
first aid step, as many emergencies do not deprive the person of oxygen. Additionally,
administering oxygen may cause the body (and therefore the blood) to take in too much oxygen
and this may harm the person. However, under specific circumstances, oxygen administration
may be beneficial but should be provided by a specifically trained first aid provider.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Oxygen administration - Guidelines
● A first aid provider should not give supplementary oxygen to an adult with a suspected
stroke unless the first aid provider is trained and recognizes the person as hypoxic.*
● If the first aid provider is trained and oxygen is available:
○ The provider may give oxygen to a person experiencing chest pain if they recognize
the person as hypoxic.*
○ The provider may administer oxygen to a person who has drowned and is having
difficulty breathing or is in respiratory distress until arterial oxygen saturation or the
partial pressure of arterial oxygen can be measured.*
○ The provider may give oxygen to a person who is in cardiac arrest during CPR, but
doing so should not delay CPR.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Oxygen administration - Good practice points
● Although high-flow oxygen should in general be avoided in patients with chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease with difficulty breathing in the out-of-hospital setting,
high-flow oxygen should not be withheld in the presence of life-threatening hypoxaemia
(oxygen saturation <88%).
● Supplemental oxygen for resuscitation of a person who has drowned may be used if
available, but should not delay CPR, including opening the airway and providing rescue
breaths and chest compressions as needed.
● When available, trained providers use the highest possible oxygen concentration during
pre-hospital resuscitation for adults and children.
● Until emergency medical care is available, the administration of supplementary oxygen is
reasonable for a person:
○ after exposure to carbon monoxide
○ experiencing decompression illness (e.g. a scuba diver)
○ experiencing breathing difficulties

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Oxygen administration - Good practice points
○ experiencing severe hypoxia (SpO2 at 94% or less).
● If the first aid responder has been trained in transcutaneous pulse oximetry and has a
proper tool for measurement, it is ideal to taper oxygen supplementation to maintain
oxygen saturation at 94% (at sea level).
● When a first aid provider trained in oxygen use administers oxygen to a person with acute
difficulty breathing who confirms that they have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, it
is suggested that pulse oximetry be used, and that oxygen be titrated to maintain an
oxygen saturation between 88% and 92%.
● The use of a pulse oximeter for first aid assessment should not supersede or replace
physical assessment.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Key action
Maintain an open airway so the person can continue to breathe normally.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Introduction
An unresponsive and breathing person has normal, regular breaths (the air moves through the
mouth and/or nose at an even pace without any irregular sounds like gurgling), but does not
respond to any sound or touch from another person. A person may become unresponsive due
to an injury (e.g. hitting their head) or a medical condition (e.g. diabetic emergency) that may
indicate a greater danger to their health. Even if the person is breathing regularly, they may still
be at risk because their muscles could relax, causing their tongue to fall back and block their
airway. First aid providers should consider accessing medical care.
If the unresponsive person’s breathing stops, becomes noisy, or they sound like they are gasping
for air or hardly breathing, they may be in cardiac arrest. See Unresponsive and abnormal
breathing for baby and child or adolescent and adult or chest pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Guidelines
● If there is no risk of a spine injury, first aid providers should maintain an open airway by
moving the person onto their side and tilting their head back (recovery position).*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Good practice points
● If the first aid provider finds a person motionless, they should check for responsiveness
and breathing immediately. The provider should take up to 10 seconds to check for
normal breathing.
● In a non-traumatic incident (no risk of spinal injury), if the first aid provider cannot move
the person into the recovery position, they can use the head-tilt-chin-lift or jaw thrust
manoeuvres to maintain an open airway.
● The first aid provider should avoid moving a person with a suspected traumatic spinal
injury if:
○ Medical help will arrive soon. The head-tilt-chin-lift or jaw thrust manoeuvres can
be used to maintain an open airway on a person with a suspected spine injury. The
jaw thrust manoeuvre may result in less cervical spine movement than the
head-tilt-chin-lift manoeuvre.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Good practice points
○ Medical help is far away and there is more than one first aid provider present.
Providers can turn the person to a side-lying position while maintaining spinal
alignment.
● A person who is pregnant and unresponsive may be placed in the recovery position on
their left side. This prevents compression of blood vessels that feed the uterus.
● The cause of unresponsiveness (e.g. diabetic emergency, poisoning, head injury) should
be identified if possible.
● First aid providers should always access emergency medical services (EMS) for an
unresponsive person who is breathing normally, as lack of response may indicate a
serious condition.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Good practice points
● The AVPU scale, which stands for Alert – Verbal – Pain – Unresponsive, describes the type
of stimulus a person reacts to and can be used to determine the level of responsiveness. A
first aid provider using the AVPU scale should maintain an open airway for any person
reacting to Pain or who is Unresponsive.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Prevent and prepare
● Follow instructions from healthcare providers to manage any pre-existing health
conditions.
● Wear and use appropriate safety equipment when working or participating in leisure and
work activities.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Early recognition
Check for a response by gently shaking the person’s shoulders or, if they are a baby, tapping
their foot. Speak loudly and clearly, and ask a question such as, “Are you alright?” If the person
responds, continue with your assessment.
If the person is unresponsive, they will not move or respond to any noise or touch. If the person
does not respond:
1.
Check for breathing: Keeping their airway open, look, listen and feel for normal breathing
for up to ten seconds. Look for chest or abdominal movement; listen for breathing
sounds; feel for air on your cheek.
2. Open the airway: Start with the person on their back. Gently tilt the head back (or into a
neutral position for a baby) until the mouth falls open, and then lift the chin.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - First aid steps
If the person is breathing normally:
1.
Move them onto their side and tilt their head back (or into a neutral position if it is a baby)
to maintain an open airway. This is called the recovery position. A baby can be held in this
position in your arms.
2. Access EMS.
3. Monitor the person for any changes in their breathing or level of response. If possible, try
to establish why the person is unresponsive.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - CAUTION
If you suspect a spine injury, maintain an open airway by using the head-tilt-chin-lift or
jaw thrust manoeuvres only and access EMS.
If medical care is some time away and if there is more than one first aid provider present,
you can turn the person into a side-lying position while maintaining spinal alignment.
If the person is breathing abnormally (gasping, taking irregular breaths or not breathing),
start CPR immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Access help
● When speaking to EMS, specify that the person is unresponsive and breathing normally. If
you know what caused the person to become unresponsive, communicate that
information too.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Unresponsive and breathing normally - Recovery
If the person became unresponsive due to an existing health condition, they should try to
quickly recognize any warning signs of it occurring again. This may enable them to get into a
comfortable position and call for help.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Overview
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Key action
Immediately start chest compressions and access emergency medical services (EMS).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Introduction
If a person’s heart is unable to pump blood around the body, then this person is in cardiac arrest. The person will quickly become unresponsive and display signs of abnormal breathing (e.g. taking irregular or noisy breaths, or stop breathing altogether). When a person’s heart is not
working and they are not breathing, their body experiences a lack of oxygen. Vital organs, such
as the brain or the heart, can start to deteriorate after a few minutes. Sudden cardiac arrest is
one of the leading causes of death worldwide (Berdowski et al., 2010). Early recognition of
abnormal breathing and starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can keep the person alive
until defibrillation takes place, either by a first aid provider or professional responder. The techniques of CPR need to be adapted depending on the size of the unresponsive
person and the size of the first aid provider. In this context, an adolescent or adult is someone
you think has gone through puberty. Use the following guidelines on an unresponsive adult
or adolescent. If the person is an adolescent, consider giving rescue breaths with chest
compressions. If the person looks like they are a child, follow the guidelines for Unresponsive
and abnormal breathing (baby or child). It is most important to do something.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Introduction
In the case of someone needing CPR, it is unlikely a
first aid provider can make the situation worse for the person.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Guidelines
● If a person is unresponsive with abnormal breathing, it is reasonable to assume the
person is in cardiac arrest.**
● Taking the pulse as the sole indicator of the presence or absence of cardiac arrest is
unreliable.**
● When possible, a lone bystander with a mobile phone should call for help, activate the
speaker or other hands-free option on the mobile phone, and immediately begin CPR
with dispatcher assistance, if required.**
● If in doubt whether a person is experiencing cardiac arrest or not, the first aid provider
should start CPR without concern of causing additional harm.**
● First aid providers who are trained, able and willing can give rescue breaths and chest
compressions to all unresponsive adolescents and adults with abnormal breathing.*
● CPR may start with compressions rather than rescue breaths.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Guidelines
● Perform chest compressions in the centre of the chest (i.e. the lower half of the sternum
or breastbone) on adolescents and adults who are unresponsive with abnormal
breathing.*
● Chest compressions should be performed at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute.**
● Chest compressions should be done to a depth of approximately 5 cm (2 inches); avoid a
compression depth of more than 6 cm (2.4 inches).*
● When possible, first aid providers should perform chest compressions on a firm surface
but should not significantly delay starting chest compressions to move the person.*
● First aid providers should avoid leaning on the chest between compressions to allow full
chest wall recoil.*
● To mitigate the effects of fatigue, rotate the provider performing chest compressions
every two minutes whenever possible.**
● The use of real-time CPR feedback devices is not recommended to improve
resuscitation.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Guidelines
● For those who are willing and able to provide rescue breaths, a ratio of 30 compressions
and two rescue breaths (30:2) should be used on adolescents and adults who are
unresponsive with abnormal breathing.**
● Interrupting chest compressions to deliver two rescue breaths should take less than ten
seconds.**
● First-aid providers must give each mouth-to-mouth rescue breath within a one-second
inspiratory time to achieve chest rise. The same initial tidal volume must be used with all
persons regardless of the cause of the cardiac arrest.*
● When an automated external defibrillator is available, first aid providers should continue
to perform CPR while the defibrillator is set up and pause only when it is ready for analysis
and, if indicated, provides a shock.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Guidelines
● In any setting, chest compressions should be resumed immediately after shock delivery
for adolescents or adults who are unresponsive with abnormal breathing. Any pauses in
chest compressions before and after the shock should be as short as possible.**
● First aid providers should use standard CPR protocols with obese persons.*
● First-aid providers should take appropriate safety (PPE and body substance isolation)
precautions when feasible and when resources are available to do so, especially if the
person is known to have a serious infection (e.g. HIV, tuberculosis, HBV or SARS).*
The following guidelines are specific to emergency medical dispatch centres and the
professionals who work there.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Guidelines
● Emergency medical dispatch centres should implement a standardized algorithm or
specific criteria to determine immediately if a person is unresponsive with abnormal
breathing at the time of an emergency call.**
● Emergency medical dispatchers should be educated to identify unresponsiveness with
abnormal breathing. This education should include recognition and significance of
agonal breaths across a range of clinical presentations and descriptions.**
● Emergency medical dispatch centres should have systems in place where dispatchers
can provide instructions to callers who will provide CPR.**
● Emergency
medical
dispatchers
should
provide
chest
compression-only
CPR
instructions to callers for adults and adolescents with suspected cardiac arrest.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Good practice points
● First aid providers should perform chest compression for all patients in cardiac arrest.
● To achieve more effective chest compressions, the dominant hand should be placed
against the sternum with the non-dominant hand over the dominant hand.
● If the person is an adolescent, CPR with rescue breaths is preferred.
● Adults receiving CPR will require advanced medical care. In contexts where this care is
unavailable, first aid providers should prioritize the dignity of the person they are caring
for.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Prevent and prepare
● There are national and global organizations that research how to reduce the likelihood of
cardiac arrest and set up national and regional cardiac arrest registers to define a strategy
of intervention. Refer to your country’s health authority for more information.
● Make healthy lifestyle choices to minimize certain risk factors such as high blood pressure,
obesity, blood sugar level, hyperlipidaemia and renal dysfunction. Avoid activities such as
smoking.
● Promote emergency phone numbers and other means to access help fast.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Early recognition
Two main mechanisms of cardiac arrest result in unresponsiveness and abnormal breathing.
The first is when the heart stops (e.g. from a heart attack) and prevents the oxygen-rich blood
from pumping around the body. This is the most common type in adults. The second type is
when a person is unable to breathe oxygen into the body (e.g. due to drowning or strangulation).
The person will have very little oxygen remaining in their blood and appear lifeless.
In the first few minutes after cardiac arrest, a person may have agonal breathing (an irregular
and laboured breathing pattern, or gasping noisily). This type of breathing is not normal. If there
is any doubt about whether breathing is normal, assume it is not. Similarly, if professional
responders are unsure if a pulse is present, they should assume it is not. A short period of
seizure-like activity may occur at the beginning of a cardiac arrest. Once the seizure stops,
continue to assess the person.
Check for a response by gently shaking the person’s shoulders. Speaking loudly and clearly, ask a
question such as, “Are you alright?”.
If the person responds, see the general approach.
If the person does not respond:

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Early recognition
1.
Open their airway: Gently tilt their head back and lift the person’s chin. (You may need to
turn the person onto their back to do this.)
2. Check for breathing: Keeping the airway open, look, listen and feel for normal breathing
for up to ten seconds. Look for chest or abdominal movement; listen for breath sounds;
feel for air on your cheek. Professional responders may also do a pulse check at this time.
Identify whether the person is an adult or adolescent. If they are a child, follow the approach for
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby or child).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - First aid steps
If the person’s breathing is abnormal or they are not breathing:
1.
Immediately shout for help and ask bystanders to access EMS. If you are alone, access
EMS yourself, either using a telephone with the speaker function or–if there is no phone
available nearby–leave the person to access EMS. Do this as quickly as possible.
2. Begin chest compressions without delay; push down on the centre of the person’s chest
at a fast and regular rate (100–120 compressions per minute).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - First aid steps
3. If able and willing, combine chest compressions with rescue breaths at a ratio of 30:2 (30
compressions followed by two breaths). Rescue breaths may be particularly beneficial for
unresponsive individuals whose condition is related to hypoxia, such as drowning,
choking, strangulation or opioid overdose. They may also be beneficial when a delay in
defibrillation is anticipated. Each rescue breath should be delivered over approximately
one second, producing visible chest rise. The provision of rescue breaths should not
interrupt chest compressions for more than 10 seconds. If the first aider is unable or
unwilling to provide rescue breaths, chest compressions alone should be continued.
4. If one is available, ask a bystander to bring an automated external defibrillator as soon as
possible. Follow the voice prompts, interrupting chest compressions as little as possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - First aid steps
5. Continue to give chest compressions and breaths unless otherwise instructed to pause
(either by an automated defibrillator or professional responder). Pause compressions if
the person shows signs of recovery, such as coughing, opening their eyes, speaking or
moving purposefully and breathing normally.
6. If two or more first aid providers are present, alternate giving chest compressions and
breaths every two minutes to prevent getting tired. Ensure that there is no interruption in
compressions as the next person takes over.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Local adaptation
These local adaptations underscore the importance of safety, quality and respect in resuscitation
efforts, particularly in challenging or remote scenarios.
Manual CPR during transport: Delivering manual CPR during transport poses significant risks to
providers and can reduce the quality of compressions. EMS systems must assess these risks and,
when feasible, use strategies to avoid them. Resuscitation is best performed at the scene unless
there is a clear and justified need for transport. If transport is required, EMS providers should
prioritize maintaining high-quality CPR throughout the journey.
Remote area transport: In circumstances where EMS or other advanced care options are
unavailable, and transport from a remote location to medical care is necessary, continuous CPR
should be performed on a firm surface during transit.
Dignity and respect: When EMS or advanced care is not accessible, it is critical to uphold the
individual’s dignity during all aspects of care and transport.
Drowning and Hypothermia cases: In situations involving drowning or hypothermia, there
remains a possibility of a positive response to CPR even when defibrillation is not feasible.
Continue to perform CPR in these situations for the best possible outcome.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Access help
● When speaking to EMS, very clearly explain that the unresponsive person is not breathing
normally; this will prompt EMS to prioritize your case appropriately.
● Ask bystanders for help accessing EMS and providing CPR, as well as bringing and using
an automated external defibrillator.
● An unresponsive person who is not breathing is unlikely to achieve spontaneous
circulation from CPR alone. Their heart needs an electric shock from a defibrillator. It is
vital that EMS arrive and a defibrillator is used.
● The survival of the person depends upon immediate and effective CPR; when accessing
help, keep any interruptions to chest compressions minimal.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child) - Recovery
● Even if the first aid provider has performed CPR and defibrillation and the person is now
responsive and breathing normally, you must continue close monitoring until EMS arrives
as the person may stop breathing again.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Overview
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child)
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Key action
Immediately start rescue breaths and chest compressions and access emergency medical
services (EMS).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Introduction
If a baby or child is unresponsive with abnormal breathing (e.g. taking irregular or noisy breaths,
or has stopped breathing altogether) and has no signs of life, it indicates they are in cardiac
arrest. When a baby or child is in cardiac arrest, their heart stops beating and cannot pump
blood around their body. This means that vital organs, such as the brain, do not get enough
oxygen and can start to deteriorate within minutes. While cardiac arrest occurs less frequently in
babies and children compared to adults, it is still life-threatening. Typically, cardiac arrest in
babies and children is the result of a breathing problem, whereas in adults, it usually has to do
with their heart itself. The causes vary by age, setting and any underlying health problems of the
baby or child; however, some common ones include choking, drowning and disease. Since the
cause of cardiac arrest is likely to relate to their breathing, rescue breaths play a critical role in
CPR for babies or children. Survival to hospital discharge is primarily linked to the early initiation
of CPR.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Introduction
● The techniques of CPR need to be adapted depending on the size of the unresponsive
person and the size of the first aid provider. If the person looks like a baby (less than
about one year old), treat them as a baby. If the person looks like they are a child, treat
them as a child.
● If the person looks like an adolescent (they may have been through puberty) or an adult,
use the guidelines provided in unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and
adult).
● It is most important to initiate the chain of survival behaviours.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Guidelines
● First aid providers should use a response check and breathing check to ascertain whether a
baby or child is unresponsive and breathing abnormally. Checking for a pulse is not needed.*
● CPR should be performed on a baby or child who is unresponsive with abnormal breathing
(e.g. taking irregular or noisy breaths or has stopped breathing altogether).**
● Lay providers should perform both rescue breaths and chest compressions for a baby or a
child in cardiac arrest. If they are unable to provide rescue breaths, they should at least
perform chest compressions.**
● For a baby, chest compressions can be performed with the two-thumb-encircling hand
method or with the two-finger technique. In newborns, the two-thumb-encircling hand
method is preferred.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Guidelines
● For a child, chest compressions may be performed with one or two hands. For example, if the
first aid provider is small or the child is large, the first aid provider may use two hands.*
● A compression-to-rescue-breath ratio of 30:2 (30 compressions and two rescue breaths) may
be used on a baby or child who is unresponsive with abnormal breathing.*
● For a baby, chest compression depth should be at least one-third of the chest’s depth or
approximately four cm (one and a half inches).*
● For a child, the chest compression depth should be one-third of the chest depth, or
approximately five cm (two inches).*
● The rate of chest compressions should be 100–120 per minute for babies and children (this is
the same as for an adolescent or adult).**
● Chest compression should be performed on a firm surface when possible.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Guidelines
● All emergency medical dispatchers should provide CPR instructions (referred to as
dispatcher-assisted CPR) to first aid providers who call regarding an unresponsive baby or
child with abnormal breathing.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Good practice points
● While it is preferred to start with rescue breaths and then compressions, it is also acceptable
to start with compressions and then give rescue breaths. Both components are important
when providing CPR to children.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Prevent and prepare
● Refer to your local or national health authority to identify the main causes of baby and
child cardiac arrest in your region. Preventable and preparable causes include choking,
drowning or disease.
● Follow recommended baby and child safety practices, including supervision near water
and safe sleep habits for infants.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Early recognition
In the first few minutes after cardiac arrest, a baby or child may have agonal breathing (meaning
they are barely breathing or gasping noisily and irregularly). This type of breathing is abnormal. If
there is any doubt about whether breathing is normal, assume it is not.
Check for a response.
● Baby: Pick the baby up or tap on the sole of their foot. An unresponsive baby will be limp
and of an abnormal colour.
● Child: Gently tap the child’s shoulders. Speak loudly and clearly, asking a question such as,
“Are you alright?”
If the baby or child does not respond or react:
● Open their airway: For a baby, tilt their head slightly to a neutral position and lift their chin.
For a child, tilt their head back and lift their chin.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Early recognition
● Check for breathing: Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Look
for chest or abdominal movement, listen for breathing sounds, and feel for breath on your
cheek. If you have any doubt whether breathing is normal, take action as though it is not.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - First aid steps
If the baby or child’s breathing is abnormal (or they are not breathing):
1.
Immediately shout for help and ask bystanders to access EMS. If you are alone, access
EMS yourself, either using a telephone with the speaker function or–if there is no phone
available nearby–leave the person to access EMS. Do this as quickly as possible.
2. Give 30 chest compressions; push down on the centre of their chest at a fast and regular
rate (100–120 compressions per minute).
○ If you are a trained responder, you may use a ratio of 15 compressions to two rescue
breaths.
3. Give two initial rescue breaths using a mouth-to-mouth-and-nose technique for a baby or
a
mouth-to-mouth
technique for a child. Blow steadily into the mouth or
mouth-and-nose for one second until you see the chest or abdomen rise.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - First aid steps
4. Continue with cycles of 30 chest compressions and two rescue breaths until emergency
help arrives or the baby or child shows signs of life (such as coughing, opening their eyes,
speaking or moving purposefully) and starts to breathe normally.
● If an automated external defibrillator is available, ask a bystander to bring it as quickly as
possible. Follow the voice prompts, interrupting CPR cycles as little as possible.
● If you are unwilling or unable to give rescue breaths, give chest-compression-only CPR at
a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute.
● If more than one first aid provider is present, change providers every one to two minutes
to prevent fatigue. Ensure there is minimal interruption to CPR as the next person takes
over.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - First aid steps
● If you are alone and do not have a way to call EMS while performing CPR (e.g. no
speakerphone), perform CPR for one minute before pausing to call for help.
● While performing rescue breaths, be alert to any signs of life such as movement or
coughing.
● If the baby or child is unresponsive and breathing normally, maintain an open airway.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Local adaptation
● In contexts that do not have an EMS or other higher level of care, if CPR has not been
effective within the first 20 minutes, then (except in cases of drowning and hypothermia)
the first aid provider could stop CPR as it is unlikely to be successful.
● Other guidance allows greater flexibility, accepting either a compression-first or
ventilation-first approach, and permits pulse checks by trained providers. Overall, some
guidance prioritizes early ventilation, while other approaches allow more latitude for
trained responders and teams.
● Recommendations for compression–ventilation ratios vary by training and context. In
some guidance, a ratio of 15 compressions to two ventilations (15:2) is recommended only
for first aid providers who have received specific paediatric basic life support training,
while others are advised to use 30:2.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Local adaptation
● 15:2 is appropriate for two rescuers and 30:2 for a single rescuer is recommended,
although some recommendations require specific training to apply the 15:2 ratio.
● It is reasonable to perform compression-only CPR if the first aid provider is unable or
unwilling to give ventilations.
● Some recommendations prioritize the two-thumb encircling technique for all
compressions in all situations, using a one-hand (heel-of-hand) technique only when the
two-thumb technique is not possible, including during dispatcher-assisted CPR. Either
technique can be used, with the one-hand technique when chest encirclement is not
possible. Overall, some approaches consistently favour the two-thumb technique, while
others allow greater flexibility based on the situation and the first aid provider’s ability.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Local adaptation
● Guidance may include different levels of detail on anatomical positioning, but both
anterolateral (front and side of chest) and anteroposterior (front and back of torso)
placements are accepted. Electrode pads must not overlap and a small gap (about one to
two cm) between pads is recommended.
● If transporting the baby or child from a remote area to medical care, continuous CPR on a
firm surface must be provided during transit.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Access help
● When accessing EMS, very clearly explain that the baby or child is unresponsive and
breathing abnormally; this will prompt EMS to prioritize the case appropriately.
● Ask bystanders for help accessing EMS and providing CPR, as well as bringing and using
an automated external defibrillator.
● The survival of the baby or child depends upon immediate and effective CPR; when
accessing help, keep any interruptions to chest compressions minimal.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult)
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing (adolescent and adult) - Recovery
Even if the first aid responder has performed CPR and defibrillation and the baby or child is now
responsive and breathing normally, you must continue close monitoring until EMS attends to
them, as they may stop breathing again.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available - Overview
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing when a defibrillator is
available

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available - Key action
Use a defibrillator in the sequence of giving CPR to improve the person’s chance of survival.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available - Introduction
An automated external defibrillator (defibrillator or AED) is a portable device that analyses the
heart’s rhythm and, if necessary, sends an electric shock (or defibrillation) to help re-establish a
normal heart rhythm. Rapid use of a defibrillator can improve the chances of survival for those
experiencing sudden cardiac arrest. A bystander with little or no training can use a defibrillator.
Public access defibrillators are proven to be safe and effective, allowing defibrillation to take
place immediately.
The automated devices have voice prompts and visual aids to follow and are easy to use. Once
the defibrillator detects a shockable rhythm, it will automatically deliver a shock (fully automated
defibrillator) or instruct the first aid provider to push the shock button (semi-automated
defibrillator). A defibrillator does not replace the need for CPR. First aid providers must provide
CPR with as few interruptions to chest compressions as possible while setting up and using the
defibrillator.
This topic should be used in conjunction with unresponsive and abnormal breathing
(adolescent and adult) or unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and child).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available - Guidelines
● The implementation of public-access defibrillation programmes is recommended to
improve the outcomes for people with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.**
● For a person who is unresponsive with abnormal breathing (taking irregular or noisy
breaths, or they stop breathing altogether), CPR should be provided until the defibrillator
is ready to start analysing the heart.*
● For adults and children, automatic external defibrillation with self-adhesive pads can be
used and is very safe.**
● For babies and children younger than eight years of age, a paediatric defibrillator should
be used.**
● For babies and children younger than eight years of age, if a paediatric defibrillator or
paediatric pads are not available, a standard defibrillator and pads could be used.*
● For adults and children (eight years or older), a standard defibrillator should be used.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available - Guidelines
● Fast removal of excessive chest hair can be done before the application of pads, so long as
the delay to shock delivery is minimal.*
● For optimal defibrillation in adults, pads greater than 8 cm are more effective.*
● Pads should be placed on the chest according to the description given on the defibrillator
or pads. For babies and children, the anterior-posterior placement of self-adhesive pads
may be used (one pad on their front, and one pad on their back).*
● For large-breasted individuals, the left electrode pad should be placed beside or
underneath the left breast, avoiding breast tissue.*
● First aid providers should continue to perform CPR while the defibrillator is set up and
pause only when it is ready for analysis and, if indicated, provides a shock.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
topic: Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available
text:
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing with defibrillator available - Guidelines
● After the defibrillator administers a single shock, the first aid provider should resume with
