the wound was dirty, the person should receive a tetanus update every five years. If the wound
was clean, it is usually every 10 years.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Cuts and grazes - Recovery
Cuts and grazes usually heal within a few days. Check the outside of the dressing each day:
● If it is still clean, do not change it.
● If it is visibly stained with a bit of blood or some clear fluid, remove the dressing. Clean the
wound again (using tap water or a disinfectant) and put on a new dressing.
Monitor the wound for any signs of infection. If the skin around the wound becomes red, purple
or darker and is warm and painful, or if the person develops a fever, this indicates an infection.
Never cover an infected wound; seek medical help.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Key action
Store the tooth temporarily and advise the person to seek help from a dentist as soon as
possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Introduction
Dental avulsion is the complete displacement of a tooth due to it being forcefully knocked out.
This type of injury is common, particularly in children. However, it is only necessary to replant a
tooth if it is a permanent one. A permanent tooth that has been knocked out can often be
successfully re-implanted by a dentist if it is done quickly.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Guidelines
● The first aid provider may temporarily store the tooth in:
○ propolis (from 0.04 mg to 2.5 mg per mL of 0.4% ethanol)*
○ oral rehydration salt solutions, such as Ricetral (a commercial form of oral
rehydration salt)*
○ solutions containing sodium chloride, glucose, potassium chloride, citrate and
extruded rice*
○ clingfilm*
● If none of these options are available, the first aid provider may temporarily store the
tooth in cow’s milk (with any percentage fat or form).*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Good practice points
● First aid providers may encourage the person to apply gentle pressure to the bleeding
gum with gauze to stop the bleeding.
● If the avulsion has created any sharp edges in the person’s mouth, advise the person to
apply a compress of gauze or clean cotton to protect their mouth from further injuries.
● When picking up the tooth, it should be held at the crown (the area that sits above the
gum), not at the root.
● First aid providers must NOT re-implant the tooth.
● The tooth should NOT be cleaned as this could damage vital tissues still attached to the
tooth.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Good practice points
● If none of the recommended storage solutions or cow’s milk are available, first aid
providers may temporarily store the tooth in a container with the person’s own saliva.
Unless there are no alternative options, do NOT let the person keep the tooth in their
mouth, as there is a chance that the person will swallow it (e.g. if the person is not fully
responsive, or if they are a child). Instead, use a small jar or another container.
● Refer the person to a dentist or advanced care. Advise them to seek help as soon as
possible to encourage successful reimplantation.
● There is no need to consider emergency dental treatment if the tooth is not a permanent
one (such as in young children). However, advise the person to seek dental care anyway,
particularly if the tooth’s root has broken off.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Prevent and prepare
● Know what solutions are available to you for storing an avulsed tooth, and have a suitable
container available for transportation.
● Wear a mouth guard for contact sports such as boxing, rugby, karate and taekwondo.
● Wear a helmet when riding a motorcycle, bicycle or horse, and for skateboarding.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - First aid steps
1.
Help the person to stop the bleeding in their mouth by applying a compress of gauze or
clean cotton.
2. If the avulsion has created any sharp edges in the person’s mouth, advise the person to
apply a compress of gauze or clean cotton to protect their mouth from further injuries.
3. Find the tooth and pick it up carefully by the crown. Store it in a salt solution, an oral
rehydration solution or clingfilm. If none of these options are available, store the tooth in a
container with cow’s milk or the person’s own saliva.
4. Advise the person to access a dentist or emergency care facility as soon as possible, and
to take their tooth with them. If travelling with the person:
○ Maintain a clear airway above all else. If the only option to safely transport the tooth
is in the person’s mouth, the person must be an adult, fully awake, cooperative and
able to do so safely.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - First aid steps
○ Check the surrounding tissues (lips, mouth) for further injury
○ Dental avulsion may indicate another injury (e.g. head injury); prioritize any
additional injuries appropriately.
When using clingfilm, make sure to add enough of the person’s saliva to prevent the tooth
from drying out.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dental avulsion - Access help
● If a dentist is not available right away, access any available medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Key action
Keep the blister clean and covered to prevent infection.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Introduction
A friction blister is a small pocket of fluid that forms in the outer layers of skin caused by
continuous rubbing or pressure over time. Friction blisters commonly appear on feet during or
after walking long distances, or on hands after using a tool for a long time during work or
recreation.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Guidelines
● If a friction blister does not cause serious discomfort, the first aid provider should consider
keeping the blister intact. This may decrease the risk of bacteria and infection, compared
to draining it (aspiration) or removing the top layer of the blister (deroofing).*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Good practice points
● Friction blisters can lead to an open wound, bleeding or infection, limiting a person’s
mobility. In these situations, the person should stop the activity causing the blister, and if
possible, cover the blister with a clean dressing. Then seek medical advice.
● If a friction blister filled with fluid causes significant discomfort (e.g. it is painful to walk) or
is at risk of self-draining, the first aider should consider draining it (except if the person
has a chronic disease such as diabetes). This may reduce the pain associated with the
blister. If drained, the blister should be covered with a clean dressing to ensure the roof
attaches to the underlying skin and that the blister does not refill with fluid and to avoid
infection

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Good practice points
● A small (up to two cm) friction blister can be punctured by a first aid provider, preferably
after cleaning the surface of the blister. Large friction blisters should be treated by a
medical professional.
● Materials like moleskin or commercial hydrocolloid blister-plasters may be applied to
minimize additional trauma to the blister and to relieve discomfort.
● If the person must walk to access help, avoid using a very sticky dressing, such as a
commercial hydrocolloid blister-plaster, as these are difficult to remove from the skin.
Removing the blister-plaster repeatedly can cause further damage. Walking for extended
periods also may allow bacteria to get under the blister bandage, increasing the risk of
infection.
● Treat an open friction blister as a cut or graze.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Prevent and prepare
● Before starting the activity, wear shoes that are well-fitting and do not rub. Protect the
parts of the feet or hands that are likely to rub by using a barrier over those areas. This
may include wearing dry socks or gloves, or taping parts of the feet or hands.
● Carry appropriate dressings if doing an activity likely to cause blisters.
● Repetitive activities increase the risk of blisters. Frequently check the areas of the skin
most likely to rub. Minimizing repetitive actions can decrease the chance of significant
friction blisters.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Early recognition
● The person has been doing an activity likely to cause continuous rubbing or pressure for
some time, which would irritate the skin.
● A small pocket of fluid can be seen in the upper layers of skin caused by the friction.
● Many blisters will self-drain if hands and feet continue to be used.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - First aid steps
1.
Wash the blister and the surrounding area with clean water and gently pat it dry.
2. If the blister is intact, cover it with moleskin or a blister pad. If the blister has self-drained,
clean the wound and cover it with a sterile dressing. A layer of moleskin or tape on top of
the dressing may help provide further padding if the person must walk on the blister.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Access help
● Seek medical advice:
○ if the blister becomes an open wound or shows signs of infection, such as
becoming hot and more painful
○ if the person has diabetes or their immune system is compromised. In these
people, wounds are more likely to become infected or have trouble healing.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Friction blisters - Recovery
● Monitor the blister over several days to check for signs of infection (such as heat,
continuous pain or onset of fever). If these appear, seek medical care immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Key action
Cool thermal burns with running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20 minutes.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Introduction
Four of the main causes of burns are heat (fire, steam), chemicals (acid), radiation (radioactive
materials, the sun, sunlamps) and electricity. Mild burns in adults generally do not require
medical care; however, even burns that appear small or mild can be very harmful to a baby, child
or the elderly. The depth and size of the burn determine its severity. It is important to note that
even after being removed from the burn source, the burning process can continue in the layers
of the skin.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Guidelines
Thermal burns
● Thermal (heat) burns should be cooled with running water for a minimum of ten
minutes, ideally 20 minutes.**
● After cooling, vaseline or honey may be beneficial substances to apply to a thermal burn.*
● Aftersun lotion (Hamamelis-free lotion), aftersun cream (e.g. aloe vera cream), or aftersun
gel (diclofenac 0.1% Emulgel) can be applied to sunburn according to the instructions and
may help reduce pain.*
Chemical burns
● Chemical burns on the skin or in the eyes should be rinsed with running water and, if
available, a solution (e.g. Dihoterine) that neutralizes and removes harmful chemicals
from the area. Rinse the area until the pain eases.*
Aftercare
● After cooling, a dressing that maintains moisture, contours easily to the wound and is
non-stick (e.g. hydrogel) should be used on burns.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Guidelines
● Silver sulfadiazine should not be used because it seems to be associated with poorer
healing outcomes than other treatments.*
● Blisters should not be deroofed or aspirated, as this may increase the risk of infection. If
they affect the function of the injured body part, the person should consider seeking
medical advice. See Friction blisters.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Good practice points
● When possible and safe to do so, the source of danger should be dealt with to prevent
further injury. For example, cover a pot of hot oil.
● The first aid provider should avoid direct contact with any chemical substances.
● If rinsing a chemical substance from the skin, the first aid provider should take care that
any diluted substance does not harm healthy tissue.
● Potable (clean) water should be used to rinse out eyes that have had contact with a
chemical substance.
● If a chemical substance was ingested, do not make any attempt to dilute it. Access the
poison control centre, emergency medical services (EMS) or local equivalent. See
Poisoning.
● If cold running water is not available, any cold liquid can be effective in cooling thermal
burns (e.g. juice, milk).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Good practice points
● As long as they are not stuck to the skin, clothing and jewellery on or near the burned skin
should be removed to support treatment and reduce further discomfort.
● Covering a burn with a clean wet cloth or plastic cling wrap can protect it during transit to
medical care. Cover rather than wrap an extremity as it may swell.
● If the burn is large, deep or close to the face, mouth/throat or genital area, or if it is the
result of chemical products, electricity or flames, the first aid provider should access EMS.
● If warmth or pain develops around the burn area, or the person develops a fever, this is an
indication of infection and the person should seek medical advice immediately.
● After cooling the burned area, honey, aloe vera or banana leaves can be used for aftercare.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Good practice points
● Young children with thermal burns being actively cooled with running water should be
monitored for signs and/or symptoms of excessive body cooling.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Prevent and prepare
● If possible, try to avoid cooking at floor level. If cooking at floor level, ensure small children
and babies are supervised and kept away from the fire (Bitter & Erickson, 2016; Forjuoh,
2006).
● Be cautious when using kerosene and heating devices as these can cause burns.
● Keep clothing away from flames and intense heat sources. Ensure the safe handling of
pressure stoves and coal-burning stoves. Construct kitchens safely, taking into account
the proximity of electric cables and fireplaces (Ghosh & Bharat, 2000).
● Place fire safety equipment (e.g. extinguishers, fire blankets or the local equivalent) in
high-risk areas, such as the cooking area, to limit the spread of fire and potential harm.
● Cover skin with long clothing, sunscreen (SPF 30 or more) or zinc oxide when in the sun.
● Avoid long periods in the sun. Choose a time of day to be outside when there is more
shade.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Prevent and prepare
● Wear protective equipment (e.g. gloves) when using chemical substances or hot objects.
● Review safety information on chemical products before use.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Early recognition
● Thermal burns caused by direct contact with a source of heat or chemical burns will
immediately be sore and the skin may react with blisters or irritation after contact with a
chemical.
● The injured person may tell you or indicate they have been burned.
● Burns vary in size and depth. Do not delay treatment. There are several methods used to
recognize the severity of a burn such as the Wallace scale; however, we have no evidence
on which is most effective.
● Sunburn can occur quite quickly or over a longer period. The person may not notice they
are getting sunburned until they see a change in their skin colour or realize the area is
painful.
● Note the age of the person and the location of the burn, as these will impact the severity
of the burn.
● Be aware that burns may appear different on different skin tones.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - First aid steps
1.
Cool the burn with clean running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20 minutes.
2. Access EMS if the burn is large, deep or close to the face, mouth, throat or genital area, or
if it is the result of chemical products, electricity or flames.
3. As long as they are not stuck to the skin, remove any clothing and jewellery on or near the
burned skin. It will be much harder to remove jewellery once the inflammatory process
has set in.
4. After cooling, cover the wound with a dressing that maintains moisture, contours easily to
the wound and is non-stick (e.g.hydrogel).
5. If necessary, cover the burn with a wet cloth or plastic cling wrap while transporting the
person to medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - First aid steps
6. Reassure the person and monitor their responsiveness, breathing and temperature,
especially if it is a child or a vulnerable person (e.g. older adult, person with diabetes).
During cooling, letting the water flow over the burn may be more comfortable for the person
than aiming the water flow directly on top of the burn. Do not use ice-cold water, as this may
lead to hypothermia, particularly in children or in the case of large burns.
Do not apply ice, as this may aggravate the injury.
For burns on the fingers, place a clean, moist cloth or sterile gauze between the fingers to
keep them from sticking together. This is especially important for severe burns.
If the burn has blisters, leave them intact and seek medical advice.
If the burn is large, there is a risk that the person will develop Shock. To help a person with
shock, it is necessary to assist them to lie down and keep them warm. If possible, prevent the
burn from coming into contact with the ground to keep the burn clean.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Local adaptation
● If there is no running water available, use alternative cool liquids (juice, milk) to cool the
burn.
● If water or other liquid is in short supply, put a bowl under the burn and pour the liquid
over the burn into the bowl so that the water can be used again. This is more effective
than putting the burn into the bowl of water as the body part will warm the water.
Pouring it keeps the water temperature lower.
● If there is no dressing available, use locally available substances such as aloe vera, honey
or banana leaves to dress the burn.
Chemical burn to eye
● In the case of a chemical burn to the eye, immediately rinse the eye with sterile saline eye
wash devices or clean running water. If only one eye is injured, be careful not to
contaminate the other eye when rinsing.
● Remove any contact lenses during the rinse.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Local adaptation
● When rinsing a chemical substance, take care that the now diluted substance does not
harm you or the person’s healthy tissue by making contact with unaffected skin or the
uninjured eye.
● Use diphoterine for cooling if available, following the instructions on the container.
● Do NOT apply any other products without consulting medical care.
Sunburn
● Apply aftersun lotion according to the instructions.
● If the sunburn is extensive or if it happens to a baby or a vulnerable person (e.g. older
adult, person with diabetes), access medical care as quickly as possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Access help
● If the burn is large, deep or close to the face, mouth, throat or genital area, or it is the
result of chemical products, electricity or flames, access EMS or the nearest medical care.
● Seek medical advice if the burn happens to a baby or a vulnerable person.
● In the case of a chemical burn to the eye, be aware that the person will need some
assistance. They should not drive a vehicle themselves.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Burns - Recovery
● Monitor for signs of infection. If warmth or pain develops around the site of the burn, seek
medical advice.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Flash eye - Introduction
Flash eye, also called snow blindness or arc eye, is a painful condition in the eyes caused by
overexposure to ultraviolet (UV) light. It is like the cornea (the transparent outer layer of the eye)
has a sunburn. Flash eye is most likely to happen to people who take part in outdoor sports or
activities in relatively high altitudes or at sea, where surfaces reflect light into the eyes. At high
altitudes, there is less air to filter light and so it is much more intense. Man-made sources of UV
radiation, such as a welder’s torch or sun lamps, have the same effect.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Flash eye - Good practice points
● If applicable, the person should remove their contact lenses.
● The person should protect their eyes and let them rest as much as possible, by:
○ staying indoors and wearing sunglasses to relieve pain or discomfort
○ keeping their eyes closed as much as possible
○ covering their closed eyelids with a cool, damp cloth.
● The person’s eyes should stay moist (e.g. using saline solution or eye drops).
● The person should avoid rubbing their eyes.
● If symptoms last longer than a day or if they worsen, the person should seek medical
advice.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Flash eye - Prevent and prepare
● Wear protective eye gear when in the sun or undertaking tasks that expose the eyes to
UV light. Protect the eyes from direct or indirect radiation that might reach them from
above and below, as well as sideways.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Flash eye - Early recognition
The person may have:
● a feeling that something is in their eyes
● a burning sensation in their eyes
● blurred or loss of vision
● red and watery eyes
● sensitivity to light
● headaches
● swelling around the eyes.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Flash eye - First aid steps
1.
Move the person away from the source of light and reassure them.
2. If they are wearing contact lenses, advise them to remove them.
3. Help them protect their eyes and let them rest as much as possible by:
a. staying indoors and wearing sunglasses to relieve pain or discomfort
b. keeping their eyes closed as much as possible
c. covering their closed eyelids with a cool, damp cloth
d. putting saline solution or eye drops in their eyes to keep them moist.
4. If their condition does not improve in 24 hours, seek medical advice.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Flash eye - Access help
● Flash eye usually passes, but if it lasts longer than a day or the symptoms worsen, access
medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Introduction
Sprains and strains are considered minor injuries, while fractures can range from minor to major.
While often not life-threatening, injuries to the extremities (arms, legs, fingers or toes) can lead
to disabilities if left untreated. A fractured bone is often painful and can cause internal or
external bleeding (when the broken bone breaks through the skin). If a long bone is injured,
such as the femur, the bleeding from the bone itself can be life-threatening. See also spine
injuries.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Good practice points
● Any injury to an extremity should be approached as a potential bone fracture.
● The injury should be stabilized to minimize any movement and pain either manually (e.g.
self-splinting) or mechanically (e.g. using a sling and bandages).
● As soon as possible, first aid providers may ice or cool the sprained joint or soft tissue
injury for up to 20 consecutive minutes, as this may decrease the pain. Cooling for longer
than this may damage the skin.
● A compression dressing may be applied to a strain or sprain if this provides comfort.
● All fractures should be assessed for internal and external bleeding and the injured person
treated for Shock, especially if the fracture involves long bones such as the femur.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Good practice points
● In situations where the injured person must be moved, and transport is expected to be
bumpy or jarring, first aid providers should protect the limb (particularly a leg) by
splinting. Splinting should be done in a way that limits pain, reduces chances for further
injury and facilitates safe and quick transport.
● When in a remote environment (or one with limited resources) and the limb below the
angulated fracture is cool, pale or the first aid provider is unable to splint for movement,
the first aid provider may consider straightening it if trained to do so.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Prevent and prepare
● Be prepared to care for fractures, sprains and strains in the context in which they occur.
For example, sprains and strains are common in sports and it is advised to have cooling
therapy equipment (e.g. ice packs) available. Conversely, if going on a trip to a remote
location, find out about local rescue organizations and practise immobilizing limbs before
the trip.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Early recognition
The person may have twisted a limb, fallen or taken a blow from an object.
The person may have:
● deformity, swelling, haematoma or bruising at the site of the injury
● pain and or difficulty in moving the body part
● shortening, twisting or bending of the limb
● a broken bone or bone fragments sticking out of the skin
● the sound of a snap or a pop when the injury happened
● a sensation or sound of bones grating.
First aid providers are not expected to be able to diagnose whether a person has a fracture or a
sprain or a strain. The only accurate way to diagnose a fracture is with an X-ray. When in doubt,
assume it is a fracture.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - First aid steps
1.
Help the person keep the injury still.
2. Support the injury in a comfortable position to prevent any movement. Keeping the limb
elevated may help reduce swelling.
3. Apply ice or something cold for up to 20 minutes. Cooling for longer than this may
damage the skin. Ask the person to rest.
4. Access emergency medical services (EMS) if the person has a lot of pain or swelling, signs
of shock, the fracture is in the femur or if the limb is in an abnormal position.
5. Reassure the person and ensure they are comfortable.
● There are many instances when the use of ice or something cold may benefit bruising,
strains, sprains, dislocations, haematoma, swelling or closed fractures.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - First aid steps
● To be effective, the application of ice or something cold must be done as soon as
possible after the trauma. Stop cooling if the person finds it too painful. If the pain
returns and the skin’s temperature has come back to normal, you may start cooling
again.
● Dislocations and fractures should always be treated by a medical professional.
● If the injury is an open fracture, your priority is to stop the bleeding and limit infection. As
for any fracture, stabilize the limb. Treat the person for Shock.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - CAUTION
● Always wrap an icepack in a cloth to avoid damage to the skin.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Local adaptation
● In remote areas where the injured person must be moved a long distance over bumpy
terrain, protect the limb by splinting it in a way that limits pain, reduces chances for
further injury and facilitates safe and quick transport.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Access help
● If you are in doubt whether the injury is a fracture, sprain or strain, access medical care.
● Record the time of injury, as this information can be helpful for medical professionals
when comparing the injured limb to the healthy one.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fractures, sprains and strains - Recovery
● Mobilization exercises can help with recovery from a sprain or strain; however, avoid
weight-bearing exercises as these could worsen the condition (CEBaP review, 2015).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Key action
Help the person to keep as still as possible to prevent further damage to their spine.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Introduction
Spinal injuries can be caused by falling or diving from a height, being crushed by machinery or a
heavy object, or being involved in road traffic collisions or sporting accidents. Spinal injuries can
result in damage that can be permanent and may include disability, such as the loss of use of
the arms or legs. Ensuring normal breathing and blood circulation of the person with a
suspected spinal injury remains vital to their survival.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Guidelines
● First aid providers should not apply a cervical collar.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Good practice points
● The person may have a suspected spinal injury if they have been involved in a traumatic
incident, such as being the driver, passenger or pedestrian in a motor vehicle or bicycle
collision, or they have fallen from a height greater than standing.
● A person experiencing the following signs or symptoms following a traumatic incident
may have a spinal injury:
○ tingling sensation in the extremities or other parts of the body
○ pain or tenderness in the neck or back
○ an obvious deformity to the head, neck or spine
○ other painful injuries, especially at the head or neck
○ Loss of sensation or weakness in the torso or arms.
● First aid providers should always access emergency medical services (EMS) when
suspecting a spinal injury.
● A person with a suspected spinal injury who is alert and awake should keep as still as
possible and may not require manual stabilization.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Good practice points
● A person with a suspected spinal injury who is not sufficiently alert or awake may benefit
from gentle support of the head (manual stabilization) to prevent inadvertent movement.
First aid providers should not strap the person’s head or neck.
● A person with a suspected spinal injury who is unresponsive but breathing normally
should only be moved once EMS arrives or if they are in harm’s way. The first aid provider
should open the person’s airway and monitor their breathing.
● In cases of suspected spinal injury, a head injury should also be considered.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Prevent and prepare
● Promote and practise safe behaviours, such as wearing a seatbelt and using a headrest
when travelling by car or wearing back protection when travelling by motorcycle or horse.
● Players should not play sports if they experience spinal pain.
● Junior sports coaches should consider when the introduction of tackling is appropriate
and should endeavour to teach the correct technique (Harmon et al., 2019).
● Remove trip hazards from places of work and home, particularly where elderly people or
people with a disability live, to reduce the chance of trips and falls.
● Always ensure ladders are stabilized before climbing them.
● Supervise children who are climbing on frames or furniture.
● Never dive into shallow water, or water with an obstructed view or high flow (e.g. rivers)
● Take particular care when diving into water in the dark.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Early recognition
● You may suspect a spinal injury if the injured person has:
○ fallen from a height greater than standing height
○ been involved in a road traffic collision
○ injured their head while diving headfirst into shallow water
○ been involved in a traumatic event (e.g. explosion or mechanical incident).
Older adults (over the age of 65) and people with an underlying bone condition may be more
susceptible to spinal injuries following minor traumas such as a slip, trip or fall.
The person may also have:
● a tingling sensation in their arms or legs or other parts of the body
● pain or tenderness in their neck or back
● obvious deformity to their head, neck or spine
● other painful injuries, especially at the head or neck

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Early recognition
● sensory deficit (e.g. numbness) or muscle weakness (e.g. paralysis) in the torso or upper
extremities. This may be accompanied by loss of control of urine or stool.
However, some people with a spinal injury may not experience any symptoms.
Be alert as babies and young children may be unable to recognize they have a spinal injury.
Likewise, someone with an altered mental status (under the influence of alcohol or substances)
may be less likely to be able to recognize they have a spinal injury.
Pelvic fracture
First aid providers need specific training to recognize a pelvic fracture. Pelvic fracture may be
associated with spinal injury.
A person with a pelvic fracture may:
● Experience pain at the hip, pelvis, groin or even the knee. This gets worse when moving.
● Not be able to support their legs. Sometimes, the foot (on the side of the fracture) is in an
abnormal position.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Early recognition
● Experience sensory disturbances and tingling sensations in the legs.
● No longer be able to pass urine. Sometimes, there is a spontaneous loss of urine. In some
cases, there is blood in the urine.
● Show signs of shock.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - First aid steps
1.
If the person is responsive and alert, reassure them and ask them to stay as still as
possible. If the person is a child, has an altered level of consciousness or does not follow
instructions, gently support their head to keep the neck and spine from moving.
2. Access EMS.
3. Ensure minimal handling or movement of the person at all times. Monitor their breathing
and level of response for any changes.
4. Reduce shock symptoms by maintaining a normal body temperature.
● Do not move the person if you suspect a spinal injury.
● If the person must be moved (e.g. due to danger), it is best done with at least two first aid
providers, with one keeping the person’s head in line with their spine.
An unresponsive and breathing person with suspected spinal injury
If the person is unresponsive and breathing normally:
1.
Leave the person as you have found them (e.g. on their back or side).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - First aid steps
2. Maintain an open airway using the head tilt/chin lift or jaw thrust manoeuvre. The jaw
thrust manoeuvre may cause less spinal motion.
3. Gently support their head in this position to prevent any movement.
4. Access EMS and follow their instructions.
5. Monitor their breathing and level of response for any changes.
Pelvic fracture
1.
Help the person to lie down on their back and to keep still with their legs straight.
2. Place padding between their legs and then immobilize their legs by binding them
together at their knees and feet.
3. Access EMS.
4. Monitor the person’s breathing, circulation and level of response, particularly looking for
any signs of shock.
If you suspect a pelvic fracture, do not “rock” or rotate the pelvis as this can restart or worsen
bleeding.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Spinal injury - Access help
Injuries to the spine may be difficult to confirm and difficult to manage in out-of-hospital
settings. Help should be sought as soon as possible if an injury to the spine is suspected.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Key action
Remove the person from their activity and observe them for signs of a concussion or other brain
injury.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Introduction
Head injuries are common across all age groups, but particularly in young children,
sportspeople and older adults. They can range from being minor (requiring rest and pain relief)
to severe (becoming unresponsive and requiring medical care). A concussion is a common type
of head injury. It can be difficult to identify a concussion because there are many signs and
symptoms which vary and are not always immediately apparent. In addition, some people do
not recognize or admit to experiencing symptoms of a concussion. This can lead to a delay in
proper treatment or accessing medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Good practice points
● It is critical that a concussion is recognized and managed appropriately.
● Any person suspected of sustaining a head trauma (a forceful bump, blow or jolt to the
head or body that results in the rapid movement of the head and brain), along with any of
the signs of a concussion, must be presumed to have a severe head injury or concussion.
● When attempting to determine if a concussion has occurred first aid providers may
consider utilizing a three-question screening process.
1.
Did a potential injury occur?
2. Was the mechanism associated with a potential head injury?
3. Was there any altered mental status?
● If the answer to all three questions is “yes,” these individuals should be removed from the
activity and EMS should be activated, or the person should be referred to a qualified
healthcare professional.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Good practice points
● Since concussion symptoms vary, first aid providers who are unsure if a concussion
occurred may consider removing the individual from the activity until a qualified
healthcare professional can evaluate them.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Good practice points
● Emergency medical care should be accessed immediately following a blow to the head if
the person:
a. becomes unresponsive, even for just a few seconds
b. has an altered mental status (e.g. they become aggressive, have slurred speech,
have a seizure; children may have an abnormal attitude or be very quiet and stop
playing)
c. has a motor or sensory deficit of one or more limbs (e.g. tingling in a limb, or
balance or coordination problems)
d. has a severe headache for more than two hours despite taking pain relief
e. has impaired vision (e.g. sensitivity to light, blurred or double vision)
f.
has blood or a clear fluid coming out of their nose, ear or mouth
g. vomits more than once
h. is unresponsive with abnormal breathing.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Good practice points
● If the person has a mild headache, a bump on their head or feels nauseous following a
blow to the head, they may rest and continue to be observed for any change to their
symptoms or behaviour requiring medical care.
● If the person shows none of these signs following a blow to the head, they may carry on
with their day, but should be observed in case any of the above signs develop over the
next 24 hours.
● In instances of head injury, a Spinal injury should also be considered.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Prevent and prepare
● Promote and practise safe behaviours, such as wearing a seatbelt and using a headrest
when travelling by car or wearing a helmet when travelling by motorcycle, bicycle or
horse.
● Consider athletic body protection (i.e. helmets, face masks) when participating in contact
sports. Sports coaches should be aware of the risks, and players should discontinue their
involvement in sports if a head or spine injury is suspected.
● Junior sports should consider at what age the introduction of tackling is appropriate and
should endeavour to teach correct techniques (Harmon et al., 2019).
● Remove trip hazards from places of work and home, particularly where there are small
children, elderly people or people with disabilities to reduce the chance of trips and falls.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Prevent and prepare
● Never dive into shallow water, or water with an obstructed view or high flow (e.g. rivers)
and take particular care when diving in the dark.
● Learn how to recognize the signs of a concussion.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Early recognition
The person has a forceful bump, blow or jolt to the head or body that results in the rapid
movement of the head and brain. This could include incidents such as a fall, a road traffic
accident or an explosion.
Mild head injury:
● a bump on their head.
● a mild headache.
● feels nauseous.
● bleeding.
If the person has a mild headache or feels nauseous following a blow to the head, they may rest
and continue to be observed for any change to their symptoms or behaviour requiring medical
care.
Severe head injury (or concussion):
● becomes unresponsive, even for just a few seconds
● has an altered mental status (e.g. they become aggressive, have slurred speech, have a
seizure; children may have an abnormal attitude or be very quiet and stop playing)
● has a motor or sensory deficit of one or more limbs (e.g. tingling in a limb, or balance or
coordination problems)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Early recognition
● has a severe headache for more than two hours despite taking pain relief
● has impaired vision (e.g. sensitivity to light, blurred or double vision)
● has blood or a clear fluid coming out of their nose, ear or mouth.
● vomits more than once
● is unresponsive with abnormal breathing.
Other signs could also indicate a head injury and the signs may present differently in people.
The main thing to look for is a change in the person. The signs of a severe head injury can
happen immediately or can develop over several hours or days.
The possibility of a spinal injury should always be considered in the case of a forceful impact or
fall.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - First aid steps
1.
Remove the person from their activity and ask them to rest.
2. Monitor the person for signs of a concussion and changes in their level of response and
breathing.
3. If the head injury is severe:
○ Access emergency medical services (EMS).
○ Reassure the person and encourage them to keep their head and neck as still as
possible. If the person is lying down, you may also use your hands or knees to keep
their head as still as possible.
○ Monitor the person’s level of response and breathing until EMS arrive.
Every bump or knock to the head does not cause a concussion or other severe head injury.
If the person has had a blow to the head but the signs are not present or are mild, help
them rest and then continue with their day, treating any minor injuries (e.g. bleeding from
the cheek). However, they should be observed as a concussion can develop over several
hours or days.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Access help
● Observe the person for signs of concussion and access help if any of the signs are present.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Head injury and concussion - Recovery
● In many cases, rest from activity is the most effective initial treatment. However, injuries to
the head are difficult to confirm and difficult to manage in out-of-hospital settings.
● Signs and symptoms of a head injury should have been resolved before returning to
activities with associated risks (e.g. some work activities, driving or operating machinery or
contact sports).
● Be aware that normal cognitive function may take time to be fully restored and that there
may be residual learning and behavioural challenges in the short term (Harmon et al.,
2019).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Key action
Help the person take the recommended dose of painkiller or apply heat wrap therapy to relieve
back pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Introduction
Lower back pain is common, and many adults experience it at some point in their lives.
Common causes of back pain include injuries to the soft tissues in the back, such as muscles or
ligaments. These injuries can result from lifting heavy objects or stress to the body from
repetitive actions or positions. These guidelines focus on the management of acute lower back
pain from low-risk injuries, such as the ones listed previously.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Guidelines
● When lifting heavy objects, people should bend their knees and keep their back straight
to prevent lower back pain.*
● Paracetamol (also known as acetaminophen) may be effective at relieving some subsets
of acute lower back pain.*
● Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen) may be effective at
relieving acute lower back pain but may cause side effects, including gastric irritation,
potential kidney interactions and high blood pressure.*
● Heat or cold application may provide short-term pain relief and reduce disability in those
with a combination of acute and subacute (pain that continues between four to 12 weeks)
low back pain.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Good practice points
● The person should sit or lie down in a position most comfortable to them.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Prevent and prepare
● Exercise regularly.
● If working at a desk, use an ergonomic chair.
● Learn how to reduce the risks of lower back pain.
● Lift items by bending the knees and keeping the back straight.
● Wear a combination of accessories to protect the back, such as back belts or shoe insoles.
● Change positions regularly and avoid holding a certain position or movement for too
long.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Early recognition
The person was involved in a high-speed, direct impact incident, or may have been using their
back for physical activity such as lifting or stretching. They may experience:
● sudden back pain
● back pain combined with neck pain or a tingling feeling running down the back of one
leg
● sudden inability to walk due to lower back pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - First aid steps
1.
Comfort and reassure the person.
2. Determine the cause of the back pain. If it is the result of a fall or other traumatic incident,
follow the first aid steps for Spinal injury.
3. Help the person move into a comfortable position and take the recommended dose of
painkiller (such as paracetamol or ibuprofen).
4. Apply a heat source (e.g. heating pad) or cold source to the lower back.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Access help
● Access emergency medical care if the acute lower back pain is severe or the result of a
traumatic incident (e.g. a fall or car accident).
● The person should seek medical advice if the back pain:
○ is related to an incident that occurred some time ago (e.g. car accident), or they
have been experiencing it for four weeks or more
○ spreads to one leg, especially if the leg feels weak
○ is combined with weak legs, sensory disturbances, or the person experiences
bladder or bowel problems, or issues with sexual functionality
○ is in combination with a fever.
The person should seek medical advice if they have a history of cancer, a weakened immune
system, osteoporosis or have used steroids (e.g. prednisolone) for a long time.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute lower back pain - Recovery
● If the back pain does not improve within four weeks, seek medical advice.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Key action
Clean the bite wound by rinsing it with clean water as quickly as possible to minimize the risk of
infection.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Introduction
Bites and scratches from mammals, such as dogs, cats, monkeys, camels, bats and humans, are
common and can cause infections. Most animal bites in adults and children are from dogs, and
young children are most likely to be bitten by an animal they know. Adults are more likely to be
bitten on the hand or wrist, while children more often receive bites on the face or neck (Elcock et
al., 2022; Ortiz & Lezcano, 2023). There are 4.5 million people bitten by dogs every year, with
885,000 seeking medical care, and cat bites make up to 50%of animal-bite injuries across the
world (World Health Organization, 2018). Bacteria can cause skin infections or complications to
the whole body, such as sepsis or tetanus. Depending on the local context, first aid providers
may also need to consider the risk of rabies.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Good practice points
● People should avoid approaching stray or wild animals and take extra care to keep from
getting bitten.
● Bleeding from an animal bite should be treated as per the guidelines for severe bleeding.
● Depending on availability, the first aid provider should clean the wound with either
potable (clean) water, saline or soap and water. Ideally, human and animal bite wounds
should be cleaned with potable water and soap to minimize the risk of bacterial and
rabies infections.
● The person should seek further medical care as soon as possible if vaccination is required
or if the wound is open or deep.
● If available, a water source should be used to clean the bite area (e.g. from a tap, squirting
device or water bottle).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Good practice points
● If warmth or pain develops around the bite area, this is an indication of infection and the
person should seek medical care immediately. The bite area should be monitored as
infection can happen in the hours or days after the bite occurs.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Prevent and prepare
● Avoid approaching stray or wild animals.
● If there is a prevalence of rabies in the area, people should follow the advice of local health
authorities.
● Be aware of specific diseases transmitted by animals in your area (rabies, anthrax,
hantavirus, bovine encephalopathy, etc.).
● Always supervise babies and children around animals.
● Teach children how to behave safely around animals. If in a new environment, ask local
people for advice on how to behave around the animals located there. Animals often bite
as a reaction to human behaviour they perceive as threatening.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Early recognition
● The person tells you they were bitten by an animal or human.
● The person has visible teeth marks on their skin.
● Crush injuries or skin, muscle or soft tissue that has been ripped open may indicate dog
bites, while deeper puncture wounds usually indicate cat bites.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - First aid steps
1.
If the wound is bleeding, apply pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding. Follow the
steps for severe bleeding. Once the bleeding has stopped, follow the first aid steps for
cuts and grazes.
Animal bites can transmit a number of diseases, such as Bartonellosis (transmitted by cats) or
Herpes B (transmitted by monkeys).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Access help
● Seek further medical care as soon as possible if skin closure is required.
● If the injured person has not been vaccinated against tetanus, seek further medical care.
● If the bite came from a wild animal, rabies is common in the area and the injured person
has not been vaccinated against it, seek further medical care.
● Monitor for signs of infection. If warmth or pain develops around the bite area, seek
medical advice.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Mammal bites - Recovery
● Change the dressing on the bite area as necessary.
● Seek psychological support if necessary.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Key action
Remove the stinger or insect from the person to prevent the further spread of venom or disease.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Introduction
Insect bites and stings can transmit diseases (such as malaria, encephalitis or Lyme disease) and
can cause wounds that can become infected. Certain insect bites and stings can also cause an
allergic reaction in individuals who have been bitten or stung before.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Guidelines
● A bee’s stinger should be removed as soon as possible.*
● A tick may be removed with tweezers or by using a commercial tick removal device,
according to the manufacturer’s instructions.*
● The following tick-removal methods must be avoided: using gasoline, petroleum or other
solvents to suffocate the tick, using ice and burning the tick with a match.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Good practice points
● If no commercial tick removal device is available, the first aid provider may grab a tick as
close to the skin as possible with very fine forceps or tweezers and pull it gradually and
firmly out of the skin.
● To remove a stinger from a person, the first aid provider may gently scrape the sting area
with a flat object, such as a bank card or butter knife. Using tweezers or any other object
that can pierce or press down on the venom bag should be avoided, as this may
aggravate the symptoms.
● The bitten or stung area should be thoroughly cleaned with potable (clean) water and
then an antiseptic solution. If no clean water is available, use an antiseptic solution.
● In the case of a bite or sting to the throat or mouth that starts to swell, the first aid
provider should immediately access emergency medical services (EMS) and apply ice to
the affected area to reduce the swelling.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Good practice points
● First aid providers should monitor the person for signs of an allergic reaction or
anaphylaxis and provide the appropriate care.
● The person should avoid scratching the bite as this can cause an infection, especially if the
fingernails are dirty.
● The skin may become redder, purple or darker, as well as warm and painful at the site of
an insect bite or sting. This should improve over a day or two. However, if it gets worse, the
person should seek medical advice, as this could be a sign of infection. Antibiotics or
vaccinations may be needed.
● Travellers should check to see what insect-related risks are prevalent in the area to which
they are travelling and seek medical advice. They may need vaccinations or medication
before leaving home.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Prevent and prepare
● To prevent diseases caused by insects, such as malaria and Lyme disease, use insect
repellent and mosquito nets, and promptly remove any ticks.
● Avoid tick-infested areas and wear long clothing in a "downward cascade" configuration.
● Consult local authorities for information on landscaping and pest management to
support any locally recommended behaviour or places to avoid to reduce risk.
● In some countries, per local regulations, report any tick bites to the authorities. Some
authorities request that you send the biting tick or ticks for identification and testing.
● Consider using anti-malarial medication when travelling. Consult a medical professional
for the recommended medication.
In first aid education, explore the following information with learners on avoiding bites and the
behaviours to adopt during an insect attack:

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Prevent and prepare
● Keep away from flowering plants, ripe fruit bushes and trees, rotten fruit, compost and
food waste. If this is not possible, wear long trousers and long-sleeved clothes and cover
your hands and face.
● Wear shoes when walking outside, particularly on grass or flowering ground.
● When outside, cover your drinks and food and check them before drinking or eating.
● Wipe off any food from the clothes, hands and faces of children, as this may attract bees
or wasps.
● Before moving objects with your hands (such as containers that have been left outside),
check underneath and inside them for insects that may bite or sting.
● Shake out shoes, socks and clothing before putting them on to remove any insects.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Prevent and prepare
● Do not touch or disturb bee or wasp hives. If you want to harvest honey, protect yourself
by wearing long trousers and long-sleeved clothes and cover your hands and face as
much as possible.
● Remain calm if attacked by a bee or wasp, as they react to movement. Do not wave your
hands in an attempt to brush them away.
● Run and find shelter if attacked by a swarm.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Early recognition
A tick bite is not painful and is often not detected, or only discovered by accident. Initially, many
ticks are only a pinhead in size, making it difficult to spot. An engorged tick is about the size of a
small pea. After a few hours, the bite may start to itch.
A person who is bitten or stung by an insect may experience:
● initial sharp pain
● swelling, itching or a rash at the site of the bite or sting.
The person may develop a mild or severe allergic reaction following an insect bite or sting.
Observe the person closely for any development of an allergic reaction. A rash can be more
difficult to see on black or brown skin (Nolen, 2020). Checking lighter areas of skin, such as the
palms of hands or soles of feet, may help you to see it.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - First aid steps
Tick bite
1.
Reassure the person and remove the tick as quickly as you can. Use a manufactured tick
removal device to remove the tick according to the manufacturer’s instructions. If a
manufactured device is not available, use tweezers to grab the tick as close to the skin as
possible and pull it gradually and firmly out of the skin.
2. Wash the site of the bite with soap and water. See cuts and grazes.
3. Write down the date and the area where the person was bitten in order to monitor the
area around the bite.
4. Seek medical advice if there is concern about an infection (fever, inexplicable fatigue or
joint pain) or if a rash appears. The Lyme disease rash is a circular rash that appears as a
patch surrounded by a ring. However, this "classic bull's-eye" rash does not always appear.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - CAUTION
● Do not squeeze the body of the insect, as this may trigger the release of the
disease-causing organisms onto the skin.
● Do not use chemicals or heat to numb or kill the tick.
● Note that insect bites are treated differently from snakebites.
Other insect bite or sting
1.
Reassure the person and advise them not to scratch, as this may aggravate the injury.
2. If the stinger is still in the person, remove it as quickly as possible. Gently scrape the area
with a flat object, such as a bank card or the blunt side of a knife.
3. Thoroughly clean the site of the bite or sting with water. If no clean water is available, use
an antiseptic solution.
4. Cool the stung area with ice cubes in a bag of water or a cooling bag to limit swelling,
itching and pain. If the sting is on the hand, remove the rings.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - CAUTION
When removing the stinger, avoid using tweezers, your fingers or any other object that can
pierce or press down on the venom bag, as this will make symptoms worse.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Access help
● Access EMS immediately if:
○ The person is bitten or stung in the mouth or on the throat. It can be dangerous as
any swelling could block their airway. While waiting for medical care, try to cool the
injured area with ice (e.g. by letting the person suck on an ice cube) to reduce
swelling.
○ The person shows any signs of a severe allergic reaction.
● Access medical care if:
○ The stinger will not come out.
○ The person develops a painful, itchy swelling or a rash.
○ The person feels progressively worse after being bitten or stung (this can occur up
to 24 hours after the bite or sting).
○ The person was bitten or stung many times.
○ The person suspects he is not sufficiently protected from tetanus.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Insect bites or stings - Recovery
● Monitor for signs of infection. The skin may become red, purple or darker, as well as warm
and painful at the site of an insect bite or sting. This should improve over the course of a
day or two. However, if it gets progressively worse, the person should seek medical advice,
as this could be a sign of infection.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Key action
Rinse the area with seawater to reduce pain and remove any stinging cells from the skin.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Introduction
Aquatic animals include those found in both salt and freshwater. Most are harmless; however,
some jellyfish and venomous fish can produce stings that are painful and cause minor or severe
allergic reactions. Stinging injuries are a common occurrence on many beaches worldwide and
are problematic for people whose livelihoods depend on activities in which they can be stung.
For bite injuries from a non-venomous aquatic animal, see cuts and grazes or severe bleeding.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Guidelines
● Rinse the area that was stung with seawater.**
● For non-life-threatening jellyfish envenomation, either rinsing with, showering or placing
the area that was stung in heated water (40-45° C, 104-113° F) may relieve the pain.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Good practice points
● First aid providers should protect themselves from being stung when removing any
tentacles or stinging cells from the skin.
● First aiders should remove all stinging cells from a jellyfish from the skin. They may cover
the stinging cells with sand or shaving foam and then scrape the cells off with cardboard
or a bank card.
● To remove visible jellyfish tentacles, use tweezers.
● The first aid provider may place the injury in heated water (up to a maximum of
45°C/113°F) for at least 20 to 30 minutes or apply a heat pack.
● If a heat pack or hot water are not available, it is reasonable to apply a cold pack to relieve
the pain.
● The choice of an agent applied to a jellyfish injury should be specific to the jellyfish.
○ Salt water may relieve pain from some jellyfish stings.
○ Vinegar may relieve pain for some jellyfish stings (e.g. box jellyfish).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Good practice points
● Avoid using aluminium sulphate, meat tenderizer or cold fresh water for pain relief.
● First aid providers should discourage the person from rubbing the site of the injury.
● In areas with deadly aquatic animals, when a person has been bitten or stung, medical
care should be accessed immediately. This is also the case if the person experiences any
signs of a severe allergic reaction. First aid providers should assess the person’s airway,
breathing and circulation while providing care for any other symptoms caused by the
injury.
● There is a risk of tetanus from an aquatic animal injury, so tetanus vaccinations might be
suitable as a preventive measure.
● The injury should be monitored as infection can happen in the hours or days after the bite
occurs.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Good practice points
● If warmth or pain develop around the site of the injury after the initial first aid treatment,
this is an indication of infection and the person should seek medical advice immediately.
If injured by a sea urchin or sea star, the first aid provider should remove all foreign
material. Clean the injury with soap and fresh water. Seek medical attention if a spine has
punctured the person’s joint.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Prevent and prepare
● Injuries from venomous marine and freshwater animals can be related to livelihoods and
economic activity in addition to tourism and leisure, so target preventive measures and
education at local people at risk as well as visitors.
● For people at risk, protective clothing should be worn.
● Follow local guidelines about the risks of entering the water.
● Even if dead, a jellyfish can still sting due to the small capsules in the stinging cells of their
tentacles (nemotocysts).
● Be aware when near stingrays. A stingray injury is caused by the venomous tail spines and
depending on its size, usually stings people in the lower limb region.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Early recognition
The person has pain associated with puncture wounds from the stinging cells. You may be able
to see stinging cells attached to the skin.
For a stingray injury, symptoms may include extreme pain, muscle cramps and a laceration at
the site of the injury.
The person may develop a mild or severe allergic reaction following a sting. See Allergic reaction
and anaphylaxis. Observe the person closely for any development of an allergic reaction. A rash
can be more difficult to see on black or brown skin (Nolen, 2020). Checking lighter areas of skin,
such as the palms of hands or soles of feet, may help you to see it.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - First aid steps
1.
Remove all the stinging cells from the person’s skin. Protect yourself from being stung as
you do this.
2. Rinse the area of the sting with seawater.
3. If possible, apply heat such as warm water, a heat pack or ash (up to a maximum of
45°C/113°F) to the site of the injury for 20-30 minutes. You could also immerse the injury in
the water. The temperature of the water is hot enough to relieve pain, but should not
burn the skin or cause pain to other uninjured areas of the skin.
4. Advise the person to seek medical care if there is a risk of tetanus or persistent pain that is
not relieved by treatment.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Access help
● If the sting injury is from a deadly species of aquatic animal, or if there is any doubt,
access emergency medical services (EMS) immediately.
● If the person experiences a severe allergic reaction, access help immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Aquatic animal injuries - Recovery
Monitor for signs of infection. The skin may become red, purple or darker, as well as warm and
painful at the site of the sting. This should improve over the course of a day or two. However, if it
gets progressively worse, the person should seek medical advice as this could be a sign of
infection.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Key action
Help the person keep as still as possible to slow the spread of the venom.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Introduction
Most snakes are harmless to humans, but some are venomous. A venomous snake injects
venom through its fangs, and the bite can be life-threatening. Identifying the type of snake will
help medical professionals determine whether the snake is venomous, the type of venom
produced and the best way to help the person who has been bitten.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Guidelines
● Limb injuries can be kept still as much as possible to slow the spread of venom. For a bite
to the arm, use a sling. For a bite to a lower limb, advise the person to limit any
movement, including walking.*
● If they are properly trained to do so, first aid providers may use the pressure
immobilization technique, by firmly applying a cotton or rubber pad under a non-elastic
bandage for special situations such as remote locations and wilderness environments.*
● A tourniquet should not be applied to snake envenomation because it may not be
effective and may result in an extended hospital stay.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Good practice points
● The person should limit physical activity to prevent the spread of toxins. If the bite is on
the person’s leg, they should not walk on the immobilized leg unless no other option is
available.
● It is reasonable to keep the injured area at or lower than the level of the heart.
● It is reasonable to remove jewellery, watches or tight clothing to prevent blood flow from
being restricted if there is swelling.
● In areas with limited resources (e.g. a wilderness or remote environment with longer wait
times to emergency medical care), it is reasonable to wash the wound.
● Suction should not be applied to a snakebite because it does not allow complete removal
of the venom and it might aggravate the damage to the skin.
● A cold compress should not be applied to a snakebite because this may cause the blood
vessels to contract and make the venom spread more quickly through the body.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Good practice points
● The wound should not be rubbed as this may cause the venom to spread more quickly
through the body.
● Cutting the wound with a knife to increase bleeding is not recommended. It does not
reduce the effect of the venom and aggravates the injury.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Prevent and prepare
● Wear appropriate footwear in areas where snakes are present.
● Learn to identify local snakes and determine if they are venomous.
● Keep away from snakes that you encounter, trying not to disturb them. Do not kill or
injure them.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Early recognition
A person with a snakebite may:
● be in pain
● have a visible bite mark
● experience swelling or discolouration of the skin around the area of the bite.
A venomous snake may also cause:
● thirst
● nausea and vomiting
● blurred or double vision
● sensory disturbances or paralysis
● sweating and excessive production of saliva
● a sudden drop in blood pressure, leading to Shock
● Seizures.
If possible and safe to do so, identify the type of snake that bit the person. Do not try to
catch or kill the snake. Consider taking a photo or making a note of its features for a
medical professional to identify. However, it is more important to provide care to the person
than to figure out what kind of snake caused the bite.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - First aid steps
1.
Ensure the area is safe or move to a safer location.
2. Help the person lie down in a comfortable position. Advise them to move as little as
possible.
3. Access emergency medical services (EMS).
4. Remove jewellery, watches or tight clothing to prevent blood flow being restricted if there
is swelling. Do this while moving the limb as little as possible.
5. Mark the site of the wound to track any changes and note the timing of the bite.
6. Monitor the person’s level of response and breathing. Encourage them to remain as still
as possible and provide emotional support as a snakebite can be a traumatic experience.
● There are many resources available to learn more about poisonous snakes, including
online databases and local resources (e.g. medical professionals, snake handlers,
exterminators or poison centres).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - First aid steps
● Be aware that snakes are traded and move around the world. You may encounter a
snake that is not common to your area.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - CAUTION
The following actions are not effective and may even cause further harm:
● applying a tourniquet
● sucking out the venom
● applying a cold compress
● rubbing the bite
● cutting the wound with a knife to increase bleeding.
Local adaptations
● If in an area with limited resources (e.g. a wilderness or remote environment with longer
wait times to EMS):
○ wash the wound with potable (clean) water
○ immobilize the limb with a non-elastic bandage to reduce the spread of the
venom and risk of infection. If this is unavailable, use clothing such as trousers or a
shirt.
● If necessary, carry the person, for example, by making an improvised stretcher.
● Dispel any non-evidence-based local ideas about snakebites, particularly on the use of
activated charcoal and black stone.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Snakebites - Access help
It is important to tell medical professionals about the type of snake that bit the person. This will
help them provide the best care as quickly as possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Key action
Quickly try to identify the poison, the amount and when (or how long) the person was exposed
to it and access advanced care, such as emergency medical services (EMS) or a poison centre.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Introduction
Poisoning is when a person is exposed to a substance that can quickly damage their health or
endanger their life. Most poisons are swallowed or inhaled; however, they can also be absorbed
through the skin. Many poisonous substances are found in homes and workplaces, including
some cleaning products, illicit substances, medications and even some plants.
Opioids act as poisons when taken in excessive amounts or by people for whom they are not
prescribed, as they depress the central nervous system and can rapidly lead to respiratory
failure and death. See unresponsive and abnormal breathing with suspected opioid overdose.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Guidelines
● For a person who has swallowed a poisonous substance, the first aid provider should
consider laying them on their left side.*
● If the person ingested a chemical substance (one that could burn from the inside), the
first aid provider can give them a dilutant if advised to do so by a healthcare provider,
such as a poison centre.*
