doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Good practice points
● The first aid provider should stop or limit further effects of the poison by stopping
continued exposure. In the case of inhalation of toxic gas, the person should be removed
from the area, but only if it is safe for the first aid provider to do so.
● In rooms that are potentially filled with unknown gases or vapours, exposure to all sources
of ignition, such as naked flames, electrical equipment, oxidizing chemicals and the
smoking of tobacco products, should be prevented.
● The nature and time of exposure and the name of the product or toxic substance should
be described to the poison control centre, or local equivalent, or EMS. All bottles,
packages or containers with labels or any other information about the poison should be
given to EMS.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Good practice points
● If life-threatening conditions are present (e.g. unresponsiveness or breathing difficulties),
the first aid provider should access EMS. The first aid provider should start CPR or provide
other first aid as necessary, taking the necessary steps to avoid cross-contamination.
● If non-life-threatening conditions are present, the first aider should access and follow the
instructions of the poison control centre (or local equivalent) or EMS.
● Rescue breaths should be avoided if poisoning by toxins such as cyanide, hydrogen
sulphide, corrosives or organophosphates is suspected. The bag-valve-mask device may
be used by those who are trained to do so.
● If the person is responsive, the first aid provider should remove any poisonous liquid
remaining in the person’s mouth by allowing the person to use water to rinse and spit out
any remaining toxin.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Good practice points
● First aid providers should not give any diluents such as milk, water or activated charcoal
to a person who has swallowed a poisonous substance unless they are instructed to do so
by the poison control centre or equivalent poison expert.
● The person should NOT be encouraged to vomit as this may damage their throat.
● Button batteries contain poisonous chemicals which may leak into the body. If they are
swallowed, this should be treated as poisoning.
● First aid providers with appropriate training may administer oxygen to people who have
carbon monoxide or carbon dioxide poisoning.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Prevent and prepare
● Ensure that all poisonous substances (such as cleaning products and medicines) are
locked away and inaccessible to children. This includes brightly coloured or scented
chemicals such as washing machine tablets, e-cigarette liquids or any drug-infused
“treats” like THC gummies, also known as weed gummies or marijuana gummies.
● Carefully read the information leaflet that comes with any new medication to avoid an
overdose.
● Regularly service cooking and heating appliances that use fossil fuels and install a carbon
monoxide detector.
● Store chemicals out of access to any person who may accidentally or purposefully swallow
or sniff them and ensure they have child-resistant lids.
● Hand sanitizers should be kept out of reach of children under the age of six at all times
and used only with adult supervision.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Prevent and prepare
● Depending on the type of work or hobbies, learn how to prevent direct contact with
poisonous substances. This may include contacting the person who is responsible for
workplace safety to teach specific safety regulations.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Early recognition
● Upon entering an environment where there may be poisonous substances, assess the
area. There may be open packaging near the person (e.g. a packet of tablets) or spilled
chemicals. A confined space may smell of gas (note that carbon monoxide is odourless, as
well as colourless and tasteless). The person may also be able to tell you that they have
had contact with a poisonous substance.
Poisoning signs and symptoms can include:
● burns around the mouth and lips
● breath that smells like chemicals, such as gasoline or paint thinner
● vomiting
● drowsiness
● difficulty breathing
● confusion or other altered mental status.
Poisoning signs and symptoms can mimic other conditions, such as Seizure, Stroke or an
insulin reaction.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - First aid steps
1.
Help the person reduce or stop further exposure to the poison.
2. Try to identify the poisonous substance, the amount and when (or how long) the person
was exposed to it. Only touch the packaging if it is safe to do so. If not, wait for EMS.
3. Access the poison control centre (or local equivalent) or EMS and report all of the
information about the poison and situation. Follow their instructions.
4. Help the person into a comfortable position on their left side if possible, and monitor
them for any change in their breathing or level of response.
5. Gather any bottles, packages or containers with labels and any other information about
the poison to give to EMS.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Special cases
● If the person is unresponsive, open their airway and check for breathing. See
Unresponsiveness topics.
● If the person has a chemical substance in their eye or around their mouth, see burns.
● If the person is having an opioid overdose, see Unresponsive and abnormal breathing
with opioid overdose.
● If the person has been bitten by a snake or stung by a jellyfish, see snakebites or aquatic
animal injuries.
● If the person vomits while lying on the ground, turn them on their side to prevent
choking.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - CAUTION
● If a toxic substance is suspected, the first aid provider may need to wear personal
protective equipment such as a mask or gloves. If a harmful substance is suspected in or
around the mouth, providers should use chest compression-only CPR to avoid contact.
● Do not make the person vomit as this may damage their throat.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Poisoning - Access help
● It is important to tell the poison control centre (or equivalent) or EMS as much as you can
about the type of poison the person may have been exposed to. This allows the
professionals to give the most appropriate help based on the person’s needs.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Key action
Encourage the person to sit with their head leaned forward slightly and pinch their nostrils for
10-15 minutes.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Introduction
A nosebleed (epistaxis) is one of the most common ear, nose and throat emergencies
encountered in both primary care and emergency settings. A nosebleed is bleeding from the
nostrils or nasal cavity that may occur spontaneously or as a result of trauma and can sometimes
be severe. The person experiencing the nosebleed is usually able to treat it themselves. They are
most common in people between the ages of 10 and 60.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Good practice points
● Applying pressure to the lower third soft portion of the nose is the only first aid
intervention needed in most cases.
● Reassure the person. Nosebleeds can be alarming, especially for young children.
● A person experiencing a nosebleed should sit with their head slightly forward with their
nostrils pinched for 10 to 15 minutes (maximum). If the bleeding does not stop after 15
minutes of continuous manual pressure or the person becomes lightheaded from loss of
blood, they should seek medical attention.
● A person with a nosebleed due to trauma should seek medical attention if they
experience signs of brain injury, obvious nasal deformity or signs of a facial fracture.
● A person experiencing a nosebleed that does not stop and is taking anticoagulant or
antiplatelet medication, or who has a blood clot disorder, should seek help from a
healthcare professional or activate EMS.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Good practice points
● The use of cryotherapy as a first aid intervention for sudden, severe nosebleeds is not
recommended.
● The person should lean forward, breathe through their mouth and spit out any blood.
Leaning forward may decrease blood flow to the airway and stomach, which can cause
breathing difficulties and vomiting, respectively.
● A severe nosebleed may be linked to a traumatic brain injury and facial bone fractures.
Signs of traumatic brain injury, including altered mental status, loss of consciousness,
repeated vomiting, changes in vision, difficulty moving or walking or severe headache,
indicate the potential of a medical emergency and the person or first aider should access
emergency medical services (EMS).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Prevent and prepare
● Prevent trauma to the nose by using guards or facemasks during recreational activities.
● Avoid picking or forceful blowing.
● Be aware that a nosebleed may occur spontaneously due to climate (temperature or
humidity) or may be caused by chronic issues like allergies or a reaction to medications.
● Ongoing nosebleeds can lead to anaemia and shock due to blood loss.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Early recognition
● The person has blood coming out of their nose.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - First aid steps
1.
Advise the person to sit and lean their head forward slightly while pinching their nostrils
for 10 to 15 minutes (maximum).
2. If the nosebleed continues after 15 minutes of continuous pressure or the person
becomes lightheaded from blood loss, seek medical attention.
3. If the nosebleed was due to trauma and there are signs of a brain injury, obvious nasal
deformity, facial fracture or the person is taking anticoagulants, access EMS immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Nosebleeds - Access help
Contact a general practitioner or out-of-hours medical service immediately if:
● The nosebleed does not stop after pressing the nose twice for 10 to 15 minutes each time.
● The person is taking a medicine (e.g. anticoagulants, such as Warfarin or aspirin) that
helps prevent blood clots or the person has a condition that means the blood cannot clot
properly (haemophilia).
Schedule an appointment with a general practitioner if:
● The person experiences frequent nosebleeds within a short period of time, for example,
several times within a month.
● If a child under two years old has had a nosebleed.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Key action
Recognize the symptoms that may indicate a heart attack and access emergency medical
services (EMS) immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Introduction
Chest pain can indicate a range of conditions related to the heart, lungs or rib cage. For first aid
providers, the most critical risk is a heart attack. A heart attack is usually caused by a blockage in
one of the blood vessels supplying the heart muscle, resulting in damage to the heart. Prompt
recognition and management of a heart attack can save lives. Delayed treatment increases the
probability of complications such as sudden death or later heart failure. Other common causes
of chest pain include trauma, angina and indigestion.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Guidelines
● While waiting for EMS to arrive, consider having the person suspected of having a heart
attack take an oral dose of acetylsalicylic acid. Acetylsalicylic acid should be avoided if the
person is allergic to it or if the person takes acetylsalicylic acid regularly and has just taken
the recommended dose.*
● If the first aid provider is trained and oxygen is available, the provider may give oxygen to a
person experiencing chest pain if they recognize the person is hypoxic, after calling for
advanced care and providing acetylsalicylic acid (ASA, Aspirin).*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Good practice points
● If a heart attack is suspected, EMS should be accessed immediately, especially if the pain
is intense, the person has shortness of breath, the person’s skin is pale or ashen and
clammy, they have a bluish colour to the skin on their lips, ears, fingers or toes, or they feel
a pulsing pain in their jaws and teeth. Access EMS even if the pain has only lasted a
couple of minutes.
● The first aid provider should help the person get into a comfortable position; the person
should refrain from physical activity.
● If the person has medication, is diagnosed with angina and is experiencing acute chest
pain, the first aid provider should assist them in taking their medication.
● While waiting for EMS to arrive, consider having the person suspected of having a heart
attack take an oral dose of 150–500 mg acetylsalicylic acid.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Good practice points
● If available, get an automated external defibrillator and keep it close to the person in case
it is needed.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Prevent and prepare
● There are national and global organizations that research how to reduce the likelihood of
heart conditions. Refer to your country’s health authority for more information.
● Exercise and a healthy diet, combined with low or no alcohol consumption and not
smoking, can help reduce the chances of a heart attack.
● If you have family, friends or colleagues who have angina or heart disease, be aware of
where they keep their medication in case of an emergency.
● Keep acetylsalicylic acid on hand if you are diagnosed with heart disease.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Early recognition
Ask the person about their chest pain. If they have been diagnosed with angina or another heart
condition, they should be able to tell you this. If the chest pain continues even after taking
medication, it is important to quickly recognize the possibility of a heart attack and access EMS.
Signs and symptoms that may indicate someone is having a heart attack include:
● chest pain
● chest pain in combination with pain in the arm or shoulder
● chest pain in combination with sweating
● chest pain in combination with palpitations.
Pain may be described as discomfort, vice-like pressure, cramping, squeezing or burning. A
heart attack can start with non-specific complaints, especially in females:
● nausea
● shortness of breath
● pain radiating to the jaw
● pain in the upper abdomen
● pain between the shoulder blades

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Early recognition
● pain that lasts more than a few minutes or it may come and go.
People may also experience the following signs and symptoms.
● paleness
● anxiousness
● bluish colour to the skin on their lips, ears or fingers.
● Heart attacks can occur in people who have not yet been diagnosed with heart disease.
● Heart attack symptoms may include any of the ones listed above and EMS should be
accessed immediately.
● Symptoms may be more subtle or uncommon in some populations, such as people who
are female, elderly or have diabetes.
● For angina, the pain is often familiar and improves when the person rests. For a heart
attack, the pain is often more persistent.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - First aid steps
1.
Help the person to sit down in a comfortable position and take their medication.
2. Access EMS immediately if you suspect a heart attack. Ask a bystander to bring a
defibrillator if available.
3. Suggest the person consider chewing a dose of 150-500mg of acetylsalicylic acid if a heart
attack is suspected.
4. Reassure the person and monitor their breathing and responsiveness.
● If the person becomes unresponsive with abnormal breathing, start CPR.
● Do not give acetylsalicylic acid to the person if they are allergic to it, have a bleeding
disorder or have already taken the recommended dose.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Access help
● Ask bystanders to help you access EMS, monitor the person and get medication or a
defibrillator.
● Emphasize that you suspect it is a heart attack when you access EMS, so they can
appropriately prioritize your case. Update EMS if the person’s condition changes (e.g. they
collapse and stop breathing).
● It is important to access help quickly to minimize any damage to the heart.
● If the person has been diagnosed with angina and has their medication, it may not be
necessary to access EMS. However, you should access EMS if the pain does not subside, as
it usually does within a few minutes of taking medication.
● If the person has taken medication for indigestion but the pain does not subside, access
EMS. Note that a heart attack is often mistaken for indigestion.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Chest pain (cardiac) - Recovery
● If angina pain patterns have changed, a change in medication or treatment may be
needed. Suggest that the person seek medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Key action
Recognize the early signs of stroke and access emergency medical services (EMS) for help
immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Introduction
A stroke occurs when the blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted. This can be caused by
bleeding in the brain or a blockage of a blood vessel, such as a blood clot. It can be very serious
and requires immediate medical care. Stroke is the second leading cause of death and the third
leading cause of disability (loss of vision, speech or partial or complete paralysis) (Johnson et al.,
2016). Early admission to a medical facility greatly increases the chance of a positive outcome, so
it is important for first aid providers to quickly recognize stroke symptoms and access EMS.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Guidelines
● First aid providers should use a stroke assessment system to recognize the symptoms of a
stroke.**
○ First aid providers should use a stroke assessment system, such as FAST or CPSS
(see below), to recognize the symptoms of a stroke.**
○ First aid providers may use stroke assessment systems that include blood glucose
measurement, when available, such as MASS or LAPSS, to increase the specificity of
stroke recognition.*
● First aid providers should NOT administer oxygen to a person experiencing a suspected
stroke.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Good practice points
● Mild stroke-like symptoms that last less than a few minutes indicate a transient ischaemic
attack (TIA) or “mini stroke”. The person experiencing these symptoms should seek
medical care as soon as possible to decrease the risk of more permanent outcomes.
● For a person showing stroke signs and/or experiencing stroke symptoms, EMS must be
accessed as soon as possible.
● First aid providers should help the person get into the best possible position, keeping in
mind the person’s comfort and physical and cognitive abilities. This may include lying on
their back or sitting.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Prevent and prepare
● There are national and global organizations that conduct research on how to reduce the
likelihood of stroke. Refer to your country’s health authority for more information.
● Make healthy lifestyle choices to minimize certain risk factors such as high blood pressure,
obesity, blood sugar level, hyperlipidaemia and renal dysfunction. Avoid activities such as
smoking.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Early recognition
● There are a variety of acronyms in the English language to help recognize the signs and
symptoms of stroke. FAST is recognized as an effective acronym for first aid providers. It
reflects the need for early recognition and medical care, which improves the person’s
chances of a positive outcome.
FAST
F
Face
Facial numbness or weakness, especially on one side: ask the
person to smile or show their teeth.
Check if the person’s mouth is crooked and whether one corner of
their mouth is drooping.
A
Arm
Arm numbness or weakness, especially on one side: ask the
person to extend both arms at the same time, straight out in front
of them and ask them to turn their palms upwards.
Carefully look if one arm is sagging or drifting around.
S
Speech
Abnormal speech, difficulty speaking or understanding others or a
loss of speech.
Ask the person or companions if there are any changes in their
speech.
T
Time
Facial numbness or weakness, especially on one side: ask the
person to smile or show their teeth.
Check if the person’s mouth is crooked and whether one corner of
their mouth is drooping.
CPSS
The CPSS (Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale) tests three signs for abnormal findings that may
indicate that the person is having a stroke (FACE, ARM and SPEECH).
Signs of stroke

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Early recognition
● Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm or leg, especially on one side of the body.
The probability of stroke is likely if the person, when asked to:
○ show their teeth, the corner of their mouth droops
○ lift both arms with palms turned upwards while eyes are closed, one arm drifts or
droops.
● Sudden confusion, trouble speaking or understanding. The probability of stroke is likely if
the person, when asked to:
○ repeat a simple sentence, speech is unclear or slurred, or the words do not come
easily.
● Sudden trouble in seeing with one or both eyes.
● Sudden trouble walking or experiencing dizziness, loss of balance or coordination.
● Sudden, severe headache with no known cause.
● Seizure (of a non-epileptic person).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - First aid steps
1.
Use a stroke assessment system to recognize the symptoms of a stroke.
2. If you suspect a stroke, access EMS immediately. Note the time it started.
3. Help the person get into the best possible position, keeping in mind the person’s comfort
and physical and cognitive abilities. Support them if they are at risk of falling.
4. Monitor the person’s breathing and reassure them. Keep talking to the person.
If the person becomes unresponsive, open their airway and check their breathing. See
unresponsive and breathing normally and Unresponsive and breathing abnormally
(adolescent and adult). Note that similar symptoms may be caused by high or low blood
sugar.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Access help
● Emphasize the signs and symptoms of stroke to the medical professional.
● The faster the person can get medical help, the less damage to the brain there may be, so
it is important to get help quickly.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Stroke - Recovery
● The signs of stroke indicate brain injury. Even if the person seems to have recovered, they
should still access medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Key action
Stop further contact with the allergen and help the person to use their medication.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Introduction
Allergies are relatively common, presenting on the skin (hives, itching, swelling), or in the airways
(sneezing, snuffles) and sometimes accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms (cramps,
diarrhoea). Chronic allergic disease (e.g. atopic eczema) sometimes deteriorates suddenly. Some
people can also be severely allergic to something, resulting in a life-threatening anaphylactic
reaction (a very severe allergic reaction). Many people with a history of anaphylaxis carry a
lifesaving epinephrine autoinjector.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Guidelines
Anaphylaxis
● First aid providers should have repeated training sessions and encounters with people
experiencing anaphylaxis before they are expected to recognize the signs and
symptoms.**
● Epinephrine should be used intramuscularly to treat anaphylaxis using the person’s
prescribed autoinjector.**
● For a person with symptoms of anaphylaxis who has been treated by, but did not respond
to, epinephrine within five to ten minutes, a second dose may be considered if
emergency medical services (EMS) have not arrived yet.*
Mild allergic reaction
● Using moisturisers in case of atopic eczema or dermatitis may relieve the symptoms.*
● Rinsing the eyes or nasal cavity with saline may relieve symptoms of hay fever.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Guidelines
● If local regulations allow, a trained first aid provider may give common antiallergic
medication (antihistamine or corticosteroid tablet) if the person does not have these with
them.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Good practice points
● The person should be asked about any known allergies and prescribed medication.
● Epinephrine can be used intranasally to treat anaphylaxis using the person’s prescribed
medication.
● If appropriate, the allergen should be removed (e.g. from the skin) or the person should
be removed from the environment containing the allergen (e.g. a chemical).
● The first aid provider should help the person to get into a comfortable position and to
take their prescribed medication if the person has it with them.
Anaphylaxis
● First aid providers should be trained in recognizing the signs and symptoms of
anaphylaxis.
● First aid providers should be familiar with the epinephrine autoinjector, so that they can
help someone having an anaphylactic reaction self-administer their epinephrine, if local
law permits.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Good practice points
● First aid providers may be permitted to use an epinephrine autoinjector if the person is
unable to do so, provided that a doctor has prescribed the medication and local law
permits.
● Epinephrine should be given when symptoms of anaphylaxis are present. Inappropriate
use of an epinephrine autoinjector (in a case of misdiagnosis, incorrect route of
administration, inadvertent intravenous administration or administration of an excessive
dose of epinephrine) may result in adverse reactions.
● The epinephrine auto-injection may be administered through the person’s clothing if the
clothes are not thick.
● First aid providers should access EMS when a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is
suspected or recognized in a person.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Good practice points
● Unless the doctor’s prescription is different, for children between 15 kg and 30 kg
bodyweight, an epinephrine dose of 0.15 mg is recommended intramuscularly. For
children over 30 kg, epinephrine is recommended in a dose of 0.3 mg, and for adults, the
recommended dose is 0.5 mg.
● First aid providers should be aware that an anaphylactic reaction can be biphasic
(symptoms recur after complete improvement) between one and 78 hours after the initial
onset. Biphasic anaphylaxis is associated with the initial presentation of anaphylaxis that
is more severe or needs more than one dose of epinephrine. In these instances, the
person should be observed in case of a second reaction.
Mild allergic reaction
● In case of an allergic reaction to the skin, advise the person not to rub the skin, as this may
exacerbate the itch.
● In the case of hay fever, rinsing the eye or nose may offer some relief.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Good practice points
● The first aid provider should monitor the person closely, as a mild allergic reaction can
develop into a severe allergic reaction.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Prevent and prepare
● Prevention is of utmost importance. Anyone with a known allergy should avoid any
contact with the allergen.
● Ensure a person with a known allergy carries an allergy card (describing their allergy) and
their prescribed medication at all times, and that caregivers know where the medication
can be found.
● Teach those with a known allergy, as well as their caregivers, to recognize the signs and
symptoms of a severe allergic reaction, when and why to access EMS and how to use the
epinephrine autoinjector.
● Consider food labelling at home and about.
● Be aware of the most common allergens causing anaphylaxis (foods, insect venoms,
medication and latex).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Early recognition
Unless the allergic reaction is the first one in the life of the person, the person usually knows they
are allergic to a certain substance and may carry some antiallergic medicine with them. Ask the
person if they have any known allergies.
You may notice the person has had contact with a common allergen.
A mild allergic reaction will vary depending on what is causing it but may include:
● red, itchy eyes
● sneezing, snuffles or runny nose
● abdominal cramps, diarrhoea and vomiting
● itching, swelling or hives on the skin, including the face.
A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is likely to develop further and include life-threatening
conditions such as:
● difficulty breathing, including shortness of breath, wheezing or asthma-like appearance

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Early recognition
● airway narrowing, swelling of the tongue, throat and larynx, causing hoarseness, noisy
breathing. Often, the first symptom to occur is difficulty swallowing.
● signs of shock including confusion or agitation, pale or ashen skin, which may lead to
collapse and unresponsiveness.
The severity of anaphylaxis can differ from one person to another, and even in the same person
from one episode to another. A mild allergic reaction may unpredictably progress to
life-threatening anaphylaxis in minutes. Therefore, high alertness is required in treating a
suspected anaphylactic reaction.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - First aid steps
Anaphylaxis
1.
Access EMS as soon as you recognize that the person is experiencing a severe allergic
reaction.
2. Help the person to lie down unless they are experiencing breathing difficulties. In that
case, help them to sit down.
3. If the person has an epinephrine autoinjector, help them use it. The best place for
injection is the middle of the outer side of the thigh. The injection can be administered
through clothes if the clothes are not thick.
4. If a person with symptoms of severe allergic reaction was treated with but did not
respond to the first dose of epinephrine within five to ten minutes, a second dose may be
considered.
5. Keep monitoring the person’s responsiveness and breathing regularly until EMS is
accessed.
Follow the usual rules for drug and medical device disposal after the autoinjector has been
used.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Local adaptation
If an epinephrine autoinjector is not available, access EMS immediately.
While waiting for medical assistance, alternative medicines can be used after medical advice,
such as antihistamines or corticosteroids.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - CAUTION
First aid providers should be aware that use of epinephrine may have side effects (some of
which may also result from an anaphylactic reaction):
● faster (pounding), sometimes irregular heartbeat
● excitement, anxiety or fear
● weakness or shakiness
● nausea and vomiting
● throbbing headache
● dizziness
● paleness
● sweating.
Mild allergic reaction
1.
Ask the person about known allergies and any prescribed medication.
2. If appropriate, remove the allergen (e.g. by rinsing from the skin) or remove the person
from the environment containing the allergen.
3. Help the person get into a comfortable position and take their medication if they have it
with them. If trained to do so and local regulations permit, offer the person common
antiallergic medication or remedies.
4. In case of an allergic reaction to the skin, advise the person not to rub the skin, as this may
make it itch more.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - CAUTION
5. Monitor the person closely, as a mild allergic reaction can develop into a severe allergic
reaction.
● An antihistamine or corticosteroid medication may be given to the person.
● For hay fever, rinsing the eyes or nasal cavity with saline may relieve symptoms.
● In the case of hives, an anti-itch ointment might help. Advise the person to seek help
from their doctor or pharmacist.
● In the case of eczema, applying moisturiser or using an anti-itch ointment may help.
● Advise the person that some antihistamines could cause drowsiness and diminish the
reflexes needed for safe driving or working with a dangerous machine. This is more
pronounced with the first generation of antihistamines. Even a small amount of alcohol
may enhance these side effects.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Access help
Anaphylaxis
● Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening condition requiring urgent medical attention. As soon as
you suspect a severe allergic reaction, access EMS.
● Ensure you tell EMS if the person has received an epinephrine injection.
Mild allergic reaction
Advise the person to seek medical advice:
● In the case of hives: if the allergic reaction to the skin is very bothersome and does not
improve over a couple of days.
● In the case of eczema: if it is the first time the allergic reaction occurs, or if the skin lesions
are accompanied by signs of infection, such as fever or feeling unwell.
● In the case of hay fever: if it is the first time the allergic reaction occurs.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis - Recovery
● Ensure that a person who has a severe reaction or requires an epinephrine injection is
monitored for the three days following a reaction, as a severe allergic reaction may recur.
● A person who has experienced a severe allergic reaction should keep an allergy card
(explaining their allergy) with them at all times.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Key action
Identify the signs of shock and provide care to minimize stress on the body and support blood
circulation to the brain and heart.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Introduction
A person experiences shock when their circulation system fails and major organs and tissues do
not receive enough blood (and therefore, oxygen). A common cause of shock is severe bleeding,
including external and internal bleeding. Very serious burns cause leaking of fluids from the
blood vessels into the burn and may result in shock. A person experiencing problems with their
heart (e.g. a heart attack) may not have enough blood pumped around the body, which may
also cause shock. Anaphylaxis is also a cause of shock as the blood vessels dilate, which causes
low blood pressure. The first aid provider’s priority needs to be on identifying shock and initiating
care of the cause if it is evident.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Guidelines
● The person in shock should be placed in a supine position (lying on their back).**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Good practice points
● Emergency medical care should be accessed immediately if it appears the person shows
signs of shock.
● As shock is caused by many other conditions, the first aid provider’s priority should be to
identify and manage the cause if possible.
● If a heart attack is suspected of causing shock, consider placing the person in a supine
position with the upper body slightly elevated.
● If the person has difficulty breathing or is uncomfortable lying on their back, they may be
placed in the position most comfortable to them, such as sitting while leaning back or
leaning forward.
● After the person has been helped to lie on their back, if it makes the person feel better,
the first aid provider may raise the person’s legs 30 to 60 degrees (also called passive leg
raising), provided there is no history of trauma.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Good practice points
● First aid providers should help the person maintain a normal body temperature (i.e.
prevent heat loss in a cold environment and prevent overheating in a hot environment) to
reduce stress.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Prevent and prepare
● Shock is caused by many other conditions and it is vital to provide care for the condition,
such as:
○ If a person is losing a lot of blood, the first aid provider should apply pressure to the
bleeding and keep the person warm. Observe for signs of shock.
○ If the person is having a severe allergic reaction and has a known allergy
requiring them to carry epinephrine or other medications, help them to take
their own medication.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Early recognition
Shock is caused by other conditions, usually severe bleeding. Sometimes heart attack, severe
burns, an infection such as sepsis or a severe allergic reaction.
In addition to the signs of one of these conditions, the person may also:
● have ashen or pale skin with bluish lips, ears and fingers
● have cool or clammy skin
● sweat and shiver
● feel weak, tired or dizzy
● Have rapid breathing and pulse
● display an altered mental status (anxious, sleepy).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - First aid steps
1.
Help the person to lie down on their back (or in a comfortable position).
2. Provide care for the cause of shock if possible. For example, apply pressure to a severe
bleed or help them take their medication if they are having a severe allergic reaction.
3. Access EMS immediately.
4. Continue to provide care for the cause of the shock if possible.
5. Keep the person warm. Cover them with a blanket or clothing and protect them from the
ground if it is cold.
6. Reassure the person by talking to them. Monitor their responsiveness and breathing
regularly.
● If the person is unresponsive with abnormal breathing, begin CPR.
● After the person has been moved to lie on their back, if it makes the person feel better,
you could raise their legs 30 to 60 degrees if they are uninjured.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Shock - Access help
Clearly explain to EMS about the person’s condition, signs of shock and what the cause may be.
Shock is a life-threatening condition so emergency medical care is needed.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Key action
Give the person something sweet to eat or drink to raise their blood sugar level (in the case of
low blood sugar).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Introduction
Diabetes is a chronic condition in which the body struggles to produce or respond to insulin, the
hormone that regulates blood sugar levels. A diabetic emergency happens when a person’s
blood glucose level goes outside the normal range, resulting in either too much sugar in the
blood (hyperglycaemia) or too little sugar in the blood (hypoglycaemia). 442 million adults have
diabetes worldwide, or one in 11 people. The number of diabetes cases worldwide has
quadrupled since 1990 (World Health Organization, 2024a). A high blood sugar level
(hyperglycaemia) may evolve gradually and can be asymptomatic for several hours or even days.
A low blood sugar level (hypoglycaemia) is usually sudden and life-threatening and therefore
forms the focus of this topic.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Guidelines
● Oral glucose administration (swallowing or eating glucose) should be used for an adult or
child with suspected hypoglycaemia who is responsive and able to swallow.**
○ First aid providers should give glucose tablets to a person who has symptoms of
hypoglycaemia and is responsive.**
○ If glucose tablets are not available, various forms of dietary sugars such as Skittles,
Mentos, sugar cubes, jellybeans or orange juice can be used to treat the symptoms
of hypoglycaemia in a responsive person.*
● If oral glucose (e.g. tablets or dietary sugars) is not available, a glucose gel can be given to
an adult or child with suspected hypoglycaemia who is responsive and able to swallow.
These gels are both absorbed into the cheeks (buccal) and swallowed (oral).*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Guidelines
● Sublingual glucose administration (putting glucose under the tongue) may be used for
suspected hypoglycaemia in children who may be uncooperative with swallowing a
glucose substance.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Good practice points
● 15g to 20g of glucose tablets should be used to treat symptomatic hypoglycaemia in
responsive babies, children and adults.
● Glucose administration should be repeated if symptoms continue after 15 minutes.
● If it is unclear whether the person is hypoglycaemic or hyperglycaemic, the first aid
provider should provide care for hypoglycaemia.
● If the person has specific medication, support them in self-administering.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Prevent and prepare
● People who are diabetic should be encouraged to carry blood testing kits with them, as
well as insulin or other oral medication or sugary food.
● People who are diabetic should be advised to alert their family and friends to their
condition and inform them on how to respond in an emergency.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Early recognition
Talk to the person. They may be able to tell you they are having a diabetic emergency and how
you can help them. You can also look for medical alert jewellery on the person.
Someone with low blood sugar may show signs of:
● sweating with cold, clammy skin
● weakness, faintness or hunger
● drowsiness, restlessness, aggressiveness (often resembling drunkenness)
● headache
● rapid pulse
● muscle tremors
● deteriorating level of response and leading eventually to seizures or unresponsiveness.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - First aid steps
1.
Help the person into a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down.
2. If the person has their own glucose or another sugar source, help them to take 15-20
grams of it. If they do not, give them a sugary (non-diet) drink, such as fruit juice, or some
sugar (such as three teaspoons of sugar or three pieces of candy, like jellybeans).
3. If symptoms continue after 15 minutes, give the person a repeated amount of glucose or
sugar substance.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - CAUTION
● Only give the person something to eat or drink if they are responsive and able to swallow.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Access help
If the person’s condition does not improve quickly (around 30 minutes) or they become
unresponsive, access emergency medical services (EMS). Monitor the person’s level of
responsiveness, breathing and circulation while waiting for help to arrive. Advise the person to
seek medical help if their symptoms are occurring more frequently than usual or if they have a
fever.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Diabetic emergency (hypoglycemia) - Recovery
If the person starts to feel better, advise them they can eat some slow-acting sugars (e.g. a slice
of bread or a waffle). Encourage them or their companion to measure their blood sugar level.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Introduction
A seizure is caused by a disruption in the brain’s electrical activity and can result in
unresponsiveness, muscle twitching, loss of bodily control (e.g. bladder release, limb flailing) or
blank staring. The severity varies from person to person, with some experiencing seizures of
greater intensity. Several conditions can cause seizures, including a head injury, infection,
poisoning or fever. A condition called epilepsy can also cause seizures and is usually treated with
medication. Babies and young children are particularly prone to seizures if they experience a
sudden increase in body temperature (febrile seizures). While a seizure is usually not harmful
and passes after a short time, it may cause the person to injure themselves further (e.g. hit their
head on the ground if they collapse).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Guidelines
● First aid providers should not force anything into the person’s mouth.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Good practice points
● The person experiencing a seizure may be placed on the floor to prevent injury from
falling.
● Once the seizure has ended, first aid providers should check the person’s breathing and
treat them accordingly.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Prevent and prepare
● Those who look after a person prone to seizures should learn to recognize what regular
seizure activity looks like for that individual, as well as their prescribed treatment and first
aid action plan. If the seizure activity is abnormal or the recommended intervention is
ineffective, the caregiver should access help immediately.
● Schoolteachers and other caregivers should be trained in first aid learning (where
appropriate) to build their confidence and comfort in emergencies (Berhe et al., 2017;
Kaleyias et al., 2005).
● Raise awareness among caregivers that a fever can cause seizures in babies and children.
Prevention includes treating the fever and dressing babies and children appropriately for
their environment.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Prevent and prepare
● In contexts where malaria is prevalent, one of the most common causes of seizures in
children
is
a
fever
caused
by
malaria.
Therefore,
malaria
prevention
(e.g.
insecticide-treated mosquito nets or mosquito repellents) may be effective at preventing
episodes in settings where anti-epileptic treatment is unavailable (Ba-Diop et al., 2014).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Early recognition
People with epilepsy may experience a warning sign before an epileptic seizure, known as an
“aura”, causing them to feel strange or experience a particular taste or smell. Other than
epilepsy, a seizure may also be the result of a head injury, disease, infection, poisoning or fever
(especially in babies and children). Conversely, there may be no apparent reason for the seizure.
Seizures may look different from one individual to the next.
Signs of a seizure include:
● sudden loss of responsiveness
● sudden collapse
● involuntary muscle movements such as twitching, jerky movements, stiffness, arching of
the back and a clenched jaw
● noisy, difficult breathing
● saliva foaming around the mouth
● incontinence.
Following the active stage of a seizure the person may:
● fall into a deep sleep
● start to breathe normally or deeply
● become responsive again, often after a few minutes

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Early recognition
● be unaware of what has happened.
Someone who experiences an absence seizure may:
● have a blank stare
● have mild twitching
● be unaware of their surroundings.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - First aid steps
1.
For those in active seizure, protect the person from harm by moving any nearby objects
that may hurt them. Avoid moving the person unless they are in immediate danger (e.g.
they are in oncoming traffic).
2. Place soft padding (e.g. a cushion or sweater) under the person’s head to protect it.
Remove eyeglasses and loosen any restrictive clothing around their neck. Do not restrain
the person.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - First aid steps
3. Access emergency medical services (EMS) in any of the following cases:
a. the person has hurt themselves
b. it is the person’s first seizure
c. the seizure lasts more than five consecutive minutes
d. the person does not regain responsiveness after the seizure
e. the person experiences repeated or different types of seizures than usual, or the
seizures have increased in frequency
f.
the person is diabetic, pregnant or recently pregnant
g. the person has a high fever
h. the person is under the influence of alcohol or substances
i.
when in doubt.
4. Note the start and stop time of the seizure, as well as if it recurs. Communicate this
information to EMS.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - First aid steps
5. When the seizure is over, check the person’s breathing and keep checking this regularly.
Remove the padding from under their head if it may interfere with their breathing.
a. If they are breathing normally, move them onto their side and ensure their airway
is open.
b. If they have abnormal breathing, see unresponsive with abnormal breathing.
6. If present, ask a family member or caregiver if the person has any anti-seizure medication.
There are many ways this medication can be administered, including orally, a spray in the
nose, an injection or rectally. Assist the caregiver if you feel comfortable doing so.
Babies and children
In addition to the steps above, check the baby or child’s temperature. If they are too hot, cool
them by removing any excess clothing and exposing them to fresh, cool air. Treat any fever if
necessary.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - First aid steps
● If the person is unresponsive, focus on maintaining an open airway.
● Do not force anything into the person’s mouth.
● If you do not know the person, look for any medical information they may have on them,
such as a medical bracelet with details of their condition, while accessing help.
● Protect the person’s dignity. For example, move bystanders along or cover any signs of
incontinence (accidental urination).
● Stay with the person until the seizure has passed and they are back to their normal
baseline.
● Be aware that, once the seizure is over, a person may be confused or aggressive. Mind
your own safety and avoid touching the person excessively.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Seizure - Access help
● A person with epilepsy may wish to manage their condition independently and request
that you do not access help. If they are with a companion (e.g. partner, parent or
caregiver), listen and support what this person says as they are more familiar with the
condition than you are. If the person having a seizure is alone, a medical bracelet or
necklace may provide you and EMS with information.
● A seizure that lasts longer than five minutes is called “status epilepticus”. It is a severe
condition and requires immediate medical assistance. Access help right away.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Key action
Help the person get into a safe and comfortable position and ask them to do physical
counterpressure manoeuvres to increase blood flow to their brain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Introduction
Fainting is a temporary loss of responsiveness due to a fall in blood supply to the brain. More
often, the person does not become completely unresponsive and usually becomes fully
responsive immediately after. Usually, a person will experience a short period of feeling faint
before they faint. This is the ideal time to provide first aid, before the person collapses. Feeling
faint and fainting are common occurrences and may happen as a response to a variety of
conditions, including pre-existing chronic issues, stress, pain, hunger or exhaustion. It can also
occur if a person stands still for a long time, especially in warm temperatures.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Guidelines
● First aid providers should assist the person who is feeling faint in doing physical
counterpressure manoeuvres.**
● While in a safe and comfortable position, a person feeling faint can perform
counterpressure manoeuvres on their own to lessen the feeling.*
● Lower-body physical counterpressure manoeuvres (such as leg crossing and tensing, or
squatting),
rather
than
upper-body
and
abdominal
physical
counterpressure
manoeuvres, should be used to lessen the faint feeling.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Good practice points
● A person who is feeling faint should be helped into a safe and comfortable position, such
as sitting or lying on the floor, so they cannot fall.
● For a person who is feeling faint accompanied by chest pain or palpitations, contact
emergency medical services.
● If counterpressure manoeuvres are not possible, the first aid provider may ask the person
to lie down and raise the person’s legs (30-60 degrees), which may increase blood flow to
the person’s brain and may improve the person’s condition.
● If the person faints, it should be brief with almost immediate recovery. If the person
becomes unresponsive, the first aid provider should immediately check their breathing.
See Unresponsiveness.
● The first aid provider should speak to the person to find out why they may feel faint (e.g.
low blood sugar or fatigue) and address their needs (once they have recovered from
feeling faint).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Good practice points
● Water may be offered to the person if they are responsive and able to swallow.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Prevent and prepare
● Take precautions to avoid the conditions that may cause a person to feel faint. Ensure
people have enough to eat and drink, get enough rest and avoid standing for long
periods.
● Stay hydrated.
● Maintain a normal temperature.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Early recognition
The person may have just experienced something shocking or painful. They may be hungry,
tired or have been standing for a long time.
Suddenly the person may become pale or ashen. They may tell you that they feel faint.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - First aid steps
1.
Help the person to sit or lie down in a safe and comfortable position, where they cannot
fall.
2. Ask the person to do physical counterpressure manoeuvres to improve blood flow to their
brain. Alternatively, you could offer to raise their legs for them if they lie down.
3. Reassure the person and observe them closely for changes in their level of response or
breathing. If possible, try to establish why they feel faint and whether there is anything
further you can do to help them.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - CAUTION
● A person who recovers from feeling faint should resume their activity only gradually as
they may feel faint again.
● If the person faints and falls, be alert to the potential injury they may sustain. See Head
injury or fractures, sprains and strains.
● A person who faints should become responsive again very quickly. If the person is
unresponsive,
check
their
breathing
and
provide
first
aid
accordingly.
See
Unresponsiveness.
PHYSICAL COUNTERPRESSURE MANOEUVRES
Lower-body counterpressure manoeuvres may be more effective than upper-body manoeuvres.
Physical counterpressure manoeuvres include:
Squatting
● Advise the person to squat.
Leg tensing
● Advise the person to cross their legs and tense
the leg, abdominal and buttock muscles. The
person can also try raising their legs if seated or
lying down.
Arm tensing

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - CAUTION
● Advise the person to tense and release their arm
muscles by gripping one hand with the other
and pulling their arms in opposite directions. If
squatting or leg exercises are not possible, arm
tensing can be used as an alternative.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Access help
● Feeling faint and fainting does not usually require medical care.
● If the person does not become responsive immediately after fainting, they may be
experiencing something more severe (e.g. a heart attack). Access help immediately.
● In a public place, you could ask bystanders to help you protect the person’s dignity, for
example, by blocking the view of people passing by.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Feeling faint - Recovery
● The person should get some fresh air.
● After the first episode, the person should try to recognize the signs of fainting as early as
possible. In that way, in the future, they can quickly get into a comfortable and safe
position and consider using counterpressure manoeuvres.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Key action
Assist the person to take paracetamol (also known as acetaminophen) to control their fever.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Introduction
When a person’s body temperature is above 38°C (100.4°F), the person has a fever. Medical
conditions, such as viral infections or sepsis, can cause a fever. A fever is a common and normal
response to fight infection and, in most circumstances, is not harmful (El-Radhi, 2012). For more
information on fevers due to environmental conditions, see Hyperthermia.
While fever can affect people of all ages, it is common in children. It rarely reaches 41oC (105.8°F).
Many healthcare providers and parents view fever as a dangerous condition or a symptom to be
stopped, despite evidence that fever is the body’s natural method of fighting and overcoming
acute infections (Green et al., 2021). Fever has the potential to cause a seizure in children
because their bodies cannot yet regulate their temperature. First aid providers should consider
the possible causes of a high temperature (e.g. infection or disease) and help the person access
medical care if necessary.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Guidelines
● Paracetamol may be given to a person with a fever who is feeling unwell.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Good practice points
● A cold cloth on the person’s face may be used but sponging or placing the person in cool
or cold water on them should be avoided. The cold water can cause the person to shiver,
which will make them warmer, or cause their blood vessels to constrict and decrease
blood flow to the skin and therefore decrease heat loss.
● People with a fever should rest and drink fluids to replace the fluid loss caused by
sweating.
● People with fever should dress lightly and the first aid provider should avoid layering
them with excessive blankets or coverings.
● Access emergency medical care if a person with a fever also has any of the following signs
and symptoms:
○ a rash
○ a change in mental status
○ difficulty breathing
○ severe abdominal pain
○ sensitivity to light and vomiting
○ signs of Shock.
● A baby, child or adult should receive medical care as soon as possible if:

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Good practice points
○ the baby with a fever is under three months of age
○ the child has a temperature higher than 39°C (102.5°F)
○ the person with fever is over 65 years of age
○ the person with fever has cancer, a weakened immune system, sickle cell disease
or is taking medications which affect their immune system
○ the fever does not decrease with paracetamol or lasts more than three days
○ additional symptoms occur that are concerning.
● Depending on the local context (e.g. areas where malaria is present), people with fever
should seek medical care, even if they have no other symptoms.
● A high fever may cause a child to experience a seizure. While the seizure could be an
indication of a more serious infection, such as meningitis, it is often the result of an
increase in temperature only. See Seizure.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Prevent and prepare
● Know the causes of fever in children and take any available precautions, such as
vaccinations or medication against particular illnesses in areas where there is a risk.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Early recognition
If possible, check the person’s temperature. A fever above 39°C (102.5°F) can be harmful and may
indicate a serious infection or disease. Consider this as you assess the person.
In the early stages of fever, the person may have a high temperature but tell you they feel cold,
or they may be shivering or have chattering teeth or goose pimples.
The person may experience:
● a high temperature above 38°C (100.4°F)
● hot, flushed skin and sweating
● headache or other aches and pains
● loss of appetite
● fatigue.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - First aid steps
1.
Advise the person to rest and dress lightly.
2. Offer the person fluids to drink to replace lost fluids from sweating.
3. In many cases, medication is not necessary. If the person is feeling unwell, you can control
their fever by giving them the recommended dose of paracetamol. You can also sponge
the person with lukewarm water, as long as this does not upset them.
4. Monitor the person’s condition and be aware of any additional signs and symptoms that
occur.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - CAUTION
● Do not overheat the person with layers of clothing or blankets.
● Do not use cold water to sponge the person, as this may cause them discomfort and
may stop their body from releasing some heat.
● Paracetamol is preferred and safe, particularly when administered at recommended
doses. Ibuprofen can cause gastrointestinal irritation and kidney damage and needs to
be used with caution (Loya et al., 2022).
● Often, one antipyretic medication (e.g. paracetamol or ibuprofen) is effective. Combining
or alternating antipyretics should only be done with careful coordination to ensure there
is no double-dosing (Green et al., 2021).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Fever - Access help
Sometimes a fever can indicate a more serious condition. Access emergency medical services
(EMS) immediately if the person has a fever combined with any of the following:
● a rash, especially if the spots are raised or firm (palpable) or the rash does not blanch
when you push on it
● a change in mental status
● difficulty breathing
● severe abdominal pain
● sensitivity to light and vomiting
● signs of shock.
Access medical care if:
● a baby with a fever is under three months of age
● a child has a temperature higher than 39°C (102.5°F)
● the person with fever is over 65 years of age
● the person with fever has cancer, a weakened immune system, sickle cell disease or is
taking medications which affect their immune system
● the fever does not decrease with paracetamol or lasts more than three days
● additional symptoms occur that are concerning.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Key action
Reassure the person and make them comfortable.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Introduction
Abdominal pain is a broad term referring to pain felt anywhere in the belly, specifically in the soft
tissues located below the lungs and above the pelvis. A variety of conditions, such as gas,
constipation, overeating, menstrual pain or an infectious stomach illness can cause acute
abdominal pain. Occasionally, abdominal pain is the result of a more serious disorder affecting
the organs in the abdomen, like kidney stones, an inflamed appendix or an inflamed
gallbladder.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Guidelines
● In case of stomach or abdominal pain, the person should remain in a position most
comfortable for them. Sitting or lying on the right side may improve gastric emptying.*
● A hot water bottle or heated wheat bag held against the lower abdomen or an abdominal
massage may relieve menstrual pain.** This can be done with or without the use of
essential oils (aromatherapy).*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Good practice points
● The first aid provider should reassure the person and help them to be more comfortable.
● In case of pain after eating a meal, it may help to keep moving (e.g. walking or running at
a moderate pace) instead of lying down or staying seated. If a person with pain after a
meal decides to lie down, it may help to have them lie on their right side.
● Upper abdominal pain and/or nausea may be symptoms of a heart attack.
● If the person has heartburn (acid-induced pain in the upper abdomen), it may help to lie
down on their back with their upper body raised.
● Emergency medical services (EMS) should be accessed if the person:
○ vomits blood
○ has chest pain or risk factors/concerns for heart attack
○ was involved in an accident/trauma
○ has severe abdominal pain
○ shows signs and symptoms of shock
○ has blood with bowel movements (this can appear as black, tarry bowel
movements or red blood)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Good practice points
○ experiences high fever (higher than 40°C for babies, children and older people)
○ is bleeding while pregnant
○ has an altered level of responsiveness.
● First aid providers should help the person access medical care if:
○ the pain does not subside
○ the abdomen is tender
○ abdominal pain is accompanied by severe diarrhoea and repeated vomiting, which
can lead to dehydration, especially in older people or young children
○ the person has a fever (higher than 38°C).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Good practice points
● Paracetamol may be effective in relieving mild menstrual pain. Non-steroidal
anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen, etc.) may also be effective;
however, they may have side effects (e.g. upset stomach or conflict with other
medications). The person may take these painkillers with fixed regularity on the days with
pain according to the recommended dose and time interval. Aside from menstrual pain,
the person should not take ibuprofen, painkillers or laxatives for abdominal pain. If
menstrual pain disrupts daily life every month, the symptoms progressively worsen, the
medication is not as effective as usual, or severe pain starts after age 25, the person
should seek medical advice.
● To prevent infectious gastrointestinal illness, personal (and group) hygiene should be
practised.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Prevent and prepare
● Keep hydrated.
● Practise food hygiene.
● Practise hand hygiene.
● Avoid contaminated or rotten food.
● Take part in regular physical activity.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Early recognition
Abdominal pain is identified by pain in the abdomen. To help decide if the abdominal pain is an
emergency and determine the first aid that will be most effective, establish what type of pain it
is by asking questions such as:
● Is the pain sudden (new) or more severe?
● What does the pain feel like?
● Was this a result of trauma?
● Are there concerns for a heart attack?
● How long have you had the pain?
● What do you think may be causing the pain?
● Do you have gas or feel constipated?
● Are you having or expecting your period?
● What have you eaten recently and how much?
● Are you experiencing any other symptoms? If so, what are they?
Common types of abdominal pain
● Menstrual pain: throbbing or cramping pains in the lower abdomen.
● Gas: pain that sometimes moves throughout the abdomen, bloating or cramping.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Early recognition
● Infectious gastroenteritis: (sometimes intense) pain accompanied by nausea, bloating
and vomiting.
● Inflamed appendix: abdominal pain that often begins around the belly button area and
moves to the right lower part of the abdomen, progressively getting worse.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - First aid steps
1.
Reassure the person and help make them comfortable.
2. Access EMS if the person:
a. vomits blood
b. has chest pain or risks/concerns for cardiac pain
c. was involved in an accident/trauma
d. has severe abdominal pain
e. shows signs and symptoms of shock
f.
has blood with bowel movements (this can appear as black, tarry bowel
movements or red blood)
g. experiences high fever (higher than 40°C for babies, children and older people)
h. is bleeding while pregnant
i.
has an altered level of responsiveness.
3. In the case of menstrual pain, give the person a hot-water bottle or a heated wheat bag to
hold against their abdomen.
● If the abdominal pain is accompanied by vomiting or diarrhoea, ensure the person keeps
hydrated by drinking small sips of water regularly.
● If the pain is menstrual pain, help the person take the recommended dose of painkiller.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - First aid steps
● If the person is experiencing pain following a meal, advise them to keep moving instead
of lying down or staying seated. If the person needs to lie down, advise them to lie on
their right side.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Access help
● Sudden, severe abdominal pain can occasionally indicate a more serious disorder, such as
appendicitis or kidney stones. It may be a sign of a surgical emergency, so it is important
to access medical care or EMS.
● Medical care should also be accessed if the pain does not subside, the person has a fever
(higher than 38°C), or if the abdominal pain is accompanied by severe diarrhoea and
repeated vomiting, which can lead to dehydration. Dehydration is common in older
people and young children.
● In older people and females, upper abdominal pain could indicate a heart attack and may
need to be seen by a medical professional. See chest pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Abdominal pain - Recovery
● Drink water regularly to stay hydrated.
● If taking a painkiller for menstrual pain, the person should take it on the days with pain
with fixed regularity according to the recommended dose and time interval. Taking a
painkiller before the pain has developed reduces overall discomfort.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Key action
Support the person to give birth, providing comfort to both the person and baby.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Introduction
Childbirth is a natural process that usually takes several hours. This allows time to access the
support of a midwife or to transport the person to a birthing facility. In some cases, an
“emergency birth” takes place very quickly and not in the place where it was planned. Childbirth
occurs naturally, and the first aid provider’s role is to support the person through the process.
There are three phases, starting with contractions and the person’s water breaking, the second
phase during which the person pushes the baby out, and the third phase when the person
pushes the afterbirth out (including the placenta).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Guidelines
● Support the person to contact their chosen birthing partner(s), as their continuous
support during labour contributes to a positive childbirth experience.**
● Being in an upright position (sitting, standing or walking) may help to shorten the
duration of labour and the pushing phase. This may result in fewer assisted births, vaginal
tears and incision of the perineum.*
● During labour, massage of the lower back may reduce pain intensity.*
● During labour, breathing exercises, yoga or listening to music may reduce pain intensity
and improve the overall birthing experience.*
● During labour, heat application (e.g. warm compresses to the perineal area or lower back
and sacrum area, a hot bath, the use of a hot water bottle on the lower back and
abdomen, etc.) may reduce pain intensity. A warm perineal compress may also reduce
vaginal tears.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Guidelines
● Delayed cord clamping (≥60 seconds after birth) for term and late preterm infants born at
or after 34 weeks’ gestation who are vigorous or deemed not to require immediate
resuscitation at birth may result in more favourable haemoglobin and haematocrit levels
of the baby.*
● Skin-to-skin contact between the mother and the baby may improve breastfeeding and
infant and maternal outcomes.*
● External uterine (self) massage in the immediate postpartum period may prevent
postpartum haemorrhage.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Good practice points
● The first aid provider should manage the scene to protect the dignity and safety of the
person, as well as take care to comfort them and give emotional support.
● The person should be supported to move into the positions most comfortable, even if the
amniotic sac is broken (waters have broken).
● The person may drink or eat something during labour if they want to.
● Hygiene measures should be taken where possible, such as wearing gloves and using
clean cloths or towels, both under the mother and to wrap the newborn in.
● As soon as the baby is delivered, the first aid provider should check both the person and
the baby for their responsiveness, breathing and for any bleeding.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Good practice points
● If the baby is responsive (e.g. crying) and breathing normally, there is no immediate need
to cut the umbilical cord and the baby should be dried and kept warm to prevent
hypothermia. Place the baby on the mother’s chest and cover with a blanket.
● If the baby is unresponsive, the first aid provider should rub the baby dry and tap the soles
of its feet. If the baby remains unresponsive and does not start breathing, CPR should be
provided as soon as possible.
● If the presence of the umbilical cord makes this difficult, it should be cut. If possible, the
umbilical cord should be tied twice (a hand's width apart) with a ribbon and cut in
between the ribbons with the first ribbon about a hand-width from the belly of the baby.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Prevent and prepare
● Know how to contact a locally available midwife or other community healthcare provider
