who can arrive quickly and provide support in an emergency.
● Encourage people expecting a baby to carry the contact phone numbers of their chosen
birthing partners, as well as their preferred midwife or birth attendant.
● Recommend pregnant people remain close to support as they near the end of their
pregnancy.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Early recognition
Talk to the person to try to determine whether they are starting labour (which may take several
hours) or whether they are having an emergency birth.
The following signs indicate that labour has started, and the baby has entered the birth canal:
● painful contractions occurring at increasingly short intervals
● abdominal discomfort
● localized back pains
● the person’s waters break
● sticky discharge.
In this instance, support the person in notifying their chosen birthing partner and preferred
birth attendants, or in arranging transport to their chosen birth facility.
Childbirth might be imminent when:
● the contractions quickly become more intense and painful
● the contractions come in short intervals (one contraction every five minutes)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Early recognition
● the person’s waters break.
If it becomes clear that the baby will arrive very soon or the person is in too much pain to travel,
prepare to support the person through the emergency birth.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - First aid steps
Initially, the first aid provider’s key priority is the person in labour. Once the baby is born, the first
aid provider has two people to care for: the person and the baby.
1.
Access help (such as medical facilities, emergency medical services or a midwife) in line
with the person’s wishes and follow their instructions. Support the person to contact their
chosen birthing partner.
2. In the first phase of childbirth, create a safe, comfortable, private and protected space for
the person. Help them move into a position of comfort. This may be sitting, standing or
moving around.
3. Offer to massage the lower back or offer relaxation methods such as yoga or listening to
music as this may reduce pain and anxiety and improve the overall birthing experience.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - First aid steps
4. If possible and if the person wants it, apply heat to the perineal, lower back, sacrum or
abdomen. You can use a warm compress or hot water bottle, or offer a hot bath. The heat
may reduce the pain intensity.
5. In the second phase of childbirth, help the person find a comfortable position, preferably
an upright one. If lying on their back, put a small pillow under the right hip. In this way,
you prevent the baby from pressing on important blood vessels.
6. If possible, wash your hands well with soap and water and place a clean cloth under the
person where the baby will be born. When the person is ready to push, ensure they are in
a supported position.
7. Watch the baby’s head as it comes out and ensure it is supported. Newly born babies are
slippery, so be very careful. Wipe any fluids or mucus away from the baby’s mouth and
nose.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - First aid steps
8. Use a clean cloth to dry off the baby. Wrap the baby in a clean cloth and cover the baby’s
head to keep it warm. Keep the mother warm as well and place the baby on the mother’s
chest or abdomen as soon as possible.
9. In the third phase of childbirth, support the person as they deliver the afterbirth. Keep the
afterbirth as a healthcare professional will need to check it is complete. Check to see if the
mother is bleeding. Mild bleeding from the birth canal is normal. If bleeding is severe,
help the person to lie down and keep them warm (see shock) until medical help arrives.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - CAUTION
● Hygiene measures should be taken where possible, such as handwashing, wearing
gloves and using clean cloths or towels, both under the person and to wrap the newborn
baby in.
● Do not pull the baby’s head and shoulders during delivery.
● Do not push on the person’s stomach during labour or after delivery.
● If the umbilical cord is wrapped around the baby’s neck during delivery, check that it is
loose and carefully ease it over the baby’s head to prevent the baby from strangulation.
● Do not pull on the umbilical cord. The afterbirth usually comes out by itself within about
30 minutes of the delivery.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - CAUTION
● If the baby is responsive and breathing normally, there is no immediate need to cut the
umbilical cord, which should be performed by a medical professional, if possible.
The person may drink or eat something during labour if they want to. This will help keep up
their strength.
Unresponsive and abnormal breathing baby
● If the baby is quiet, open their airway and check for breathing. If the baby is breathing
abnormally (gasping, taking irregular breaths or not breathing), place the baby on a firm
surface and begin CPR as described in unresponsive and abnormal breathing (baby and
child).
● If CPR is difficult because of the umbilical cord, cut the cord. To do this, if possible, tie a
ribbon or string around the cord in two places, a hand's width apart, so blood can no
longer flow through the cord. Then cut the cord in between the two ribbons.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Emergency childbirth - Access help
● Emergency medical services (EMS) may be appropriate in many childbirth cases, or the
person may have a preferred midwife or birth attendant. Consider contacting another
local midwife or other community health worker if these are not available.
● Phone EMS, medical facilities or another healthcare provider, as they will be able to tell
you what to do and support you.
● Tell EMS (or chosen healthcare provider) about any changes in the person's or baby’s
condition.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Key action
Advise the person to take the recommended dose of paracetamol (also known as
acetaminophen) to relieve their pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Introduction
A sore throat is characterized by a dry, scratchy pain in the throat, often worse when swallowing.
It can be caused by several conditions such as a viral or bacterial infection (also known as a cold)
and generally does not need medical treatment. Roughly four out of five people recover well
within a week (Gunnarsson et al., 2023). However, a bacterial infection can be serious. Individuals
between the ages of five and 24 are most likely to get a sore throat, especially during the early
spring or winter months (Rughani, 2019). Sometimes a sore throat can be severe enough to
cause the airway to swell. In these instances, the person should access medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Guidelines
● Paracetamol can reduce the pain caused by a sore throat.**
● Drinking a hot drink may relieve the pain.*
● Medicated lozenges (containing benzocaine or hexylresorcinol) or mouth sprays
(containing chlorhexidine gluconate and benzydamine hydrochloride) may relieve the
pain.*
● Antibiotics should only be given if prescribed by a medical professional.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Good practice points
● Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as ibuprofen) can be used as a second-line
treatment for sore throat, should paracetamol be ineffective.
● The first aid provider should encourage the person to drink water in small amounts.
● Harsh or high-pitched breathing sounds, the inability to swallow, severe pain or drooling
are signs and symptoms of potential airway swelling that should receive urgent medical
care.
● If a first aid provider suspects the person has a swollen airway, they should help the
person rest in a comfortable position and access medical care.
● Smoking, talking a lot, singing and shouting may make a sore throat last longer. The
person should speak as little as possible, speak at their normal volume and avoid
whispering.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Prevent and prepare
● Avoid people who are sick with an infectious illness such as influenza or strep throat
(streptococcal infection), or create a barrier (e.g. mask) between people.
● Wash your hands with soap and water or use hand sanitizer to prevent the spread of the
common cold (G. M. Allan & Arroll, 2014).
● Avoid smoking and smoky environments.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Early recognition
A person with a sore throat may:
● complain of a painful or dry, scratchy throat, especially when swallowing
● have swollen neck glands, redness at the back of the throat, swollen tonsils or whitish
spots in the throat
● experience difficulty eating and drinking.
The person may also have pain in their ear, see earache or fever. Children in particular may
experience vomiting or abdominal pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - First aid steps
1.
Advise the person to take the recommended dose of paracetamol to relieve their pain.
2. Encourage the person to drink lots of water in small amounts. A hot drink may relieve
their pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Sore throat - Access help
● The first aid provider should access medical care if someone with a sore throat:
○ has difficulty breathing
○ also experiences fever, dehydration, a painful neck or a rash
○ is not able to drink
○ has severe pain
○ is unable to manage any secretions (e.g. drooling)
○ develops an earache with pain radiating in one ear
○ has difficulty opening the mouth
○ has a high fever (39.5-41oC or 103.1-105.8oF) when taken with a thermometer that
measures heat from the tympanic membrane in the ear.
○ has severe throat pain and paracetamol has no effect
○ does not see any improvements after multiple days
○ experiences a sore throat frequently.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - Key action
Advise the person to take the recommended dose of paracetamol (also known as
acetaminophen) and seek medical attention if the earache remains or gets worse over 48 hours.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - Guidelines
● If trained and it is safe to do so, first aid providers may give the person paracetamol for
pain relief.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - Good practice points
● Advise the person not to pick their ear as this can cause damage to the ear.
● Medical advice should be sought when there is fever, fluid draining from the ear, vertigo
or loss of or decreased hearing associated with ear pain.
● The person should seek medical advice if the symptoms get worse or do not improve
within 48 hours.
● A source of heat can be held against the affected area and may reduce pain.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - Prevent and prepare
● Teach children to avoid putting objects in their ears, such as cotton swabs or buds, or
pencils.
● People using noisy equipment should use ear defenders to reduce noise below 85
decibels.
● Be alert to earaches in people who use a hearing aid or who listen to music through
headphones.
● Be alert to earaches in people who spend a lot of time in the water, have an abscess or
infection in their gums or have had a cold or flu.
● Keep ears warm and dry where possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - Early recognition
● The person may complain of pain, changes in hearing or a sensation of fullness in their
ear.
● The ear may be hot or sensitive to touch.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - First aid steps
1.
Help the person take the recommended dose of an over-the-counter painkiller (e.g.
paracetamol) to reduce pain.
2. Give them a warm compress, such as a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel, to hold
against their ear to reduce pain.
3. In the case that there is something in the ear canal (e.g. insects, beads), do not try to
remove it. Seek medical advice.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Earache - Access help
● Seek medical advice if there is discharge coming from the ear, hearing loss, vertigo or
fever. Seek medical advice if the earache does not improve within 48 hours.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Key action
Advise the person to take the recommended dose of paracetamol (also known as
acetaminophen).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Introduction
Headaches are a common condition. Typical symptoms include a mild to painful throbbing or
tight sensation in the head, pain behind the eyes (especially when looking at bright lights) or
dizziness. In more extreme cases, symptoms might include nausea or vomiting. A migraine is a
type of headache that is often reoccurring. Usually, a headache does not have a serious cause
and will pass; however, in some cases, it can indicate a more serious condition. First aid providers
should seek to understand the probable cause of the headache.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Guidelines
● If a person experiences a tension-type headache or an acute migraine headache, the first
aid provider should advise them to take 1,000 mg of paracetamol or nonsteroidal
anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Good practice points
● Paracetamol and other painkillers should only be used if a headache results from minor
causes such as tiredness or stress.
● Applying an ice pack or cold compress to the head or back of the neck may provide relief
from migraine symptoms.
● Bright lights (e.g. from an office or phone screen) may make a headache or migraine
worse. If the individual with either condition is sensitive to light, they should sit or lie in a
dark or dimly lit room to increase comfort and reduce the pain.
● Individuals with a headache should get fresh air, get enough sleep, drink water regularly
and take time to relax.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Prevent and prepare
● Understanding the causes of headaches can help prevent them from occurring.
Headaches can be caused by:
○ stress
○ poor sleep
○ flu or cold
○ meningitis
○ Hyperthermia
○ Head injury
○ Dehydration
○ alcohol consumption.
● The use of painkillers such as paracetamol is most effective when taken at the early stages
of the onset of pain. Taking a painkiller at the first sign of a headache may prevent a more
severe one from developing.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Early recognition
A person may have a headache if they:
● have pain behind their eyes
● feel a tightness around their head
● have painful throbbing in their head
● have an increased sensitivity to noise or light
● are nauseous.
The condition may indicate another more severe condition if the headache is accompanied by:
● fever
● vomiting (without diarrhoea or fever)
● skin rash
● memory loss
● neck pain or stiffness
● coordination problems
● problems with eyesight
● drowsiness or sleepiness
● trauma to the head.
The pain caused by a headache can range in frequency and severity.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - First aid steps
1.
Reduce anything that may worsen the headache (such as direct sunlight or noise). If safe
to do so, move the person to a quiet space.
2. Advise the person to take 1,000 mg of paracetamol.
3. Advise them to rest in a dark, quiet room. It may help to place an ice pack or cold
compress on their head or neck.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Access help
Headaches can sometimes indicate a more serious underlying disorder. Access emergency
medical care if the headache is severe and is accompanied by:
● vomiting (without diarrhoea or fever)
● a sore or stiff neck
● a rash, as this may indicate meningitis
● memory loss
● double or blurred vision
● fever
● signs of a Stroke.
Or if the severe pain:
● follows a head injury
● becomes worse very fast
● occurs during exertion (e.g. exercise) or a change in posture
● started suddenly within the last three months of pregnancy
● does not go away even after taking painkillers or reducing potential causes
● occurs regularly, without explanation, in children under the age of six.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Headache - Recovery
● The person may take painkillers for frequent tension headaches as required, following the
advice provided with the medication regarding frequency and over what time period.
However, if the headache persists or new patterns emerge, the person should seek a
medical assessment.
● Follow any recovery instructions from the healthcare professional.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hiccups - Introduction
A hiccup (or hiccough) is a sudden contraction of a muscle called the diaphragm that helps a
person to breathe in and that repeats several times per minute. During a hiccup, the muscle
contraction causes the person to take in a quick breath. This breath in is then interrupted by the
epiglottis closing over the windpipe, making a “hic” sound. Hiccups can occur “spontaneously”,
after eating or drinking, or in the context of a wide variety of illnesses or medical interventions.
Short hiccup spells are commonly experienced by healthy children and adults. Adult males are
more likely to experience episodes of hiccups (Lee et al., 2016).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hiccups - Good practice points
● Home remedies such as holding one’s breath for a couple of seconds, doing the Valsalva
manoeuvre for a short time, sipping ice-cold water, swallowing some granulated sugar,
biting into a lemon or tasting vinegar may be effective.
● The use of gripe water is not recommended.
● A person with hiccups should seek medical advice if hiccups last longer than 48 hours or
if they have other symptoms in combination with hiccups, such as chest pain, weakness
in their limbs or face, headache or trouble keeping balance.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hiccups - Prevent and prepare
● Giving babies a break from feeding and burping them may reduce the amount of air in
their stomachs and may help prevent hiccups.
● Eating slowly and avoiding alcohol may help reduce the likelihood of hiccups.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hiccups - Early recognition
● A person with hiccups will take a short breath inward, followed by a “hic” sound. This can
occur between two and 60 times per minute.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hiccups - First aid steps
1.
Comfort the person and reassure them that hiccups usually pass after a few minutes.
2. If they can, encourage them to perform the Valsalva manoeuvre (take a deep breath in,
close the nose and mouth and gently blow out) for a short time.
There are other methods to stop hiccups that may be more suited to some contexts.
● Drink a glass of ice-cold water.
● Suck a sugar cube or an ice cube.
● Bite into a lemon.
● Hold your breath for a couple of seconds.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hiccups - Access help
● Generally, hiccups pass within a few minutes. Seek medical advice if the hiccups last
longer than 48 hours or if the person has other symptoms in combination with hiccups,
such as chest pain, weakness in their limbs or face, headache or trouble keeping balance.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Key action
Rapidly cool the person to reduce their body temperature.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Introduction
Hyperthermia occurs when the body reaches abnormally high temperatures because it is
unable to regulate its internal temperature. It occurs when the body produces or absorbs too
much heat, or a combination of both. Hyperthermia can be mild (heat exhaustion) or severe
(heatstroke). There are two types of hyperthermia: exertional heat illness (EHI), when the body
produces too much heat, and non-exertional heat illness (or “classic” hyperthermia), when the
body absorbs too much heat. Children and the elderly are most at risk for a “classic”
hyperthermia.
Exertional heatstroke is a medical emergency characterized by life-threatening hyperthermia
and central nervous system dysfunction during or directly after exercise. Early recognition and
aggressive cooling reduce the morbidity and mortality of a person with heatstroke (Van den
Bersselaar, 2020).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Guidelines
● In the case of an adult experiencing severe hyperthermia (heatstroke) due to intense
physical activity, the first aid provider should consider immersing the person from the
neck down in cold water (1-26°C/33.8-78.8°F) until a core body temperature of less than
39°C (102.2°F) is achieved. If this is not possible, cool the person using any other active
cooling technique (e.g. a wet sheet, water or ice packs placed in the armpits, neck and
groin area).**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Good practice points
● The person should stop all physical activity and be removed from the hot environment to
a cool place.
● For people with hyperthermia due to intense physical activity, first aid providers can also
consider using other immediate active or passive cooling techniques available to them
(e.g. cold-water immersion of hands or feet, ice packs, cold showers, fanning, ice sheets
and towels).
● If the person has hyperthermia due to intense physical activity and is responsive enough,
they may have something cool to drink. This may include water, a water and sugar
solution or a water and salt solution (e.g. a homemade oral rehydration solution or a
sports drink). See Dehydration.
● The first aid provider should access emergency medical services (EMS) if the person:
○ shows unusual behaviour, confusion or becomes unresponsive
○ has a seizure
○ has a body temperature above 39°C (102.2°F)

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Good practice points
○ stops sweating
○ cannot drink without vomiting.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Prevent and prepare
● The risk of hyperthermia depends on a person’s ability to adapt to heat. This adaptability
depends on four factors:
○ activity level (e.g. limit physical activities during the hottest part of the day)
○ freedom of choice of clothing (e.g. wear appropriate clothing for the temperature
and activity)
○ adaptability to the environment (e.g. take frequent breaks to drink water)
○ personal factors (e.g. a person’s health and fitness level)
● In places where there is a high risk of hyperthermia, consider making cooling methods
available so there is no delay in first aid when hyperthermia occurs.
● Be aware that EHI can also occur in cool environments.
● Monitor weather conditions.
● Plan work and rest times if working in warm conditions.
● Develop an action plan in case conditions suddenly change and there is a higher risk of
hyperthermia (e.g. a sudden heatwave).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Prevent and prepare
● Monitor urine colour for signs of dehydration.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Early recognition
The person’s condition will depend on how much the body has overheated.
Mild to moderate hyperthermia (heat exhaustion):
● normal or mildly higher temperature
● cool, pale, clammy skin
● excessive sweating
● thirsty
● headache
● muscle cramps
● rapid, weak pulse
● fainting or dizziness.
Severe hyperthermia (heatstroke or heat stress combined with an altered mental status):
● the person has stopped sweating (indicating they are severely dehydrated)
● high body temperature (above 40°C/104°F)
● dry, flushed, hot skin
● nausea
● muscle spasms
● feeling lightheaded or dizzy, disoriented
● pain throughout the body
● unusual behaviour (aggressive combativeness or drowsiness) or signs of confusion
● seizure or possible loss of responsiveness.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - First aid steps
1.
Advise the person to stop all physical activity immediately. Help them to rest in a cool
place and to remove any excess clothing.
Mild to moderate hyperthermia
1.
Cool the person down using any technique available, such as immersing their hands and
feet in cold water, applying ice packs to their neck and groin areas, encouraging them to
have a cold shower or fanning them.
2. If the person is not vomiting, give them some water, sports drink or cold tea with sugar to
drink.
3. Monitor the person’s temperature and level of response. Try to reduce their temperature
to less than 39°C (102.2oF).
4. A person with mild to moderate hyperthermia will usually recover without medical care.
Monitor them closely in case their condition does not improve or worsens. And access
EMS if in any doubt.
Severe hyperthermia

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - First aid steps
1.
Access EMS immediately. Heatstroke is life-threatening. Be alert to any unusual behaviour
(aggressive combativeness or drowsiness) or signs of confusion.
2. Help the person lie down in a cool place and remove any excess clothing.
3. Start cooling the person down immediately. Immerse the person in cold water (1-26°
C/33.8-78.8°F) for about 15 minutes, or until their temperature has dropped to less than
39°C (102.2°F). If this is not possible (e.g. cold water is unavailable or the person is confused
and refuses), cool the person using any other active cooling technique (e.g. place cool, wet
sheets or towels on the person or wet them with cold water and place ice packs on their
neck and groin areas). Fanning the person will also help cool them down.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - First aid steps
● Severe hyperthermia (heatstroke) is a time critical illness and the priority is rapid and
effective cooling prior to transfer to a hospital.
● If medical personnel are available, the person’s core (rectal) temperature should be
recorded as soon as possible as an indicator of severity and to guide treatment (DeGroot
et al., 2022).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hyperthermia - Recovery
● After cooling the person down, monitor them closely, as they may start to feel cold and
shiver, especially if they are still wearing wet clothes. If this happens, give them a blanket.
● Encourage the person to drink oral rehydration solutions, sports drinks or tea with sugar.
Start with a small amount and wait to ensure the person does not vomit the liquid back
up.
● Encourage the person to rest. In most cases, people with mild to moderate hyperthermia
will recover fully.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Key action
Give the person plenty of fluids to drink as tolerated.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Introduction
Dehydration is a shortage of water in the body and occurs when a person loses more fluid than
they take in. It can result from a range of conditions (vomiting, diarrhoea, heat stress, fever, etc.),
vigorous activity in hot and humid environments, or when wearing excess clothing. These
conditions result in a significant loss of water through sweat and other bodily fluids. They also
cause the person to lose electrolytes, which are essential for the body to function normally.
When the body is dehydrated, it can experience cramps, changes in mental capacity or even
shock (which can be life-threatening if left untreated), especially in small children or older adults.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Guidelines
● First aid providers should encourage people with mild dehydration to drink fluids (e.g.
water or diluted apple juice in children older than six months).**
● In more severe cases, first aid providers should rehydrate the person using either
commercially prepared oral rehydration salts or a pre-prepared salt package that
complies with the World Health Organization’s recommendations for oral rehydration
salts solutions.**
● First aid providers can use 4%–9% carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks to care for
exertion-related dehydration. If these are not available or not tolerated, alternative
beverages include water, 0%–3.9% carbohydrate-electrolyte solution, coconut water or 2%
or low-fat milk.*
● Breastfeeding for babies should be continued.**

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Good practice points
● Breastfed babies require more frequent feedings as they generally receive less milk each
time they feed than bottle-fed babies. Breastfeeding can be supplemented with oral
rehydration solution (ORS).
● If using formula, babies should receive normal amounts of milk (powder dissolved in
water, NOT in ORS), SUPPLEMENTED with ORS.
● Emergency medical services (EMS) should be accessed if the person’s responsiveness is
altered (trouble waking up, confusion) or they become unresponsive.
● First aid providers should seek medical advice if they are in doubt, or if the person:
○ is a baby, child or older adult
○ loses more fluid than they take (e.g. severe vomiting)
○ urinates very little or not at all, and the urine is a dark colour
○ has a fever or signs of heat exhaustion.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Good practice points
● In cases of mild diarrhoea, other juices (e.g. guava or mango) can be used as an
alternative to apple juice, or as an addition to ORS.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Prevent and prepare
● In hot weather, regularly check on older adults and babies to ensure they remain cool and
drink plenty of fluids.
● Ensure babies and young children continue to take breast or bottle milk (or other drinks)
when they have fever or diarrhoea or are vomiting, as the risk of dehydration is high.
● Avoid doing any vigorous activity outside during the hottest part of the day.
● Train and acclimatize your body in the lead up to significant sports activity.
● In hot weather, dress appropriately, take frequent breaks in a shaded area, drink plenty of
(cool) fluids and avoid activities that over-exert yourself.
● In cold weather, avoid overexertion that causes sweating or reduce the number of layers
of clothing.
● Be aware that dehydration can occur in any weather, not just hot weather. It is important
to stay hydrated in all situations.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Prevent and prepare
● Carry plenty of fluids if travelling in remote areas with limited water supply.
● Practise good food and hand hygiene, and only consume clean (potable) water to avoid
vomiting and diarrhoea (one of the main causes of dehydration).
● As the climate continues to warm, more extreme heat events are expected to occur in
locations that are unprepared for the consequences of high temperatures. It is valuable to
learn how to prepare for these changing climates.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Early recognition
The person may be in a hot environment, doing vigorous physical activity during a heatwave, or
may not have adequate access to fluids.
The person may have:
● diarrhoea or vomiting
● fever
● altered responsiveness
● headache
● dizziness
● less or no sweat (e.g. under the armpits)
● absence of tears
● dark coloured urine
● weak radial pulse
● dry mouth and tongue
● delayed time to skin re-colouration
● abnormal breathing pattern
● fatigue (in the elderly).
In babies and young children look for:
● dry mouth and tongue
● crying without tears
● sunken eyes
● unusually tired or sleepy
● a dry diaper for three hours or more.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - First aid steps
1.
Reassure the person and give them plenty of fluids to drink.
a. In mild cases of dehydration, water is sufficient.
b. In more severe cases, give the person an oral rehydration solution (ORS). If this is
unavailable, give the person apple juice, coconut water or water.
For children:
● Babies and young children who are breastfed should continue to be so. The frequency of
feeding should be increased.
● Babies receiving milk formula should drink regular amounts of milk, supplemented with
ORS. The formula should be dissolved in water, not in ORS, as the latter may cause
diarrhoea and worsen dehydration further.
● Children between the ages of two and five years should have 10 ml/kg (the caregiver will
need to estimate their weight) of water, rehydration solution, apple juice, coconut water
or water.
● Any fluids given to the person should be non-alcoholic.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - First aid steps
● To create one litre of ORS, combine:
○ half a teaspoon of salt
○ six teaspoons sugar
○ One litre of drinking water
DO NOT give an ORS to a person experiencing a diabetic hyper crisis as it could have severe
negative effects and worsen dehydration further.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Dehydration - Access help
● Access EMS if the person’s mental status changes (e.g. confusion) or they become
unresponsive.
● Seek medical advice if:
○ the person’s condition does not improve quickly
○ they are a baby, child or older adult
○ they are losing more fluid than they can take in (e.g. because of vomiting or
diarrhoea)
○ they urinate very little or not at all and the urine is a dark colour
○ has fever or signs of heat exhaustion
○ you are in doubt.
Self-recovery
● To avoid a case of new dehydration, continue to drink fluids regularly. Eat fruit and
vegetables regularly.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Key action
Gradually warm the person using the most appropriate equipment available.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Introduction
Hypothermia is a condition in which the body’s core temperature drops below 35°C (95°F) and
cannot function properly; blood circulation reduces significantly, especially in the small vessels in
the skin. It can occur when a person is exposed to extreme cold, such as in mountainous regions
in the winter. Other factors that intensify the risk of hypothermia are living in homes that lack
heating, the use of alcohol or substances or pre-existing mental health conditions (Gordon et al.,
2014). Some conditions reduce people’s ability to recognize when they have lost a significant
amount of heat.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Guidelines
● If the person has stopped shivering, the first aid provider should actively warm them,
preferably using an electric heating blanket. Hot water bottles, heating pads or warm
stones may be used as alternatives.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Good practice points
● People experiencing hypothermia should be treated with care, removed from the cold
source and have any wet clothes removed. If the person is moderately to severely
hypothermic, clothes should be cut off to minimize their movement as this could lead to
dangerous heart arrhythmias.
● A person experiencing hypothermia, who is responsive and shivering vigorously, may be
warmed passively (e.g. using a sleeping bag, a fleece or a 100% polyester blanket, with a
wind or vapour barrier). The head and body should be covered to minimize convective
and evaporative heat loss. Alternative equipment may be used, including warm, dry
clothing or reflective material. The person should contract and relax large muscles to
generate internal heat.
● Do NOT apply warm stones directly to the skin to avoid burning the person. Do NOT rub
the person’s skin, as this may damage the skin and underlying muscles.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Good practice points
● Care should then be taken to insulate the person by placing a barrier between them and
the ground (e.g. a tarp and sleeping bag) to minimize conductive heat loss.
● If the person is responsive and able to swallow, the first aid provider should give them a
warm sugary drink (e.g. hot chocolate) or some high-energy food.
● For all cases of hypothermia, emergency medical services (EMS) or equivalent should be
accessed and the person’s airway, breathing and circulation should be monitored.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Prevent and prepare
● Wear appropriate cold-weather clothing.
● Keep clothing dry. If clothing gets wet, change into dry clothing as soon as possible.
● In cold weather, check on those in insecure housing or without heating to ensure they
have ways to keep themselves warm.
● Eat high-energy foods and drink high-calorie drinks, as well as water, to prevent
dehydration.
● Avoid alcohol.
● If possible, take regular breaks from the cold to allow the body to warm up.
● When planning to visit a remote, cold area, check how to access local emergency services
and take appropriate signals and contact details with you.
● Ensure someone knows when you are venturing to a remote place, the route you plan to
take and when you expect to return.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Early recognition
Symptoms will depend on the temperature and whether the person is experiencing mild or
severe hypothermia. Take into account the surrounding environment, for example, if the person
is in a cold environment or wearing wet clothing, they are at a higher risk of hypothermia.
The person may have the following:
● shivering
● poor coordination
● slow movements
● mild confusion
● skin becomes paler, ashen or loses its colour
● bluish colouring to lips, ears, fingers and toes.
As their condition worsens, they may show the following:
● no shivering
● disorientation, lack of memory
● exposed skin becomes blue and swollen
● may become incoherent or behave irrationally
● coordination continues to worsen; the person cannot walk or use their hands.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - First aid steps
1.
Remove the person from the cold or protect them from further cooling.
2. Have the person remove any wet clothes (or help them if they are unable to do so).
Carefully dry off the person if they are wet. Cover and protect the person from the cold.
3. If a person is responsive and shivering, let them warm up using a sleeping bag or a
blanket. If they can swallow, give them a warm, sugary drink (e.g. hot chocolate) or some
high-energy food.
4. If the person is in an altered state of responsiveness and is not shivering, gradually warm
them using an electric heating blanket. Hot water bottles, heating pads or warm stones
can be used as alternatives. Be sure there is a layer between the item and the skin to
prevent burns.
5. Reassure the person and monitor their breathing and level of response.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - CAUTION
● Do not rub the person’s skin, as this may damage it and the underlying muscles further.
● Do not apply warm stones directly to the skin as this may burn the person.
● If the person becomes unresponsive, open their airway and check for breathing. See
Unresponsiveness.
● In a limited-resource setting, create a heat source (such as a campfire) to warm the
person and build a shelter to protect them from the cold. Ensure there is a layer, such as
a blanket, between the person and the ground.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Access help
For all cases of hypothermia, the first aid provider should access emergency medical care
immediately.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Hypothermia - Recovery
Most healthy people with mild to moderate hypothermia will recover fully. However, if signs and
symptoms continue or additional ones appear, seek medical care.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Key action
Gently immerse the affected area in warm water until it is rewarmed (usually 30 minutes) and
protect it from cold.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Introduction
Frostbite is damage to the skin and other tissues caused by extreme cold. When it is cold (at or
below 0°C) or there are strong winds, the human body tries to preserve its core body
temperature by constricting the blood vessels near the skin. In extreme cases, this can reduce
the blood flow in some areas of the body to dangerously low levels, resulting in frostbite. The
fingers and toes are the most vulnerable. Frostbite can lead to permanent damage, but this can
be avoided if it is recognized and treated quickly.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Good practice points
● Warming of frozen body parts should be done only if the appropriate resources are
available, medical care is more than two hours away and there is no risk of refreezing.
● Warming should be achieved by immersing the affected area in warm water between
37ºC and 39ºC (98.6ºF and 102ºF) until the affected body part takes on a red or purple
appearance and becomes soft and pliable to the touch (usually in 30 minutes).
● Other heat sources (e.g. fire, space heater, oven, heated rocks) should be avoided because
of the risk of burns.
● During warming, consider giving the person a high dose of ibuprofen (400-800 mg) or, if
unavailable, a low dose of acetylsalicylic acid (75-81mg). This may improve healing.
● After warming, the frostbitten area should be protected from refreezing and the person
should seek medical care as soon as possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Good practice points
● Topical aloe vera may be applied to the frostbite after re-warming.
● Affected body parts should be dressed in sterile gauze until the person can access
medical care. If fingers or toes are affected, the gauze should be placed between them.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Prevent and prepare
● Ensure feet, hands and face are kept warm and covered in cold conditions.
● Pack appropriate equipment and clothing for the weather conditions, including
emergency items in case conditions worsen.
● Take shelter from extreme cold or strong cold winds.
● Be aware that cold temperatures numb the nerves in the skin and reduce sensitivity. This
makes it more challenging to notice when frostbite occurs.
● Be aware that with humidity and wind, frostbite can occur at temperatures as high as 5ºC
and 7ºC.
● Be aware that metal items (e.g. glasses or jewellery) can cause the skin to suddenly freeze
when exposed to cold, damp wind, especially if the skin the metal touches is sweaty.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Early recognition
● Early frostbite may be marked by flushed skin, sensation changes such as burning,
prickling or numbness, or pain in the exposed cold area. The skin flushing can decrease as
the skin cools, and it can appear paler from decreased blood flow. Skin becomes cold,
hard to the touch, waxy and blisters can form. As frostbite progresses, the skin dies and
turns dark blue or black.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - First aid steps
1.
Protect the person from hypothermia. Do this by helping them move to a warmer place,
removing wet clothing and keeping them warm and dry.
2. Carefully remove jewellery if this is possible without causing any damage to the skin.
3. Gently warm the affected area by putting it in warm (body temperature) water until it is
rewarmed (usually 30 minutes). Avoid rubbing or aggressively handling the affected area
as this may damage the skin.
4. Dress the affected area with sterile gauze. If multiple digits are affected, place gauze
between each digit.
5. Consider giving the person a high dose of ibuprofen (400-800 mg) or, if unavailable, a low
dose of acetylsalicylic acid (75-81mg). This may improve healing.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - CAUTION
● Rewarm the frostbitten area if you have appropriate resources, there is no risk of
refreezing and you can rewarm the part faster than if they access medical care.
● Do not put the affected area near direct heat like a space heater or hot stove.
● Avoid breaking blisters that may occur.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Frostbite - Access help
● Always access medical care in the case of frostbite.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Key action
Take the person to a lower altitude as quickly and safely as possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Introduction
Altitude sickness occurs when people at a high altitude do not have enough oxygen in their
blood because the air pressure is too low. As altitude increases, the air becomes thinner and less
oxygen is inhaled with each breath. The term altitude sickness includes:
● Acute mountain sickness (AMS)
● High altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), affecting the lungs and breathing
● High altitude cerebral edema (HACE), affecting the brain, behaviour and alertness.
Individuals most affected by altitude sicknesses are those who travel to a high altitude quickly
(e.g. tourists), especially if they have pre-existing medical conditions. However, trained
mountaineers can also develop symptoms when they reach very high altitudes, such as in the
Himalayan region.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Guidelines
● People experiencing AMS, HACE or HAPE should stop their ascent immediately and start
to descend safely, with support, until their symptoms lessen.**
● If the person has prescribed medication for altitude sickness with them (such as
acetazolamide or dexamethasone), the first aid provider may assist them in taking it
based on the label instructions.*
● Where local laws, regulations, or protocols permit, specially trained first aid providers may
give medications (such as acetazolamide or dexamethasone) to individuals experiencing
altitude sickness.*
● For first aid providers trained in its use, oxygen may be administered to individuals
experiencing AMS, HACE or HAPE.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Good practice points
● People experiencing altitude sickness should be kept from getting cold or overheated.
● Gradual or staged ascent to higher altitudes may be a more effective method of
prevention than a fast ascent.
● Adequate hydration should be maintained (though not forced). The person should drink
regularly (every 20–30 minutes) and enough (more than they would normally drink).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Prevent and prepare
● Check how to access local emergency services and pack appropriate signals and contact
details when going to high altitudes.
● Ensure you have the right equipment with you to make a safe descent.
● Eat high-energy foods and drink high-calorie drinks, as well as water, to prevent
dehydration.
● Ensure someone knows the route you plan to take if you are venturing to a remote place,
and when you expect to return.
● Avoid alcohol.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Early recognition
People may start to experience symptoms at around 2,400 m (roughly 8,000 feet). Twenty-five
per cent of travellers experience AMS above 3,500 m (11,483 feet), with 50% experiencing it above
6,000 m (19,685 feet). Be aware of the signs of altitude sickness if travelling above this altitude
(Hackett & Shlim, 2019).
Several altitude sickness diagnostic-scoring systems exist. The Lake Louise Criteria for Altitude
Sickness (Roach et al., 2018) are as follows:
Acute mountain sickness
If the person chooses to remain at a certain altitude, AMS may improve with rest, hydration and
medication. However, the symptoms will improve faster by descending to a lower altitude. There
is also the risk that AMS will progress to HAPE or HACE.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Early recognition
● Headache and at least one of the following symptoms: fatigue or weakness; dizziness or
light-headedness; gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea or vomiting, loss of appetite);
difficulty sleeping; shortness of breath.
High-altitude pulmonary edema
HAPE is when fluid collects in the lungs (pulmonary edema) and causes extreme shortness of
breath. It is life-threatening and requires immediate, safe descent.
● At least two of the following symptoms: difficulty breathing while resting; coughing;
weakness or decreased physical performance; chest tightness or congestion.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Early recognition
● At least two of the following signs: crackling or wheezing heard in one or both lungs when
breathing; bluish colouring to the skin, lips and fingers; rapid breathing and elevated
heart rate.
High-altitude cerebral edema
HACE is when fluid collects on the brain, causing confusion, coma, and, if untreated, death. It is
life-threatening and requires immediate, safe descent.
● Change in responsiveness, behaviour, normal movement or coordination in a person,
either with or without acute mountain sickness.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - First aid steps
1.
Help the person move to a lower altitude as quickly and safely as possible. Encourage
them to drink water.
2. If the person has prescribed medication for altitude sickness, help them take it.
3. Have the person rest at a lower altitude until their symptoms resolve. If local regulations
permit, and you are trained to do so, administer oxygen to the person. You may do this
upon arrival at a lower altitude, or if necessary, while descending with the person.
4. Access emergency medical services (EMS) if the person’s condition does not improve.
Monitor the person’s temperature to ensure they do not get too cold or hot. See hypothermia
or Hyperthermia.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Access help
● Access help if the person is unable to descend on their own and it is unsafe for other
group members to transport them to a lower altitude. Help may take many forms,
including other hikers, search and rescue, formal evacuation teams or military assistance.
● Access EMS if the person’s condition does not improve.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Altitude sickness - Recovery
● If a person with AMS is asymptomatic, they may continue to ascend. They should monitor
themselves for signs and symptoms of AMS, HAPE and HACE.
● Once descended to a lower altitude, a person with HAPE or HACE should not re-ascend
until their symptoms have resolved and they have been examined by a medical
professional.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Key action
Access emergency medical services (EMS) immediately and administer oxygen if specifically
trained.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Introduction
Decompression illness results from a reduction in the ambient pressure surrounding a person’s
body. It is commonly caused by pressure changes that occur in scuba diving, a very popular
sport in many parts of the world. Decompression illness includes two conditions: decompression
sickness and arterial gas embolism. Decompression sickness is thought to result from bubbles
growing in the tissue and causing local damage. Arterial gas embolism results from bubbles
entering the circulation, collecting together and travelling through the arteries and causing
tissue damage by blocking blood flow to the small vessels.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Good practice points
● In the case of suspected decompression illness, specifically trained first aid providers
should administer oxygen at the highest concentration available (such as a
non-rebreather mask), which may reduce the symptoms substantially. The oxygen should
be continued until medical care is accessed.
● First aid providers should access EMS immediately, as well as the Divers Alert Network
(see Access help section below) and indicate the likelihood of decompression illness so
that transport of the person to a recompression chamber can be arranged as soon as
possible. Definitive treatment is usually oxygen therapy provided in a recompression
chamber.
● In cases of cardiac arrest after resurfacing, CPR should be administered with rescue
breaths.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Good practice points
● In locations requiring extended or complicated transport to a recompression chamber,
rapid transport to a nearby emergency department capable of resuscitation should be
prioritized for stabilization prior to transport to the chamber.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Prevent and prepare
● Be aware of and actively reduce the risk factors, including deep or long dives, cold water,
hard exercise at depth and rapid ascents.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Early recognition
Symptoms of decompression illnesses usually appear 15 minutes to 12 hours after surfacing, but
in severe cases, may appear before surfacing or immediately afterwards.
Decompression sickness
Symptoms include the following:
● unusual fatigue
● skin itch
● pain in joints and muscles of the arms, legs or body
● dizziness, vertigo, ringing in the ears
● numbness, tingling, paralysis
● shortness of breath.
Arterial gas embolism
Symptoms include the following:
● dizziness
● chest pain
● disorientation
● bloody froth from the mouth or nose
● paralysis or weakness
● convulsions
● becoming unresponsive.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - First aid steps
1.
If specifically trained, administer oxygen to the person.
2. Access EMS. If possible, call the Divers Alert Network +1-919-684-9111.
3. Monitor the person’s level of response, breathing and circulation until EMS arrives.
● If the person becomes unresponsive, open their airway and check for breathing.
● If the person becomes unresponsive with abnormal breathing after resurfacing, CPR
should be administered with rescue breaths.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Decompression illness - Access help
● Phone EMS immediately. They will be able to tell you what to do and arrange help.
● The Divers Alert Network is an international not-for-profit organization with a helpline
which can be reached 365 days a year, 24 hours a day, by phone: +1-919-684-9111. This
network provides assistance with managing injured scuba divers, helps determine if
recompression is needed, provides the location of the closest appropriate recompression
facility and helps arrange transport for the person.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Key action
Stop travelling if possible to allow the person time to recover and take corrective action.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Introduction
Motion sickness is caused when the brain’s estimate of motion is different from what the person
is experiencing. The person’s eyes, balance centre of the inner ear, and general perception of
their body’s position and movement conflict with the messages the brain receives. The
sensitivity to motion sickness varies in individuals, but most people will experience it if the cause
is strong enough. Pregnant women, children older than two years and those with migraines are
most susceptible. First aid care is often ineffective, and providers should emphasize prevention
instead.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Guidelines
● Eating a light meal, taking a dose of ginger, or chewing peppermints or ginger gum
before travelling may help prevent motion sickness.*
● Controlled breathing and distracting the ill person with an activity (e.g. listening to music)
may help to reduce symptoms of motion sickness.*
● Looking straight ahead through the windshield, keeping the eyes open, looking outside
and fixing the gaze on a central point on the horizon, as well as restricting one’s view, may
help prevent motion sickness. Sitting in a chair with a high backrest, facing in the
direction of travel, wearing an acustimulation wristband and having control over the
movement of the vehicle (driving oneself) may also help prevent motion sickness.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Good practice points
● Stopping the means of transport may decrease nausea.
● Getting fresh air during travel, with a window open and air on the face, may reduce
symptoms of motion sickness.
● Those who have used medications such as antihistamines to relieve motion sickness
previously should continue to use them if they are found to be effective.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Prevent and prepare
The following methods may help prevent motion sickness:
● Eat a light meal before travelling.
● Drive the vehicle yourself, if possible.
● Take one to two grams of ginger (e.g. tea or biscuits) before or during travel.
● Sit in a chair with a high backrest during travel, facing forward.
● Look outside and fix the gaze on a central point on the horizon.
● Wear a P6 acupressure or P6 acustimulation wristband while travelling.
Additionally, some may find it helpful to:
● take mint or peppermint before or during travel
● sleep through travel
● get fresh air during travel.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Early recognition
Initially, the person’s skin may become pale or ashen.
The person may feel dizzy or have a headache.
As symptoms progress, the person may experience nausea or vomiting.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - First aid steps
1.
Stop travelling if possible, to allow the person time to recover and take corrective action.
2. If it is not possible to stop travelling, tell the person to face forward and to look straight
ahead at a fixed point on the horizon.
3. If possible, provide fresh air and encourage the person to take slow and regular breaths.
4. Try to distract the person (e.g. play some music).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Motion sickness - Access help
Usually, motion sickness passes without the need to access help.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Key action
Provide support to those who have experienced a traumatic event. Listen, be empathetic,
maintain contact and connect the person to other resources.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Introduction
From a psychological perspective, trauma refers to any disturbing experience that results in
significant fear, helplessness, dissociation, confusion or other disruptive feelings intense enough
to have a long-lasting negative effect on a person’s attitudes, behaviour and other aspects of
functioning. Traumatic events include those caused by human behaviour (e.g. sexual and
gender-based violence (SGBV), conflict, industrial accidents) as well as by natural hazards (e.g. earthquakes) and often challenge an individual’s view of the world as a just, safe and predictable
place (American Psychological Association, n.d.-c). A traumatic event involves exposure to a perceived or actual threat of death, serious injury or
violence. Examples of such events include severe accidents, fires, robberies, physical attacks,
violent attacks, disasters and any form of sexual and gender-based violence. The word “exposure”
covers different events; it could be a direct experience, witnessing something traumatic or
learning about a loved one experiencing such an event. A traumatic event is usually unexpected,
unavoidable and dangerous. Trauma-informed practice in first aid involves recognizing and responding to the psychological
and emotional needs of individuals who have experienced traumatic events. This approach
emphasizes safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration and empowerment.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Introduction
This section provides a brief introduction on how to support people experiencing a traumatic
event. It aims to provide learners with tips to develop greater awareness and streamline first aid
procedures. It does not expect the learners to deliver psychological first aid (PFA) without formal
training.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Guidelines
● Integrating PFA principles (listening, being empathetic, maintaining contact and
connecting to other resources) to provide support to those who have experienced a
traumatic event may help to reduce trauma-related anxiety.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Good practice points
● The following interventions are recommended to support those who have experienced a
traumatic event:
○ Engage in conversation.
○ Listen to the person’s concerns.
○ Offer empathetic support.
○ Maintain contact as long as the first aid provider can, and calm the person in
distress.
○ Connect to additional support resources or networks.
○ Encourage professional support if the person continues to experience difficulties in
their daily functioning (more than one month).
● Integrating psychological first aid principles when assisting people in distress may help
them during or in the immediate aftermath of an event, and can continue to support
them in the days, weeks, months and even years that follow.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Good practice points
● Do not pressure individuals who have experienced a traumatic event to talk about the
event. Avoid asking for details of the event. Instead, focus on their current needs and
feelings and let them share their experiences on their terms.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Prevent and prepare
● Ensure that first aid providers are trained in trauma-informed care principles, particularly
in PFA. This includes understanding the impact of trauma and recognizing signs and
symptoms.
● Establish safe spaces for providing first aid, free from potential triggers or stressors.
● Before offering support to others, first aid providers should pay attention to their own
psychological well-being and readiness. Because they may also find themselves exposed
to trauma, loss and devastation, injury and even death in an emergency or crisis. It is
important for the first aid responders to work closely and communicate their conditions
and needs in challenging situations with their team (IFRC Psychosocial Centre, 2015).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Early recognition
How a person experiences and reacts to a traumatic event is unique. Some may experience
psychological distress and feelings of shock immediately after an event, but eventually adapt
well to daily life. Others may have persistent, intense post-traumatic stress reactions that disrupt
their daily functioning. Common reactions include intrusive behaviour, avoidance, dissociation,
negative mood and arousal symptoms. Specific stressors (such as the level of experienced pain),
individual characteristics, and conditions (such as the level of social support) impact a person’s
ability to cope.
● Quickly and calmly assess the situation, recognizing signs of physical injury and
emotional distress. Approach the person with a calm and reassuring demeanour,
acknowledging their distress and ensuring they feel safe.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - First aid steps
To address the immediate needs of people experiencing a traumatic event, skills and techniques
from Psychological First Aid (PFA) will be useful. Provide support with the concepts of LOOK,
LISTEN and LINK.
1.
Administer appropriate physical first aid, such as stopping bleeding, immobilizing injuries
or performing CPR, while maintaining a calm and supportive presence.
2. Provide emotional support by listening, validating feelings and offering reassurance. Use
simple and clear communication to explain each step of the care process (LOOK, LISTEN,
LINK).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Traumatic event - Access help
● If the situation requires advanced medical care, promptly call emergency services. Ensure
the person knows help is on the way.
● Work collaboratively with emergency responders, providing them with relevant
information about the person’s physical and emotional state.
● Empower the person by involving them in decisions about their care and respecting their
choices and preferences.
● If possible, involve peers or family members who can provide additional support.
Education consideration

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Key action
Engage the person in conversation, assess the suicidal threat, ensure safety and link to
appropriate resources while providing empathetic support.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Introduction
Suicidal ideation refers to the situation in which a person thinks about ending their own life. The
presentation of suicidal ideation can vary from being fleeting and vague to very concrete. Concrete ideation involves method selection, planning and/or intention to complete suicide. A
person could act upon ideation, undertaking an action in which they expect to end their own
life. Depending on the fatality of the outcome, the action is considered a suicidal attempt or
suicide. According to the World Health Organization, close to 800,000 people die due to suicide
every year (World Health Organization, 2025). It is a global phenomenon that spans multiple
countries. Yet, suicides are preventable with a comprehensive multi-sectoral prevention strategy. Vulnerability for suicidality is determined by a complex interaction of biological, psychological
and social factors. Exposure to stressful life events can contribute to the development of suicidal
ideation. During or immediately after a severely distressing event, many people react by going
into what is commonly known as a state of shock, where it feels like time stands still, along with
feelings of numbness and unreality. This can be accompanied by physical and emotional
reactions. In some cases, people may think of attempting suicide or even perform suicidal
behaviour (Howarth et al., 2020).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Introduction
Self-harm is when someone intentionally hurts themselves, for example, by cutting or burning
their skin, or poisoning themselves (IFRC Psychosocial Centre, 2018). It should be noted that not
all self-harm is suicidal behaviour, so it is important to explore what the self-harming actions
mean to the person affected. The most important distinction between self-harm and suicidal
behaviour is the intent to take one's life. Suicide is when someone intentionally takes their own life (IFRC Psychosocial Centre, 2018). Suicidal ideation refers to thoughts about or a preoccupation with killing oneself (American
Psychological Association, n.d.-b). Attempted suicide, also called a suicide attempt, is a
deliberate but incompleted attempt to take one’s own life (American Psychological Association,
n.d.-a). It is important to always take someone who threatens to harm or kill themselves seriously
and not leave the person alone till more help arrives (IFRC Psychosocial Centre, 2018).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Guidelines
● Having a confidant or someone to talk to may decrease the risk of suicidality.*
● Staying connected to and befriending the person at risk may decrease psychological
distress in people with suicidal ideation.*

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Good practice points
● Psychological first aid principles can be used when helping people with suicidal ideation.
● The following actions may help people with suicidal ideation:
○ Engaging the person in conversation.
○ Assessing the risk of suicide and harm.
■ Talk openly about suicidal thoughts.
■ Ensure personal safety in case of an immediate threat.
○ Listening non-judgmentally.
○ Encouraging the person to seek professional support and other social support.
○ Ensuring the safety and protection of the person.
In emergency and imminent risk situations:
● DO NOT leave the individual alone.
● Call emergency services.
● Remove any means of self-harm.
● Bring the individual to a safe, supportive environment, if possible.
● Include trusted supports of the individual (such as a friend or family member), if possible.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Good practice points
● Consult with and involve the supervisor or a Mental Health and Psychosocial Support
(MHPSS) specialist as soon as possible during the situation.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Prevent and prepare
● Obtain updated information about safe and available resources and referrals from
supervisors, MHPSS-trained professionals or staff.
● Before offering support to others, first aid providers should pay attention to their own
psychological well-being and readiness because they may also find themselves exposed
to trauma, loss and devastation, injury and even death in emergencies or crises. It is
important for the first aid responders to work closely and communicate their conditions
and needs in challenging situations with their team (IFRC Psychosocial Centre, 2018).

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Early recognition
Individuals may present themselves in very different ways when they are in despair and at risk of
self-harm or suicide. One person may never mention their intent to harm themselves and may
appear calm, despite how they are feeling inside. Another person may be openly expressing
their desire to end their life. There are a variety of ways that individuals may present themselves,
including:
● visibly distressed
● apathetic
● calm
● depressed
● anxious
● affected by alcohol or drug use
● erratic.
Warning signs in adults
There are certain warning signs that may indicate a person is thinking about or planning
suicide. These include:
● Threats of suicide or self-injury.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Early recognition
● Planning for suicide (e.g. searching for methods, acquiring means). The risk that
somebody will take their own life increases if somebody has a clear plan (how, where,
when), has the means to execute the plan, and/or declares the intention to act.
● Talking, writing or online posting about death or suicide.
● Making arrangements, appearing to “say goodbye”, getting affairs in order.
● Affective changes include pronounced negative feelings (e.g. hopelessness, feeling stuck
with no way out, anger, vengefulness, seeing no reason to live, feeling like a burden to
others, anxiety or dramatic mood changes.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Early recognition
● Changes in behaviour such as increased risk behaviour (e.g. recklessness, increased
consumption of alcohol or other substances), sleep problems or social withdrawal.
Warning signs in youth
Certain warning signs may indicate a young person has a higher risk of performing suicide.
These include:
● changes in sleeping and eating habits
● loss of interest in activities they previously enjoyed, such as sports or art
● isolating themselves or withdrawing from family and friends
● headaches, stomach aches and other physical symptoms that cannot be explained by a
medical condition
● refusing to go to school or beginning to do poorly in school
● talking about death often or asking questions about death
● researching or looking up ways to die
● drawing pictures, writing stories, plays, or creating other artwork about death or suicide
● hopelessness
● giving away their favourite things

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Early recognition
● saying things like "I wish I were dead" or "It would be better if I weren't here".

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - First aid steps
To address the immediate needs of people having suicidal ideation, the principles, skills and
techniques from psychological first aid (PFA) are useful. You may provide support with the
concepts of LOOK, LISTEN and LINK.
Communicate clear limits on confidentiality. The person who is at risk must understand that if
the first aid provider believes the person is in imminent risk of harming themselves, the first aid
provider will need to break confidentiality to help keep the person safe.

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - First aid steps
1.
Never leave a person alone if they have expressed that they are at risk.
a. If you are on the phone or working remotely with the person, try to get emergency
backup numbers for people in their lives with whom they trust and feel safe, if at all
possible, as well as information on their current location. [LOOK, LISTEN]
b. If the person is at home, invite someone from the household to support the
person, if it is safe to do so. [LINK]
2. Have the individual remove anything that could be used to harm themselves [LOOK,
LISTEN]. Ask carers to help with this, if possible. [LINK]

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - First aid steps
3. If you are meeting someone in person and you think they may be at risk of harm, make
the space as safe and secure as possible.
a. This may mean finding a quiet, calm place to speak, removing anything
dangerous, or perhaps moving away from a room on an upper level of a building or
from one with the windows open. [LOOK]
4. Use stabilization, calming techniques and basic helping skills to help keep the person
calm and to reduce distress. [LISTEN]
5. Always contact your supervisor or refer to MHPSS-trained professionals or staff when
responding to someone at risk. [LINK]
6. When someone has already attempted suicide (e.g. intoxication or excessive bleeding),
the main course of action is to provide first aid and medical attention immediately. After
stabilization, refer to a mental health professional for follow-up. [LINK]

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Suicidal ideation - Access help
● Ensure the person is not alone before leaving to get help. [LINK]
● Ask if the person knows where to seek help and advice. Be aware of and inform the
person about the range of professional help available. [LINK]
● Encourage the person to see a health/mental health professional. [LINK]

doc: IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025
text:
Acute grief - Key action
Support the person in experiencing their grief in a way that respects their individual needs, and
link them to their social supports.
